#### The Organizing Society: 

##### GDMB Society for Mining, Metallurgy, Resource and Environmental Technology 

The GDMB is a non-profit organization. Its activities focus on combining science with practical experience in the fields of mining, engineering, tunnelling, mineral processing, extraction, recycling and refining of metals, as well as on the manufacturing of semi and finished products. There is an increasing emphasis on associated environmental issues. The GDMB is internationally active with a European basis and covers a wide variety of topics from applied geology via processing to recycling. These include many important areas of chemistry, especially the complex metallurgical chemistry and, last not least, also analytical chemistry. As a consequence of their increasing importance, aspects of industrial minerals are addressed in addition to the traditional fields of metals and alloys. In order to remain a vibrant and attractive professional society, the GDMB draws on the experience and interests of its worldwide members.

#### Preface 

###### Copper – Indicator of the progress of civilization 

This is the motto for the 7<sup>th</sup> international copper conference, the most important copper seminar in the world, which has been organized by the GDMB, the German based Society for Mining, Metallurgy, Resource and Environmental Technology, together with IIMCh from Chile, MetSoc from Canada, TMS, SME from USA and MMIJ from Japan. 

The copper conferences bring together the highest level of science and technology: universities, metal producers, manufacturing companies, suppliers and finally the people who work with copper: scientists, technicians, engineers, traders and many more. 

An extensive programme has been arranged for this conference and an abundance of contributions from all over the world dealing with the different aspects of copper making and its use are registered already, for which we gratefully thank the authors. Apart from plenary addresses, separate sessions will be held for economics, mineral processing, pyrometallurgy, hydrometallurgy, electrowinning and -refining, downstream fabrication and application, process control and automation, recycling and sustainable development, environmental control, health and safety. Copper, one of the oldest metals used by mankind, is still today one of the most important industrial metals and indispensable for modern life. It is the indicator of industrialization and progress in every country. It is used everywhere, where electricity flows and thus is still valued so highly today. The increased economic potential of newly industrialized countries, above all East Asia and China, has increased the significance of the red metal once again. More recent technologies in production, processing and application often provide new answers to old questions. From the middle of the last century there was another innovation surge resulting in totally new technologies, a trend still going on. This has made each copper conference into an exciting adventure. It is positive and reassuring that particularly the high industrialized countries have become the vanguard, not just in technical innovation, but also protection of environment and nature and preserving resources. They repeatedly prove that ecology and economy may go hand in hand. 

Many sponsors have contributed to the conference’s success, for which I would like to express my sincere thanks! 

Hamburg is expecting its guests! Hamburg, the old Hanseatic city with a 1200 year long tradition, one of the biggest and most beautiful cities in Germany, combines a wonderful mixture of industry, commerce, nature and culture. Not only the “Copper 2010” in the Congress Centre awaits you, but rich offerings of sightseeing and shopping in a

cosmopolitan city, one of the largest harbours in Europe, the Alster lake in the city centre, green parks and plenty of cultural events, some of which we hope to show you in the companions programme. 

We are delighted that you will join us and look forward to a highly interesting conference! 

_Michael Kopke_ Chairman Copper 2010

#### Plenary Lectures (Abstracts) 

Some of the full papers will be published in Volume 7 of the Proceedings of Copper 2010 and in World of Metallurgy – ERZMETALL. 

###### Is the Copper Industry Fit for the Future? 

Dr.-Ing. Bernd Drouven, CEO, Aurubis AG, Hamburg, Germany 

The copper world has already changed a great deal during recent years. But what still lies ahead of us? What are the changes in conditions that we have to cope with and how will our solutions look? 

The rise in the demand for raw materials is unrelenting. At the same time, both the primary and secondary feed materials have a specific complexity, the customers’ needs are becoming increasingly differentiated and their orders are placed at increasingly short notice. Production times for metals have to be faster and inventories minimised. 

The volatility of the metal prices has increased significantly in recent years and we will probably have to live with that in the future as well. The LME functioned well in the crisis, but the copper price is being influenced more and more by funds. 

How can the value added chain change to adapt to this? Which consequences will that have for process technology, production planning and logistics? How will the consolidation of our industry continue? 

This keynote will go into the various effects and challenges – in particular from the perspective of a European custom smelter and fabricator – and present possible approaches for solutions. 

###### Sustainable Growth Strategy for Japanese Copper Business 

Toshinori Kato, Managing Director, Mitsubishi Materials Corporation, Tokyo, Japan 

Business environment, for any industry, has changed dramatically over the last decade. Copper industry is no exception and those involved are experiencing an unprecedented period of upheaval. The landscape of the market has completely altered, with large-scale M&As taking place among miners - creating an oligopoly situation - and a rapid expansion of smelting capacity within developing countries, driven by stron

g economic growth. Traditional copper smelters and fabricators have been facing challenges, but a long-term sustainability of Japanese copper business is achievable. 

Firstly, an immense amount of effort has been made over the years to develop the clean and one of the most environmentally-friendly processes in the industry. Mitsubishi Materials (MMC) particularly plays a great role in establishing Japanese smelters’ reputation as the most energy-efficient operations in the world. It is our strong commitment to be a leader in this expertise by sharing our technologies with the industry. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

IX 



Secondly, infrastructures for copper smelting have been utilized in developing the recycling business. Exemplified by the operations at Onahama smelter, which has the world’s largest furnace for treatment of shredder residue, the industry has worked closely with other sectors and municipalities. Building an effective structure to make the best use of our facilities is a key for success in this field. It is fair to say that Japanese copper smelters, including MMC, are now regarded as an indispensable part of national environmental policy. 

Finally, progression of integration in the copper fabrication sector has strengthened the industry’s capability of providing a variety of high-value-added products to end-users. Tight relationships with the consumers have been beneficial in developing new use of copper. Evidence of a promising future can be seen in increasing use of copper in the growing sectors such as hybrid automobiles and renewable energy. 

###### Copper Sulphide Smelting: Past Achievements and Current Challenges 

Dr. Carlos M. Dнaz, Adjunct Professor, University of Toronto, Private Consultant, Toronto, Canada 

In the last three decades, increased oxygen consumption in copper sulphide smelting and converting and the implementation of computerized process control, among other factors, have led to higher process intensity and smelter concentrate processing capacity, decreased smelting energy consumption and improved SO2 capture from process gas streams. An annual primary smelting furnace throughput of one million tonnes of concentrate is the new industry standard. Top submerged lance smelting has become an important processing route in recent years. Two new continuous converting routes were commercialized in the 1990s. However, due to substantially improved converting practice and larger converters, Peirce-Smith converting still maintains its position as the dominant technology. 

A major realignment of world copper smelting has taken place in the last 30 years. Spurred by rapid economic expansion and the resulting huge increase in demand for basic materials, a number of modern, large capacity copper smelters have been built in China, India and other Asian countries. Only moderate growth in smelting and electrorefining capacity has taken place elsewhere. Moreover, ER cathode output in the USA has substantially decreas

ed. 

In this paper, the author examines recent technological advances and industry changes and highlights issues, such as energy consumption and the corresponding greenhouse gas emissions that will become the focus of future discussion. 

###### Energy as a Key Factor of Sustainability 

Javier Targhetta, Vice President, Freeport McMoRan, Phoenix, Arizona, USA 

Energy must be seen as the prime mover for development and is therefore vital for economic equilibrium and social welfare. Energy will continue to play a key role in the coming decades being not only an environmental challenge but also a fundamental issue in terms of the progress of humanity. Nevertheless, harmonizing several aspects related to energy management will be of essence for the 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

X 



near future and will make energy one of the greatest challenges of the 21<sup>st</sup> century. It is becoming increasingly important to maintain the appropriate equilibrium between environmental issues (global warming, the future of nuclear waste, the integration of renewable energies…), coordinated governments policies to ensure that global energy costs are kept competitive and companies finding a balanced, rational and fair model of energy utilization based on the review of ethical business aspects and the establishment of social responsibility principles. 

This paper develops the idea that the rules and procedures for future energy use must be based on a reasonable equilibrium between technical aspects mainly associated to environmental issues, political decisions made by governments and public administrations and social responsibility programmes that companies themselves must assume and implement. 

###### <mark>The Supply and Copper Producer Response to a Growing Demand Scenario</mark> 

Ricardo Alvarez, General Manager, Codelco El Teniente Division, Santiago, Chile 

<mark>The prospects for medium and long-term consumption of copper are promising. A recovery projected for developed economies, starting 2010, joins the growing impact on demand generated from the process of development and urbanization of emerging countries. The intensity of copper use will also maintain the positive growth started a decade ago based on factors such as providing solutions to combat global warming.</mark> 

<mark>The objective of this presentation is to analyze how supply may react and adjust to envisaged demand scenarios, bearing in mind some distinctive elements of the copper industry like:</mark> 

- <mark>Historical supply reaction to demand and price levels</mark> 

- <mark>Availability of resources and copper ore reserves, incorporating a dynamic analysis and the effects of geological exploration and possible technological changes.</mark> 

- <mark>Pipeline of probable and possible projects, analysing the effects of projects in less developed and riskier geographical locations</mark> 

- Technological changes under development that may positively impact the amount of rese

rves available and the competitiveness of projects. - The growing role of scrap as a supply source for copper. The analysis of these points will allow us to confirm the capability of supply response to growing demand, ruling out revisited hypothesis of insufficient reserves ###### Implementation of Recent Global Copper Projects Tim J. Manafi Shahid Bahonar University National Iranian a Mineral Industries Research Centre (MIRC) Copper Industry Company b Mining Engineering Department c Energy and Environmental Research Centre d Chemical Engineering Department Kerman, Iran Kerman, Iran **Keywords** : Redox potential, copper concentrate, chalcopyrite, leaching, anodic polarization #### Abstract This research was done to evaluate the effects of redox potential, temperature and iron ions on copper and iron dissolution of Sarcheshmeh chalcopyrite copper concentrate, Kerman, Iran. In this regard, 3 series of experiments were carried out in the presence and absence of ferric

and ferrous ions. At first, the effect of redox potential (400 ± 30 mV and 600 ± 50 mV vs. Ag/AgCl) and temperature (35 °C, 50 °C and 70 °C) on copper dissolution was investigated in shake flasks at pH 1.8, stirring rate 150 rpm, solids content 5 % (w/v) and nutrient medium 9K. The potential was controlled by potassium permanganate as an oxidizing agent. Afterwards, linear sweep voltametry examinations were carried out on an electrode of carbon paste concentrate. Finally, chemical leaching experiments were investigated in the presence of ferrous and ferric ions as well as their mixture (at 420 mV) at 50 °C. The results showed that copper concentrate was leached faster at a redox potential of 400 ± 30 mV and temperatures of 50 or 70 °C than at other conditions, and it would be passive at 35 °C and a high redox potential (600 mV). Moreover, chemical leaching of copper concentrate was enhanced twofold in the presence of 0.15 M iron (ORP: 420 mV vs. Ag/AgCl) as compared to without iron addition. Anodic polarization examinations revealed a pick attributed to the formation of a passive layer at 35 °C which disappeared at 70 °C. Comparing the results showed that the polarization results well agreed with the results of chemical leaching experiments. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Chalcopyrite (CuFeS2) is the most abundant copper-bearing mineral containing approximately 70 % of the world's copper reserves [1, 2]. Traditionally, the copper extraction from chalcopyrite concentrates is done by pyrometallurgical processes such as flash smelting. Environmental, financial and 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

1725 

_Ahmadi, Ranjbar, Schaffie, Manafi_ 



technical disadvantages of these processes have caused a special attention of investigators on hydrometallurgical methods as an alternative. The principal problem for treating chalcopyrite copper concentrates by hydrometallurgical processing is that chalcopyrite is relatively refractory due to its strong lattice and dissolves very difficultly in acidic solutions under ambient conditions [1, 3]. This refractoriness is due to the formation of a passive layer on its surface that slows down the diffusion of the leaching agents and electrons to the surface of the mineral and products to the solution. The nature of this passive film has not been well known yet. However, the most probable causes are metal-deficient sulphides, polysulphides, elemental sulphur and jarosite [4]. Recently, a number of papers [5-10] have been published on electrochemical aspects of chalcopyrite leaching and found that the rate of copper dissolution is strongly dependent on the redox potential. 

Furthermore, using electrochemical techniques by massive or carbon paste mineral electrodes are very helpful to study the dissolution of conductive minerals such as chalcopyrite. These methods give some important data about the dissolution or leaching rates of minerals at a range of potentials and the results are similar to that obtained in industrial le

aching processes [11, 12]. Hence, this research was done to investigate the effect of redox and surface potentials on chemical leaching of a chalcopyrite copper concentrate in the presence and absence of iron species at different temperatures corresponding to optimum temperatures of microorganisms used in bioleaching processes. The results showed that dissolution was reduced at high redox potential. #### 2 Materials and methods ##### 2.1 Mineral A copper sulphide flotation concentrate obtained from Sarcheshmeh Copper Mine (Kerman, Iran) was used in all experiments. Chemical analysis of a representative sample is shown in Table 1. X-ray diffraction of the concentrate showed that chalcopyrite (CuFeS2) and pyrite (FeS2) are the major components and silicon oxide is the minor one (see Figure 1). The concentration of ferrous ions in the solution was determined by titration with potassium dichromate 0.01 N using sodium diphenylamine sulphonate as indicator. The difference in the concentration of total iron and of ferrous ions is equal to the concentration of ferric ions in the solution. The pH and ORP values in the leaching solution were measured with a pH meter (model: Jenway 3540) and a Pt electrode in reference to an Ag/AgCl electrode (+207 mV vs. SHE at 25 °C) respectively. For all experiments analytical grade reagents and distilled water were used. Furthermore, the stock solutions were prepared with 9K basalt salts [13] except where cited. ##### 2.3 Chemical leaching experiments by controlling redox potential The first series of leaching experiments were carried out by controlling the redox potential using periodical addition of potassium permanganate 3 M as oxidizer. Experiments were carried out in 500 ml Erlenmeyer flasks containing 200 ml 9K medium at a solids content of 5 % (w/v), initial pH of 1.8, a stirring rate of 150 rpm, temperatures of 35, 50 and 70 °C as well as redox potentials of 400 ± 30 and 600 ± 50 mV vs. Ag/AgCl. During each test, 5 ml of leach liquor were withdrawn after 10 h to measure the concentration of Cu and Fe. After 10 h the reaction mixture was filtered to separate undissolved material from the pre

gnant solution. 

The second series of experiments were done to investigate the effect of ferric and ferrous ions with a solids content of 1 % (w/v), leaching time 8 days, initial pH 1.8, stirring rate 150 rpm and temperature 50 °C in 250 ml of 9K solution in 500 ml Erlenmeyer flasks. The iron concentration in the flasks was 0, 0.15 M Fe (II), 0.15 M Fe (III) and 0.15 M Fe (total). The latter solution was prepared to obtain the redox potential of 420 mV (vs. Ag/AgCl) by mixing ferric and ferrous sulphates in which the total iron concentration was maintained at 0.15 M. The low solid to liquid ratio was chosen to avoid sharp changes of the redox potential of the liquid medium during the first instant of leaching. 

##### 2.4 Electrochemical experiments 

A conventional three-electrode cell was used at temperatures of 35, 50 and 70 °C. The linear sweep voltametry experiments were carried out using a potentiostat/galvanostat (BHP-2063 electrochemical analysis system, Behpajooh, Iran). A 200 ml 9K solution was used as supporting electrolyte. The pH was adjusted at 1.8 with H2SO4. A saturated calomel electrode and a platinum wire (from 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

1727 

###### _Ahmadi, Ranjbar, Schaffie, Manafi_ 



Azar electrode Co., Iran) were used as reference and auxiliary electrodes respectively. The reference electrode was converted to Ag/AgCl in this paper. The working electrode was made by mixing 1 g of concentrate, 1 g of graphite powder (Merck) and a few drops of non-conductive paraffin oil (Merck). The mixture was housed in a glass tube (inner diameter 4.4 mm) and polished and renewed on smooth sandpaper (No. 1000). An electric contact was made by a platinum wire silversoldered to a copper wire (Figure 2). 

To adjust the desired temperature, the electrochemical cell was located in a thermostat bath. Before each test, the solution was de-aerated with N2 and maintained in the cell during the experiments. 



Figure 2: Working electrode of concentrate carbon paste. 

#### 3 Results and discussion 

##### 3.1 Influence of solution potential and temperature on copper dissolution 



The effect of various redox potentials (no control, 400 ± 30 and 600 ± 50 mV vs. Ag/AgCl) on copper dissolution from the flotation copper concentrate have been investigated at temperatures of 35, 50 and 70 °C. These temperatures are the optimum temperatures of mesophile, moderate thermophile and extereme thermophile microorganisms respectively. As can be seen in Figure 3, at a solution potential of 400 ± 30 mV and higher temperatures especially 70 °C, copper dissolution shows a maximum; however, the lowest copper dissolution occurs at a potential of 600 ± 50 mV and a temperature of 35 °C. It seems that the surface of chalcopyrite has been passivated at the solution potential of 600 ± 50 mV. This condition is similar to that occurring during bioleaching by mesophile bacteria. The obtained result is in agreement with the other investigations in which the rate of

Linear sweep voltametry experiments were studied to investigate the effect of temperature and applied potential on the rate of copper concentrate dissolution. In all polarization experiments, the scanning was initiated from the potential of 80 mV (vs. Ag/AgCl) in the positive direction up to 680 mV at a scan rate of 20 mV.s<sup>-1</sup> . As can be seen in Figure 4, during scanning potential, three different regions could be observed. In the first region, by increasing the applied potential, the anodic current increases, while the second region which is in the potential range of 450 to 600 mV, exhibits various behaviours at different temperatures in which by increasing potential, anodic current decreases at 35 °C, flattens at 50 °C and increases at 70 °C. This region is attributed to the passiv

ation of the mineral surface. It can be concluded that the nature of the coating layer at low temperature may be different from that at high temperature and the increasing of temperature may decompose the passive layer, because by increasing medium temperature, the existing peak observed at 35 °C disappeared. 

In the third region that starts at potentials higher than 600 mV, anodic current increases with increasing applied potential rapidly. It indicates that the created passive layer has probably decomposed at high applied surface potential. Moreover, Figure 4 shows that rising the temperature from 35 to 70 °C increases the anodic current. This behaviour is explained by the formation of a passive layer at low temperature and the applied potential above 450 mV. The nature of this passive layer is not well known yet, but the most probable causes are a compacted sulphur layer [16, 17], a metal deficient chalcopyrite-like sulphide layer [18], a polysulfide like CuxSy [19] or an iron-bearing precipitate like jarosite [20]. This layer leads to slow and incomplete extraction of copper from the concentrate. This result is in agreement with the results obtained by other investigators [21-23] from studies on massive chalcopyrite electrodes and indicates that chalcopyrite dissolution is the rate limiting step in the copper concentrate leaching. Tshilombo et al [23] showed that the anodic current is proportional to the content of copper dissolved into the solution. 

The results achieved by anodic polarization examinations are in accordance to those obtained from the section 3-1 in chemical leaching by controlling the potential using potassium permanganate.

To study the electrochemistry of the dissolution process for carbon paste-concentrate electrodes, linear sweep voltametery experiments were also done in some 9K solutions containing 0.15 M of these cations at temperatures of 35 and 70 °C. #### 4 Conclusion 

The following results were obtained from chemical leaching and anodic polarization experiments for Sarcheshmeh chalcopyrite concentrate: 

In controlled potential examination by potassium permanganate, it was found that copper dissolution from the concentrate is maximal at a redox potential of 400 mV vs. Ag/AgCl and a temperature of 70 °C. It was revealed in anodic polarization experiments that a pick observed at 35 °C attributed to the formation of passive layer disappeared at 70 °C. It indicates that the structures of passive layers are different at low and high temperatures. **Keywords:** Chalcopyrite, leaching, chloride, potential 

#### Abstract 

It is well known that the leaching of chalcopyrite under ambient conditions is extremely slow even under highly oxidizing conditions. This has been attributed to so-called passivation of the mineral that occurs at potentials above about 0.65 V (SHE). However, previous reports have suggested that the mineral can be more effectively dissolved at lower potentials in sulfate solutions and mechanisms for this reaction have been proposed. This paper will report on an extensive study of the kinetics of the dissolution of a number of chalcopyrite concentrates in chloride solutions under various conditions in specially designed reactors with the objective of developing a heap leach process for primary copper sulfide ores. 

It will be demonstrated that enhanced rates of dissolution can be achieved at ambient temperature

s by the application of controlled potentials in the range 560-600 mV, depending on the concentration of chloride ions. However, control of the potential by the use of electrochemical or chemical oxidation of iron(II) or copper(I) ions is ineffective unless carried out in the presence of dissolved oxygen. The rates of dissolution are approximately constant for up to 80 % dissolution for sized fractions of the concentrates with an activation of energy of about 80 kJ/mole. Chalcopyrite from different sources appears to dissolve at approximately the same rate which is largely independent of the iron and copper ion concentrations, the acidity and chloride ion concentration but depends in some cases on the presence of additives such as fine pyrite.

#### 1 Introduction 

The generally higher reactivity of sulfide minerals in chloride as opposed to sulfate solutions has resulted in many studies of chloride systems for the hydrometallurgical treatment of sulfide minerals. A comparison of chloride and sulfate based leaching processes shows that there are various advantages associated with the former. Thus, chloride leaching can be carried out at ambient temperatures whereas sulfate processes generally require elevated temperatures. In addition, in chloride systems, the copper(I) ion is stable and this allows the use of copper(II) ions as an oxidant in addition to iron(III). In the case of chalcopyrite, several aspects still require clarification such as the role of impurities, mineral particle size and origin, the nature of the passivating layer and the deportment of sulfur. 

The dissolution of sulfide minerals, and in particular, the passivation of chalcopyrite are potentialdependent reactions and many studies have been carried out in order to establish the relationship between the solution potential and the leaching rate. It is now well known that the leaching rate in sulfate solutions is dependent on the potential and that the rate is enhanced in a certain potential range [1, 2]. Many studies have been devoted to the elucidation of the potentials at which dissolution is possible and at which apparent passivation occurs. Thus, electrochemical and chemical experiments have been used to establish the relevant leaching potential region as being 0.45 to 0.75 V under appropriate experimental conditions. However, few actual dissolution studies [1, 3, 4] have been conducted under controlled potential conditions, particularly in chloride media. 

In order to enhance the rate of leaching of chalcopyrite, several catalysts and/or promoters have been proposed such as pyrite, activated carbon and the ions of Ag(I), Sn(II), Co(II), Hg(II), Bi(III) and Mn(II). The effect of pyrite on the leaching of chalcopyrite has been investigated by some researchers [5-10]. Most of these investigations have focused principally on the role of galvanic interactions in the leaching of sulfide miner

als. It has been postulated that when chalcopyrite and pyrite are in intimate electrical contact with each other they form a galvanic couple as a result of which chalcopyrite behaves as an anode and dissolves more rapidly, while pyrite behaves as a cathode. However, none of these investigations has directly verified the formation of such galvanic couples by electrochemical experiments. A number of investigations have been conducted to elucidate the reaction kinetics and delineate the important variables for the leaching of chalcopyrite in both chloride and sulfate systems. Although relevant work has been reported by many researchers, some ambiguities still remain. In this first paper of several on this topic, the factors affecting the dissolution of chalcopyrite under controlled potential conditions in chloride solutions will be reported. _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 1738 _Leaching of Chalcopyrite in Chloride Solutions 1. The solution potential in the leach reactor was maintained at a constant Eh set point by a computer controlled system in which either flow of gas from a cylinder into the reactor is controlled by way of a solenoid valve or an air injection tube connected to a small air pump is similarly activated when the potential as monitored by an ORP probe drops below the set-point. (-) Concentrate 1, (-) Concentrate 2, (X) Concentrate 3 and (-) Concentrate 4. #### 4 Conclusions The results of a fundamental study of the rate of dissolution of chalcopyrite concentrates in chloride solutions under controlled, low potentials have been described. It has been demonstrated that enhanced rates of dissolution of copper from chalcopyrite concentrates in chloride media can be achieved at ambient temperatures by the application of controlled potentials in a “potential window” between 560 and 600 mV (SHE). The presence of dissolved oxygen is also essential for satisfactory rates of leaching under these conditions. A relatively high activation energy of 80 kJ/mole for dissolution under these conditions was established from experiments carried out in the temperature rang

e from 25 to 75<sup>o</sup> C. This has confirmed that the rate of dissolution is controlled by the rate of slow chemical or electrochemical processes. Although the presence of chloride and cupric ions are essential for adequate rates of dissolution under these conditions, high concentrations do not improve the leaching rate if conducted within the potential window. The rate is essentially independent of acid concentration in pH range from 0.5 to 2 with slightly lower rates at the lower pH values. Precipitation of iron as a poorly crystalline akaganite does not appear to inhibit the rate of dissolution. 

Addition of excess fine pyrite with a particle size of less than 25 µm to the leach system can significantly enhance the rate of dissolution of copper from the concentrate. The effect is reduced in

Petrus Basson Mintek, formerly BHP Billiton Johannesburg Technology Centre Randburg, South Africa

**Keywords:** Chalcopyrite, leaching, chloride, potential 

#### Abstract 

In a previous paper in this series, it was shown that enhanced leaching of chalcopyrite from a number of concentrates in acidic chloride solutions can be achieved by controlling the potential in a range of 560-600 mV (SHE) in the presence of dissolved oxygen. The addition of fine pyrite enhanced the rate of dissolution under these conditions. 

Based on the results of these leaching experiments and detailed mineralogical analyses of the residues, a mechanism involving non-oxidative dissolution of the mineral coupled to oxidation of the product hydrogen sulfide is proposed. The latter reaction is shown to occur predominately by a copper ion – catalyzed reaction with dissolved oxygen. The results of an independent study of the kinetics of this reaction will be presented which will demonstrate that the rates are consistent with those obtained for the dissolution of the mineral. The possible involvement of a covellite-like surface layer on the chalcopyrite under some conditions will also discussed as it relates to the mechanism. It will also be shown that fine pyrite particles can also act as a catalyst surface for the oxidation of hydrogen sulfide. This mechanism is consistent with the mineralogy which confirmed the formation of secondary sulfur which is not directly

associated with chalcopyrite except at high pH (about 2) values but is found as discrete globules and associated with fine pyrite if present. 

A comparison of this mechanism with those proposed in other more limited studies of the dissolution of chalcopyrite under similar conditions in sulfate solutions has been made.

#### 1 Introduction 

One of the most important outstanding problems with the hydrometallurgy of copper is the low temperature leaching of chalcopyrite. In a previous paper (Part 1), the results of dissolution experiments with various chalcopyrite-rich concentrates in chloride and chloride-sulfate media under controlled potential conditions were described. The main conclusion is that the leaching of chalcopyrite is enhanced in chloride solutions within a “potential window” between 560-600 mV (SHE) in the presence of dissolved oxygen and copper ions. At higher potentials, the mineral undergoes typical passivation with substantially lower rates while lower potentials are inadequate for oxidative dissolution. The addition of fine (-25 µm) pyrite enhances the rate of chalcopyrite dissolution as does low concentrations of silver ions. 

A similar potential dependence of the rate of dissolution of chalcopyrite in sulfate solutions has been reported by Kametani et al [1] and Hiroyoshi et al [2]. The latter proposed a reaction model according to which the rate of leaching is enhanced as a result of reduction of chalcopyrite by iron(II) to chalcocite in the presence of copper(II) ions. The more reactive chalcocite is, in turn, oxidized by iron(III) more rapidly than chalcopyrite. In this mechanism, the iron(II)/iron(III) couple acts, unusually, as both reducing and oxidizing. In this paper, an alternative reaction model based on a non-oxidative process in which chalcopyrite dissolves or is converted to a covellite-like species by a non-oxidative reaction coupled to oxidation of hydrogen sulfide by one of several oxidants as described by Nicol et al [3] is applied to the chloride system. A crucial step in this mechanism is the rate of oxidation of hydrogen sulfide and this paper addresses this aspect as part of the overall mechanism in chloride solutions containing copper(II) ions as the main oxidant. The study involved measurements of the rate of consumption of dissolved oxygen by hydrogen sulfide in the presence of various ions and sulfide minerals to confirm this model. Detailed mineralogical studies using mainly mineral liberation analysis (MLA) have also been carried out on the residues from the leach experiments. This data has demonstrated that elemental sulfur is formed from a soluble sulfur intermediate in the overall dissolution reaction.

#### 3 Reaction Mechanisms 

##### 3.1 High Potential Region – Oxidative Model 

It is well known [4, 5] that chalcopyrite can be oxidatively dissolved according to the overall reaction 

CuFeS2 + Ox = Cu<sup>2+</sup> + Fe<sup>2+</sup> + 2S + Red 



in which Ox and Red represent the oxidant and its reduced form respectively. In this case, the common oxidants are dissolved oxygen or ferric ions. Contrary to conventional expectation that the rate of dissolution should increase with increasing potential at the chalcopyrite surface, the rate does not follow such a trend under ambient conditions and the mineral generally requires elevated temperatures in order to dissolve at acceptable rates. During the dissolution of chalcopyrite at elevated temperatures, elemental sulfur (termed “primary” sulfur in this paper) is formed on the surface of chalcopyrite and it has been suggested that this elemental sulfur layer inhibits leaching [4] although this is no longer accepted as the reason for “passivation” which is now thought to be due to the formation of a relatively thin copper-rich polysulfide layer. A schematic depiction of this reaction model is given in Figure 3 (left).

##### 3.2 Low Potential Window – Non-Oxidative Model 

At lower potentials, especially in the region between 560-600 mV (SHE), leaching experiments described in the first paper of this series have confirmed that the rate of dissolution is significantly greater than that observed at higher potentials. It has been found that this relatively high rate of dissolution can only be sustained in the presence of dissolved oxygen, copper ions and chloride ions. 

In this potential region, direct oxidative dissolution of chalcopyrite by Equation 1 does not occur but, on the other hand, the potential is below that required for the development of a passive layer on the surface. It is proposed that dissolution occ

urs as a result of a non-oxidative process in two stages as shown in Figure 3 (right). In the 1st stage, chalcopyrite is converted to CuS or dissolves to release copper ions and H2S as shown in the following reactions. CuFeS2 + 4H+ = Cu2+ + Fe2+ + 2H2S (2) CuFeS2 + 2H+ = CuS + Fe2+ + H2S In the 2nd stage, dissolved H2S (or CuS) is oxidised by the reaction 2H2S + Ox = 2S + Red + 4H+ (4) Thus, in terms of this reaction model, elemental sulfur will only form on the surface of the chalcopyrite if the rate of reaction (4) is rapid relative to reactions (2) and (3). Under most ambient temperature conditions, reaction (4) occurs away from the chalcopyrite surface and thus the sulfur is formed by a “secondary” process. Cu 2+

This mechanism whereby H2S is oxidised to form secondary sulfur explains why there is very little primary elemental sulfur associated with chalcopyrite particles during dissolution at low potentials but that it occurs as isolated spherical globules and as layers around smaller pyrite particles. ##### 3.3 Relevant Chemistry of the Non-Oxidative Model Although the above reaction mechanism is consistent with the experimental observations, a more direct confirmation of some aspects of the chemistry is desirable in that it could also be used for the purpose of creating appropriate quantitative kinetic models for the leaching reactions involving chalcopyrite and also possibly other sulfide minerals. In the above model a key component is the kinetics of the oxidation of H2S by dissolved oxygen in the presence of homogeneous or heterogeneous catalysts. It is well known that copper(II) ions are not stable in the presence of sulfide ions even in strongly acidic solutions due to precipitation by the reaction Cu(II) + H2S = CuS + 2H+ The calculated equilibrium concentratio

ns of the soluble species in a saturated solution of CuS in 0.2 M HCl containing increasing concentrations of chloride (added as NaCl) show that the equilibrium does not allow for measurable concentrations of copper(II) ions (less than 4 x 10-9 M). However, as found in this study, addition of sulfide ions at low concentrations (less than 1mM) to acidic chloride solutions containing copper(II) ions does not result in the immediate precipitation of black CuS but a white turbidity appears after some minutes which is due to the precipitation of elemental sulfur. Thus, dilute solutions of copper(II) ions with dissolved H2S are metastable and therefore it is not surprising that elemental sulfur is often not observed on the surface of partially dissolved chalcopyrite grains. These observations are in accord with those made by Luther et al [6] who found that copper(II) ion reduction by sulfide to copper(I) occurs prior to precipitation as CuS (covellite is now accepted as a copper(I) sulfide i.e. Cu2S2) in sea water solutions. In the chloride system, CuS is also not thermodynamically stable in the presence of copper(II) ions as shown by the data presented in Figure 4 which summarizes the thermodynamics of the various possible couples involved in this system for initial concentration ratios of Cu(II)/Cu(I) = 100 and Fe(II)/Fe(III) = 1000. These ratios were chosen such that these couples and the couple CuS = Cu(I) + S + e (9) 1758 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ _Leaching of Chalcopyrite in Chloride Solutions 2. Mechanisms_ are all in equilibrium for a chloride concentration of about 15 g/L and a total copper ion concentration of 1 g/L. As a result of the increased stability of copper(I) in chloride solutions, copper(II) ions can oxidise both CuS and H2S to elemental sulfur. Obviously iron(III) can fulfill the same role but the important distinction between the Cu(II)/Cu(I) and Fe(III)/Fe(II) couples is that copper(I) ions are rapidly oxidised by dissolved oxygen whereas the corresponding oxidation of iron(II) ions is very slow at ambient temperatures. The potentials in Figure 4 confirm that CuS is not stable in solutions containing an excess of copper(II) ions even at low concentrations of chloride and that elemental sulfur should be the product of oxidation of H2S. Thus, even if CuS is the first product of reaction with H2S, it will be oxidised by copper(II) ions albeit at a slower rate than could be expected for the homogeneous oxidation of H2S by copper(II) ions. Mechanisms_ ##### 5.6 The Role of Oxygen The observation that enhanced rates of dissolution are only observed in the potential “window” **in the presence of dissolved oxygen** requires that any mechanism should identify the essential role of oxygen. A similar observation in regard to the necess

ity for dissolved oxygen was made in studies of the dissolution of chalcopyrite in sulfate solutions by Hiroyoshi et al [10] who concluded inadequately that chalcopyrite was simply oxidised by dissolved oxygen. In all subsequent publications involving their mechanism, the role of oxygen has been largely ignored. It should be recognized that the solutions used in these and the present studies are meta-stable in that the measured EH does not reflect the true equilibrium solution potential in the presence of dissolved oxygen. Thus, it is possible to have a solution which may be almost saturated with respect to dissolved oxygen (E<sup>o</sup> = 1.2  V) but still have a measured EH as low as 0.6 V. The EH in a metastable system consisting of two or more redox couples is determined mainly by that of the couple with the greatest exchange current density. In the present case, both the copper(II)/copper(I) and iron(III)/iron(II) couples have exchange current densities on a platinum surface which are orders of magnitude greater than that of the oxygen/water couple. 

In terms of the present proposed mechanism involving a non-oxidative dissolution reaction, it has been demonstrated that the crucial step involving the oxidation of H2S by dissolved oxygen is rapid in the presence of copper(II) ions but that, at the concentrations of copper ions normally present in leach solutions, the rate of the oxidation of H2S by copper(II) ions in the presence of dissolved oxygen is rapid compared to the rate of oxidation of the copper(I) ions formed in this reaction by dissolved oxygen. Thus, H2S is removed rapidly by a reaction which does not appear to involve oxygen. One possible mechanism involves the initial formation of a copper(II)-HS<sup>-</sup> complex [11] which can undergo oxidation by a second copper(II) ion or by oxygen. #### 6 Conclusions 

The rate of dissolution of chalcopyrite in chloride solutions is enhanced within a potential window between 560 and 600 mV (SHE) in the presence of copper ions and dissolved oxygen. This study has aimed at the establishment of a

mechanism which is consistent with the data obtained in an extensive study of the kinetics of dissolution. Mineralogical investigations of chalcopyrite surfaces and the residues from dissolution experiments have shown that the surface of the mineral is converted to a covellite-like phase during leaching at potentials below the potential window. Except at high pH values, the product of elemental sulfur forms largely as isolated spherical globules and as layers around smaller pyrite particles but seldom on the surface of chalcopyrite confirming that initial dissolution involves a soluble sulfur intermediate. 

These phenomena can be explained by an extended reaction model in which chalcopyrite dissolves non-oxidatively to form H2S and possibly a covellite-like surface species within the potential window. The H2S that is in equilibrium with the mineral is oxidized by oxygen in a reaction catalyzed by copper ions and other minerals such as pyrite. Confirmation of this reaction model has been enhanced by a detailed study of the kinetics of the copper-catalysed oxidation of H2S with the following main conclusions: 

1. The oxidation of hydrogen sulfide in acidic chloride solutions by dissolved oxygen is very slow in the absence of catalysts. 

2. Copper ions are very effective in catalyzing the reaction by a mechanism that involves oxidation of sulfide by copper(II) and reoxidation of copper(I) by dissolved oxygen. 

3. The rate-determining step is re-oxidation of copper(I) by oxygen at copper concentrations above about 0.1 g/L while at lower concentrations, reduction of copper(II) by hydrogen sulfide becomes rate-limiting. 

4. At high copper concentrations, the rate of the reaction is similar to and follows the published rate law for the kinetics of the oxidation of copper(I) by oxygen in chloride solutions. 

5. Rates of dissolution estimated using a modified previously published model involving mass transport coupled with chemical oxidation of H2S formed at the surface of the mineral compare favourably with those measured under similar conditions. 

6. Fine pyrite catalyses the oxidation of hydrogen sulfide. This confirms observations of the effect of fine pyrite on the leaching of chalcopyrite concentrates and the accumulation of sulfur around fine pyrite particles during dissolution of chalcopyrite.

### Enhanced Leaching of Chalcopyrite at Low Potentials in Chloride Solutions 3. Ores 

Petrus Basson, Dr. Elmar Muller Mintek, formerly BHP Billiton Johannesburg Technology Centre Randburg, South Africa 

Prof. Michael Nicol Murdoch University Parker Centre Perth, Western Australia 

**Keywords:** Chalcopyrite, leaching, chloride, potential 

#### Abstract 

It is well known that the leaching of chalcopyrite under ambient conditions is extremely slow even under highly oxidizing conditions. This has been attributed to so-called passivation of the mineral that occurs at potentials above about 0.65 V (SHE). 

A study has been made of the rate of leaching of copper in dilute chloride solutions from a lowgrade ore which contained chalcopyrite as the only copper sulfide mineral. Leaching has been carried out in batch stirred reactors using milled ore and in 1 m columns using crushed ore in solutions of chloride at various potentials. It has been observed that enhanced rates of dissolution of copper from chalcopyrite in chloride media can be achieved at ambient temperatures by the application of controlled potentials in a “potential window” between 560 and 600 mV (SHE). These results generally confirm the results presented in Part 1 of this series of papers wh

ich detailed the results obtained on the dissolution of a concentrate from the same ore. A reduced sensitivity of the rate of leaching in columns to the potential has been observed which is interpreted in terms of a potential distribution at the surface of chalcopyrite grains. This potential distribution can vary both locally due to mineralogical effects and vertically due to potential variations down the column as observed in the differences of the potential in the column inlet and outlets. 

A linear rate of approximately 0.1 % copper dissolution from a low grade chalcopyrite ore under typical heap leach conditions has been measured in a solution of 50 g/L chloride at a pH of 1 and a potential of about 600 mV for the feed solution. 

#### 1 Introduction 

A previous paper in this series [1] presented the results of a study of the leaching of chalcopyrite from various concentrates in chloride solutions. It was shown that enhanced rates of dissolution can

However, control of the potential by the use of electrochemical or chemical oxidation of iron(II) or copper(I) ions is ineffective unless carried out in the presence of dissolved oxygen. This paper will present the results of testwork on the leaching of a low-grade copper ore containing chalcopyrite as the main copper sulfide mineral. The leach process adopted is based on the results of the testwork with the concentrates as described in the first paper.

In both cases, the feed solution was adjusted to the required potential. As could be expected, oxidation of the minerals will result in a decrease in potential in the column while aeration of the solution will result in oxidation of copper(I) and iron(II) by dissolved oxygen and increase the potential. The net result depends on the relative rates of these two processes. In the case of the column operated at 750 mV, oxidation of copper(I) is slow due to the low copper(I) concentration at this potential and the solution leaving the column therefore has a lower potential than that in the feed. The opposite is true for the column operated at a low potential. It can be expected that the actual potential in the solution in the column will vary down the length of the column between these two limits. In addition, the actual potential at the mineral surface will depend not only on the solution potential but also the local environment in terms of accessibility of the solution and a distribution of mineral potentials could be expected. It is therefore not surprising that the effect of potential is not as obvious in the column tests as in the milled ore or concentrate tests. However, the general trends are as predicted in that reduced rates are observed at both low and high potentials. 

It should be pointed out that, although the rate of leaching is enhanced by control of the potential, the absolute rates are still low. Thus, the approximately linear rate at 600 mV shown in Figure 6 is only about 0.1 % copper dissolution per day which is possibly not acceptable in a heap leach under conditions of low temperature (average 15<sup>o</sup> C). 

The rate of leaching of iron from the columns roughly paralleled that of copper except in the initial stages when the pH in the column was high due to rapid consumption of acid by some gangue minerals. This resulted in temporary precipitation of iron. A limited mineralogical study of the residues showed the absence of any secondary copper sulfides while pyrite grains appeared to be unreacted as could be expected at these potentials. Consumption of acid varied between about 25 and 40 kg/t ore after 300 days which, as expected, is lower than that consumed in the leaching of the milled ore. 

#### 4 Conclusions 

A study has been made of the rate of leaching of copper in dilute chloride solutions from a lowgrade ore which contained chalcopyrite as the only copper sulfide mineral. Leaching has been carried out in batch stirred reactors using milled ore and in 1 m columns using crushed ore in solutions of chloride at various potentials. It has been observed that enhanced rates of dissolution of copper from chalcopyrite in chloride media can be achieved at ambient temperatures by the application of controlled potentials in a “potential window” between 560 and 600 mV (SHE). These results generally confirm the results presented in Part 1 of this series of papers which detailed the results obtained on the dissolution

of a concentrate from the same ore. A reduced sensitivity of the rate of leaching in columns to the potential has been observed which is interpreted in terms of a potential distribution at the surface of chalcopyrite grains. This potential distribution can vary both locally due to mineralogical effects and vertically due to potential variations down the column as observed in the differences of the potential in the column inlet and outlets.

### Treatment of High-Arsenic Copper-Gold Concentrates – An Options Review 

Ken Baxter, Hermann Scriba Ivan Vega SNC-Lavalin Australasia SNC-Lavalin Chile Level 17, 191 St Georges Terrace Av. Presidente Riesco 5335, Fl.8, Las Condes WA 6000 Perth, Australia Santiago, Chile 

**Keywords:** Hydrometallurgy, copper, leaching, arsenic, enargite, roasting, gold 

#### Abstract 

Copper resources containing elevated levels of arsenic present a difficult metallurgical problem. Smelters will generally only accept copper concentrates with arsenic grades below 0.5 % arsenic, which precludes direct smelting of concentrates from many arsenic containing deposits. Arsenic removal from concentrates is necessarily coupled with the treatment of primary copper sulphides, and both the copper and arsenic need to be separately recovered. Arsenic disposal technology must also conform to world’s best practice, and the copper must be produced in a saleable form. In addition, copper/arsenic concentrates often contain significant gold value, which also needs to be recovered economically. High arsenic concentrates can be treated utilising either a hydrometallurgy or pyrometallurgy based flowsheet when a smelting option is not available. This paper reviews some of the technologies and processing options currently available for treatment of such high-arsenic copper-gold ores and concentrates at the hand of a recent case study. 

#### 1 Introduction 

The presence of arsenic in copper and gold ores is a common deterrent to the development of such deposits. While the gold industry has largely adopted treatment routes that deal with high-arsenic concentrates, ores in which copper is the predominant element of value, have been typically avoided when they contain high concentrations of arsenic which prevent production of a saleable

copper concentrate. In addition the environmental regulations relating to treatment of arsenic containing materials and arsenic disposal have gradually become more stringent, creating additional challenges for such projects. Projects such as Tampakan, Frieda River, Chuquicamata Mina Ministro Hales, El Galeno and Caspiche are examples of projects where treatment of high-arsenic copper ores and concentrates is being considered.

1783 

_Baxter, Scriba, Vega_ 



SNC-Lavalin is involved in concept and engineering studies for clients who are considering treatment of copper ores with high arsenic content. Typically mining companies are interested in minimizing capital expenditure to produce a saleable copper concentrate. Currently, the allowable arsenic content in copper concentrates for sale to a smelter is set at 0.5 % and this figure is expected to be lowered in future with an arsenic level of 0.3 % being under consideration. When considering the exploitation of an arsenic-containing copper deposit the following approaches may typically be explored: 

- 1) Avoid the arsenic-bearing zones in the ore body. 

- 2) Exclude the arsenic bearing minerals from copper concentrate during processing. 

- 3) Remove arsenic from the concentrate by processing and produce a smeltable concentrate. 

- 4) Treat arsenic-containing concentrates in a dedicated facility to produce final products for sale. 

The approach ultimately adopted depends on a multitude of factors specific to each project, which include the abundance, occurrence and distribution of arsenic minerals, relative contribution from gold, ore behaviour during testing, etc. 

Where avoidance of arsenic-rich areas is not practical, consideration may be given to physical separation of arsenic containing minerals such as tennantite and enargite from chalcopyrite, chalcocite and pyrite by selective flotation. The selective flotation of the arsenic containing minerals may be achieved by manipulation of flotation pH, oxidation-reduction potential (ORP), temperature as well as optimisation of the grind. Such methods have recently been developed and described [1-3] while other methods remain proprietary and confidential. Applying such a method could potentially produce a smeltable arsenic-depleted copper concentrate, while the arsenic-rich concentrate may be considered for disposal or, more likely, further processing as per approaches 3 and 4. This type of approach can be considered in the first instance to reduce to quantity of arsenic containing concentrate to be treated. Production of a low arsenic concentrate for sale also reduces the overall project risk by providing part of the revenue stream via this saleable concentrate. 

When a copper concentrate is produced that contains arsenic above the smelter threshold, two approaches are possible: 3) remove the arsenic selectively from the concentrate to below the acceptable arsenic threshold and 4) leach the concentrate and sepa

rate the arsenic hydrometallurgically while producing copper and gold products for sale. 

This paper reviews some of the methods that are available for consideration for treatment of arsenicrich copper-gold sulphide concentrates (approaches 3 and 4) and highlights some of the factors that have to be considered when comparing flowsheets. Some results from a recent case study on a range of flowsheets are included below. 

The processes included in this case study are for a project in which gold and copper were present in approximately equal value proportions. Flowsheets and process models were developed in consulta-

#### 2 Arsenic - removal and disposal 

The handling of arsenic containing residues is an important consideration in any process flowsheet, particularly in light of ever tightening environmental disposal and emission regulations. 

In the past, copper smelters have dealt with high-arsenic concentrates by employing a reduction roast pre-treatment to drive off arsenic as gaseous arsenic polysulphide. In the most common flowsheet the arsenic polysulphide would be oxidised to arsenic trioxide and then condensed and removed as a white powder. Roasting was used in the eighties to successfully treat arsenic-containing copper concentrates at El Indio mine [4] which contained arsenic at over 6 %. The arsenic trioxide product was packed in drums and sold, the main market being for use in the manufacture CCA (chromated copper arsenic), a wood preservative. However, this market no longer exists, so alternative means of arsenic disposal have to be sought. 

Considerable research effort has been expended, mainly over the last two decades, in developing methods for hydrometallurgical removal and fixation of arsenic and in stability testing on arsenic bearing products from these processes to confirm their long term stability. Two recent publications by authorities in the field [5, 6] provide extensive reviews of these developments, industrial practise and recent thinking on stability of arsenic containing residues. 

Current best practice is considered to be the disposal of arsenic as a ferric arsenate waste product and storage of that residue at the plant site in a suitably designed containment facility. The ferric arsenate products that exhibit acceptable stability in TCLP tests, used routinely by the US-EPA for · suitability for landfill include crystalline scorodite (FeAsO4 2H2O) and Type II ferric arsenate (Fe4(AsO4)3·(OH)x(SO4)y) and amorphous arsenic ferrihydrite. Scorodite and type II ferric arsenate are routinely produced at elevated temperature under pressure, in autoclaves, and more recently research has focussed on developing methods for production of scorodite at atmospheric pressures [7-10] by controlling the p

recipitation conditions. Production of stable ferrihydrite, historically used in atmospheric leach operations, requires limestone or lime addition and a Fe:As ratio of > 4:1 in the precipitation reactor, however the production of scorodite at elevated temperatures can be achieved with lower Fe:As ratios. Provision of sufficient iron for arsenic precipitation is a major operating cost for any process if iron salts need to be purchased to meet this requirement. Alternatives for iron production on site can be included in flowsheets. 

There is also increasing evidence both the chemical and physical environment during storage is highly significant in limiting the possibility of arsenic release during long term storage. Microbiological activity during storage and chemical interaction between components have been shown to

produce conditions that may result in release of arsenic to ground waters. These considerations suggest the following for storage of arsenic bearing wastes: 

- Dry storage may be more appropriate than storage under water in a natural lake, due to potential biological activity. 

- Storage in a dedicated lined and monitored facility is prudent. 

- Wastes that contain materials with reducing properties, such as unreacted sulphides and elemental sulphur, may result in arsenic destabilisation and release in the long term. 

#### 3 Processes for selective arsenic removal from concentrates 

Two flowsheets are briefly described that may be used to selectively remove arsenic from a copper sulphide concentrate to produce a saleable copper concentrate. It should be noted that both of these options produce an arsenic depleted concentrate product that requires further off site treatment to produce copper and gold products comparable to that produced from the other processes described in Section 4 below. These realisation costs need to be considered in any comparison of processes to ensure a valid comparison is provided of the overall costs of copper and gold production. 

##### 3.1 Reductive roasting 

Roasting has been successfully used to treat copper concentrates from the El Indio mine which contained over 6 % arsenic, producing a saleable copper-gold concentrate [4]. Xstrata’s Altonorte smelter is still believed to toll treat high-arsenic concentrates through a roaster. Currently the expansion of Codelco’s Chuquicamata operations to treat the Alejandra Hales (formerly Mansa Mina) high-arsenic deposit is coupled to the planned construction of a roasting plant that will feed an arsenic depleted concentrate to the existing Codelco smelter. 

The Codelco approach suggests that reductive roasting may be the logical choice where an existing smelter is faced with increasing arsenic in the feed. However, it should be noted that this decision may depend on the flowsheet requirements and operating costs associated with the form of arsenic in the waste product. Current trends suggest

that a scorodite product, rather than a calcium arsenate product should be produced from the flowsheet and this can have significant capital and operating cost implications. Increasing dust containment from the roaster may also require further capital expenditure. 

While the older El Indio operation used hearth furnaces, the authors prefer a modern roasting flowsheet which utilises fluidised bed reactors. 

The objective of the flowsheet is to selectively remove over 90 % of the arsenic during reductive roasting in fluidised-bed reactors operated at ~680 °C. During the roasting process enargite is con-

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

_Arsenic Removal from Copper Concentrates_ 



verted to covellite and any pyrite contained in the concentrate is also oxidised to provide part of the heating requirements, while chalcopyrite is left essentially unreacted. 

Arsenic is volatilised from the copper concentrate as As2S3 gas. The high temperature off-gas from the roaster passes through cyclones before dilution air is added in a combustion chamber to oxidize As2S3 to As2O3 with further formation of SO2. The main purpose of the As2S3 oxidation is to avoid post-combustion in the dry electrostatic precipitators downstream. From the cyclones, the off-gas is cooled to 350-380 °C in an air-cooled heat exchanger before dust is removed in a dry electrostatic precipitator (ESP). Dust from the roaster and the ESP are routed to the calcine cooler to form a combined roaster calcine product. This arsenic-depleted product is then sold to smelters. 

The As2O3 gas is condensed and scrubbed from the off-gas stream in a scrubber, which leaves the remaining gas to be cleaned and sulphur dioxide to be recovered as sulphuric acid in a sulphuric acid plant. The solution from the gas cleaning circuit containing the arsenic is then treated in a hydrometallurgical plant, where the arsenic is first oxidised to the As(V) state using hydrogen peroxide and then precipitated with addition of ferric sulphate and limestone to produce crystalline scorodite in a waste product that is stored in a lined storage facility. 

##### 3.2 Alkaline sulphide leaching 

The ASL process as applied to enargite containing concentrates has recently been outlined by Anderson [11]. The heart of the process is the alkaline sulphide leach in which arsenic is selectively leached from the concentrate in a caustic environment with sodium sulphide as the active agent, according to the following reaction: 

2Cu3AsS4 + 3Na2S → 3Cu2S + 2Na3AsS4 



A modified flowsheet for the ASL process developed by the authors requires atmospheric leaching at elevated temperature (~90-100 °C) with addition of caustic soda and sodium sulphide. High arsenic recovery to the leach solution is expected with relatively short residence times of 2-6 hours. A significant proportion of the gold also dissolves under these conditions, but it is removed selectively from the solution using a resin based process. The flowsheet also

includes steps for reagent recovery from the spent leach solution via H2S formation and re-absorption. The flowsheet includes a small HTPOX autoclave utilising pyrite-rich cleaner concentrate to provide iron and heat into the arsenic precipitation step. This results in production of the desired scorodite precipitate, while also producing steam and acid to be used elsewhere in the process. The pressure oxidation of the copper- containing pyrite cleaner tailings also introduces additional copper into solution, which is recovered using a small solvent extraction and electrowinning circuit. 

An ASL leach process is currently being considered for use on a portion of the concentrates to be produced from the Tampakan deposit [12].

#### 4 Complete hydrometallurgical processing 

The approach to applying a complete hydrometallurgical processing solution to the treatment of high-arsenic concentrates is to leach the copper minerals and to produce a saleable copper product and a disposable arsenic-containing residue. Gold is either extracted during the copper leach or in a subsequent leach on the residue, typically using cyanidation. Where gold is a significant contributor to the revenue, particular attention should be paid to the mineralogical occurrence of the gold and the economics of its recovery. 

Dreisinger [13] reviewed the available options for leaching of primary copper sulphides. A large number of processes were considered in the review, from atmospheric leaching to total pressure oxidation. It is conceivable that each of these processes may be adapted to treat arsenic containing copper-gold concentrates; however only a selection of the more prominent processes suitable specifically for treatment of high-arsenic copper-gold concentrates is briefly described below. While the sulphide leaching step may be regarded as the heart of each process, each process requires an integrated flowsheet consisting of a unique combination of steps to effect optimal copper extraction and recovery, gold recovery and arsenic precipitation and residue disposal. 

##### 4.1 High-temperature pressure oxidation 

High temperature (or total) pressure oxidation (HTPOX) is often the first choice and the benchmark used to determine maximum extraction from total oxidation of sulphide minerals. It was originally developed and has been used extensively for oxidation of refractory sulphide gold concentrates and ores. This technology has been applied on a commercial scale on copper concentrates at Sepon, Kansanshi and Bagdad. A HTPOX plant is also planned for construction at the Chelopech mine. 

The application of this process, which is typically performed in horizontal agitated multicompartment autoclaves at temperatures of 220-230 °C, has been recommended for concentrates with enargite [14], as copper recoveries are high (>99 %) and an environmentally acceptable arsenic precipitate, scorodite, is produced. The

process is expected to result in almost total recovery of copper in a leach time of 60-120 minutes without the requirement for regrinding. The leach residue can also be expected to be amenable to high gold recovery through cyanidation at a relatively low cost, contingent on achieving good control of low concentrations of basic ferric sulphate in the leach residue. 

The process relies on oxygen injection into the autoclave under pressure. Due to the total oxidation of the sulphides to sulphuric acid the process consumes large quantities of oxygen and the acid produced has to be neutralised with limestone. If copper oxide resources are available in the area, this disadvantage can be reversed as the acid can be used to leach additional copper at low cost to the project and provide an additional revenue source. This process has typically been employed industrially in flowsheets where the acid generated can be used elsewhere.

##### 4.2 Medium temperature pressure oxidation 

Pressure oxidation at medium to low temperatures up to 160 °C has the aim of reducing the consumption of oxygen through part production of elemental sulphur and part production of sulphuric acid in the leach. This approach results in lower oxygen consumption and neutralisation costs which in turn reduce overall operating costs. 

While a large number of processes with these characteristics are available, the more prominent processes associated with treatment of copper arsenic containing concentrates and currently receiving the most attention for development are the CESL and the NSC [11] processes. The CESL process is briefly discussed below. 

###### 4.2.1 The CESL Process 

The CESL copper process operates at 150 °C and at a chloride concentration of 10-15 g/l in solution. While not installed in a commercial plant, a 10,000 t/a copper demonstration plant is currently being operated by Vale at its Sossego Mine in Brazil [15]. CESL is also presenting a paper at the current conference on a process for treatment of high-arsenic / enargite copper concentrates. 

The CESL Process has been refined over many years and many pilot and demonstration plant runs on a range of concentrate types and is marketed by CESL Limited, a subsidiary of Teck Corporation. The CESL process is expected to achieve good copper extraction and the production of a scorodite precipitate in the leach, although optimal copper extraction from enargite may be expected to involve a trade-off between extraction and regrind size and leach time. Optimisation of the leach conditions would seem an important aspect in assuring acceptable recoveries. 

The CESL copper leach produces elemental sulphur, resulting in reduced oxygen and neutralisation costs when compared to total pressure oxidation. 

As with all the medium temperature processes that produce elemental sulphur, gold recovery from the POX leach residue is an issue, as conventio

nal atmospheric cyanidation will typically result in high cyanide consumptions, mainly due to side reactions with elemental sulphur. The resultant SCN<sup>-</sup> is also difficult to destroy and Caro’s acid addition is the most likely process to be required for effluent detoxification. 

CESL appears to have overcome this issue by developing a pressure cyanidation process, coined the CESL Gold Process. This process is reported to reduce cyanide consumptions to acceptable levels when used in conjunction with a cyanide recovery process. 

The presence of chlorides in the process liquors from the CESL process requires special attention to materials of construction and poses a risk of chloride transfer to the electrowinning tankhouse via the solvent extraction circuit. It allows for use of saline water in the process, but control of chloride levels in the circuit is an important parameter to ensure high extractions.

##### 4.3 Atmospheric sulphate leaching 

Two patented processes that involve atmospheric leaching are described below. The Albion process is a relatively simple process that has undergone significant development and commercialisation. The Galvanox<sup>TM</sup> process is a more recent invention that also involves a small high temperature pressure oxidation circuit. Gold is typically recovered from leach residues by cyanidation and one of the features of the low temperature leach where the elemental sulphur is not melted would appear to be lower cyanide consumptions relative to those processes where the sulphur has been melted. 

###### 4.3.1 The Albion process 

The Albion Process has been developed by Xstrata Technologies and consists of ultrafine grinding using the IsaMill<sup>TM</sup> technology followed by atmospheric leaching in agitated tanks with oxygen injection. The process was initially developed to treat high-arsenic concentrates from the Frieda River mine [16] and has subsequently been commercialised at Mt Isa treating arsenic containing smelter flue dusts [17] to recover the contained copper as well as a number of other applications treating zinc and refractory gold concentrates. 

In order to achieve acceptable copper recoveries from an enargite-containing copper concentrate using the Albion process, fine grinding to ~10 micron is usually required followed by atmospheric leaching near the boiling point for 24 hours with oxygen injection. 

During the atmospheric leaching process, which is executed under controlled acidic conditions, iron and arsenic are also leached. The leach slurry is then neutralised with limestone, which effects iron and arsenic precipitation as ferric arsenate. The solids are separated by thickening and filtration and washed to enable gold recovery from the residue using cyanidation. High gold recovery is usually achieved at acceptable cyanide consumption levels, although gold associated with unreacted pyrite will not be recovered. Cop

per is recovered through solvent extraction and electrowinning and the acidic raffinate is returned to the leach. 

The Albion Process has been tested on numerous arsenic containing copper concentrates. It has been used successfully by Xstrata at their Mt Isa plant to leach arsenic containing smelter dusts and has full scale applications in gold and zinc processing. The possible advantage of the Albion process is the relatively low process risk of the unit processes involved and lower operating cost due to the ability to control elemental sulphur formation. 

###### 4.3.2 The Galvanox™ process 

The Galvanox™ process was recently invented by Professor David Dixon of UBC and coworkers [18]. One of the authors of this paper, Ken Baxter, was intimately involved in the development of an integrated flowsheet and engineering of the process. The Galvanox™ process is marketed by Bateman Engineering.

The Galvanox™ process was originally targeted at the processing of chalcopyrite, but has been shown to be applicable to enargite as well [19]. The heart of the process is the atmospheric leach at elevated temperature (80 °C) where the presence of pyrite is required to provide the catalytic galvanic effect which preferentially leaches any copper sulphides within 12-24 hours depending on the specific project mineralogy. Pyrite is essentially unreacted (passivated) in the leach and can be recycled to the leach process from the leach residue to provide the required pyrite to copper mineral ratio. 

A small pressure leach circuit operates in parallel to the atmospheric leach circuit, treating approximately 10 % of the feed as a minimum, and is required to treat a solution bleed stream to precipitate the arsenic and iron as disposable scorodite and hematite respectively. The autoclave also provides acid and heat to the atmospheric leach circuit. 

The Galvanox™ process has been shown to be potentially more economical than other applicable hydrometallurgical processes when applied to chalcopyrite concentrates [20]. This is mainly due to the maximisation of the formation of elemental sulphur in the atmospheric leach. Excellent gold recoveries have been achieved on combined leach residues at manageable cyanide consumption levels. In an arsenic treating flowsheet two separate residues can be produced; an arsenic-containing residue comprising largely scorodite and gypsum and a sulphide and elemental sulphur containing residue. These residues can be separately leached for gold in CIL circuits and stored separately, thereby removing the risk of interaction of sulphide residue affecting arsenic stability of the scorodite precipitate. 

The Galvanox™ process is known to be more effective on some ores than others. Testwork is essential to determine the amenability of a specific concentrate. 

##### 4.4 Atmospheric chloride leaching 

The most prominent of the more recent chloride technolog

ies have been the Outotec HydroCopper<sup>®</sup> and Intec Copper processes. These companies have recently entered into a technical co-operation agreement to better exploit similarities and synergies in their processes. Both technologies make use of the leaching of sulphide concentrates in chloride media under atmospheric conditions. The HydroCopper<sup>®</sup> process is described below. 

###### 4.4.1 The HydroCopper<sup>®</sup> process 

The HydroCopper<sup>®</sup> process has been developed by Outotec [21]. This process has been primarily developed and extensively demonstrated for chalcopyrite concentrates. The process has been studied for the Erdenet project, but remains to be commercialised. The process is significantly different from the other options above and is based on chloride metallurgy. The high chloride brine environ-
