1791 

_Baxter, Scriba, Vega_ 



ment provides for high mineral reactivity during atmospheric leaching with lower energy requirements for copper extraction and recovery than in sulphate systems. 

Outotec have developed a flowsheet to recover copper and gold from an arsenic-containing copper concentrate and produce a scorodite and elemental sulphur containing residue. The process has been engineered and recently demonstrated on the Zangezur concentrate in Outotec’s demonstration plant in Pori, Finland. 

The HydroCopper<sup>®</sup> process is performed in a concentrated chloride brine in a 3-stage countercurrent leach in which gold is also leached and recovered by absorption onto resin. The process uses chlor-alkali cells to regenerate caustic soda, chlorine, hydrogen and hydrochloric acid, which are all used in the process. Copper is continuously removed from the process by precipitation as cuprous oxide. The high purity cuprous oxide is then treated in a reduction melting process to produce copper which is cast into copper wire rod. The rod product may receive a premium over LME grade copper cathode. Hydrogen used in the reduction melting processes is also generated in the chloralkali plant. 

##### 4.5 Bacterial Leaching 

Bacterial leaching of sulphide minerals has been practiced in many forms. The most widespread application of bacterial leaching is in the processing of refractory gold concentrates with the BIOX<sup>®</sup> process the front-running commercial application. The bacterial leaching process that has undergone the furthest development for leaching of copper concentrates leaching is the BioCOP™ process, developed by BHP Billiton in South Africa [22]. 

###### 4.5.1 The BioCOP™ process 

The BioCOP™ process uses thermophile bacteria to oxidise and leach copper from sulphide concentrates. The thermophilic bacteria oxidize sulphide minerals to metal sulphates and sulphuric acid at temperatures of ~80 °C. In contrast to the mesophilic leaching of refractory gold concentrates at ~40 °C which use air as an oxidant, the BioCOP™ process uses oxygen in the leach. 

The Allianc

e Copper joint venture group (BHP Billiton and Codelco) have commercialized the BioCOP™ process at Chuquicamata in Chile in a 20,000 tpa Cu demonstration plant. The plant was specifically used in this application to treat high-arsenic concentrates and is integrated with a heap leach circuit to allow for an acid credit back to the bioleach plant. The process is proprietary and although little has been published on the extent of chemical reactions in the BioCOP™ process, the reaction is understood to proceed to full oxidation of the sulphides [13], similar to the high temperature total pressure oxidation process described above. The major difference is that additional limestone is required to assist with neutralisation during the leach and ferric arsenate precipitation.

#### 6 Conclusion 

A number of processes are available for treatment of high-arsenic copper-gold concentrates and the most prominent of these have been described and compared in a case study. The case study suggests that cost for arsenic removal to produce a saleable concentrate by known processes is costly, potentially making full hydrometallurgical treatment competitive. There is little difference between the options and testwork is recommended to distinguish between them. Also in the context of the greater cost of overall project development, selection of a robust process is recommended. 

The list of options described here is not exhaustive and selection of the appropriate option to pursue for development of a particular project may require consideration of other factors that include the following:

**Keywords:** Rhenium, ammonium perrhenate, ion exchange 

#### Abstract 

Rhenium content in the Polish copper concentrates can reach up to 15 ppm. During metallurgical processes rhenium goes to the gas phase from which it is washed out in installations for wet purification of gases directed to the sulphuric acid plant. The Instytut Metali Nieżelaznych has already conducted research and implementation works into the recovery of that metal for many years. The results were described in the paper „Recovery of rhenium from weak acid solution” presented at the conference „Copper2003-Cobre2003”. Further studies, conducted in cooperation with KGHM Ecoren S.A., resulted in the development of a new variant of the technology and launching of an installation for the recovery of rhenium in the form of ammonium perrhenate, with a current capacity at the level of 4-5 t/y. The modified method is based on an ion exchange process with a weekly basic anion resin, which is applied in place of the previously used activated carbon. The new ionite, beside the selective sorption of rhenium from acid solutions, provides also possibilities for its elution with NH3aq. As a result NH4ReO4 in ammonia solution environment is produced. Crude crystals are formed by its concentration and then refined by re-crystallization from water. The rhenium contained in the mother liquors is recovered by ion-exchange on the same resin. 

The industrial installation is composed of four columns operating in a series. It provides efficient rhenium recovery, as confirmed by the composition of the effluent, where the Re concentration usually does not exceed the level of 1 mg/L. The installation provides the possibility to exclude an individual column saturated with rhenium and to subject it to the elution process. In that way ammonium perrhenate of the highest purity is produced, meeting the requirements for the production of catalysts and metallic rhenium used for the production of superalloys. The paper presents basic information on the applied flow-sheets and technological process parameters.

#### 1 Introduction - Rhenium production and application 

Rhenium is an exceptional rare element, nonetheless thanks t

o its specific properties it is used in many fields of economy [1, 2]. Rhenium was commercially applied for the first time in the sixties of the 20<sup>th</sup> century, when Pt-Re catalysts were used in petrochemical industry for the production of high octane lead-free petrol. Until the late eighties that branch of industry was definitely the largest rhenium consumer. That scheme started to change in 1988, when rhenium-containing superalloys came into production. The superalloys are mainly used in the production of monocrystalline blades of jet engines and turbines [3, 4]. Rhenium addition in the amount of 3 to 6 % provides possibilities to operate engines at higher temperatures, which results both in better engine performance and in fuel saving. It is estimated that currently supperalloys represent 77 % of the rhenium demand whereas the catalysts for oil refining 15 % only. The remaining 8 % are consumed in other applications, e.g. rhenium is utilised in the process of hydrodesulphurization as a component of catalytic systems; it is also used in the production of thermocouples, heating components, electrodes, electric contacts and electromagnets, as well as in organic synthesis and catalysis [2, 5-7]. A large part of primary rhenium is recovered from dusts and gases generated in molybdene roasting plants. In Kazakhstan primary rhenium is also produced from copper residues. In Poland rhenium can be found in domestic copper concentrates (Table 1) where its content varies from 5 to 15 ppm. The concentrates are processed by KGHM Polska Miedź S.A. in three copper smelters, i.e.: Głogуw I smelter, Głogуw II smelter and Legnica smelter. As a result of high volatility of the oxidised rhenium forms (especially dirhenium heptoxide) rhenium is accumulated in dusts and gases during the copper concentrates pyrometallurgical treatment. In the classical shaft furnace technology (Legnica smelter and Głogуw I smelter) rhenium becomes partially distilled and is collected in the form of sulphide in the slime. The part of rhenium remaining in the copper matte – after converting – passes in the form of dirhenium heptoxide to the gas phase. 0.01-0.05g/dm3Re| |secondary dusts from lead production|100 g Re/Mg| |Fe-As alloy|up to 1000 g Re/Mg| #### 3 Rhenium technologies in Poland The researchers of the Instytut Metali Nieżelaznych (IMN) developed many technologies for the recovery of rhenium from domestic resources, mainly in the form of ammonium perrhenate(VII) [12-15], and that material was then used for the development of other rhenium technologies, such as: production of metallic rhenium, synthesis of perrhenic acid, production of other perrhenates(VII): silver, nickel(II) and cobalt(II), as well as organic rhenium catalysts [7, 16, 17]. The paper is a continuation of the previous IMN one, titled „Recovery of rhenium from weak acid solution” presented at the Copper 2003-Cobre 2003 conference and its objective is to review the current situation of rhenium recovery in Poland and to determine the possibilities of rhenium recovery development in Poland in the following years [13]. Studies into rhenium recovery in Poland started in the sixties of the 20th century [13]. Initially the main emphasis was placed on recovery of rhenium from secondary lead dusts. As a the result two technologies of dust leaching (in water and sulphuric(VI) acid) were developed and the rhenium was recovered from the produced solution using ion exchange with a strongly basic resin. The technology produced ammonium perrhenate (APR) [12, 13]. In the consequence of changing the gas 1806 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ _Development of the Technology for Recovery of Rhenium in Polish Copper Smelters_ dedusting technology from dry into wet, that method became unprofitable. Therefore investigations into recovery of rhenium from washing acids were conducted in the following years. Many new technologies were developed but the most interesting was the last one, i.e. the precipitation method, based on recovery of rhenium from the washing acid of the Legnica smelter [13]. In the first stage of the method rhenium was precipitated from a 60 % solution of sulphuric(VI) acid using Na2S2O3·5H2O. The precipitated rhenium concentrate, after filtering it out of the solution, was sent to leaching with water which contained some hydrogen peroxide. The produced solution was neutralised with ammonia until pH of 7 was reached and after filtering out it was sent to a sorption process, where a strongly basic anion-exchange resin was used. ### Dissolution of Copper Selenide in Ferric Sulphate and Chalcopyrite in Cupric Chloride Media 

J. E. Dutrizac, T. T. Chen 

CANMET-MMSL 555 Booth Street Ottawa, Canada K1A 0G 

**Keywords:** Copper selenide, ferric sulphate leaching, metastable Cu1+xSe phase, chalcopyrite, cupric ion leaching 

#### Abstract 

The dissolution of pressed disks of synthetic Cu2Se in Fe(SO4)1.5 - H2SO4 solutions proceeds in two stages: a rapid initial linear stage followed by a much slower second stage. The rate of the initial linear stage increases slightly with temperature and the apparent activation energy is 15 kJ/mol. The rate of the initial linear leaching reaction increases as the 0.79 power of the Fe(SO4)1.5 concentration, is nearly independent of the H2SO4 concentration and increases as the square root of the disk rotation speed. These variations indicate that the initial linear leaching stage is controlled by the diffusion of ferric ions through the liquid boundary layer to the surface of the selenide. Mineralogical characterization of the leached disks and sized Cu2Se fractions, as well as the molar ratios of the reaction products, indicate the sequential transformation of Cu2Se into Cu2-xSe, Cu3Se2, Cu1+xSe, CuSe, and after prolonged reaction, elemental selenium. The dissolution of closely sized chalcopyrite in CuCl2 – HCl – NaCl media obeys a linear rate law and generates cuprous chloride, ferrous chloride and >95 % elemental sulphur. The dissolution rate increases systematically with increasing temperature, and the apparent activation energy for chalcopyrite dissolution is 62 kJ/mol. At 95 °C, the chalcopyrite leaching rate increases as the 0.29 power of the CuCl2 concentration. The chalcopyrite leaching rate increases as the 0.10 power of the HCl concentration but the rate is essentially independent of the NaCl concentration for the 0.5 M CuCl2 – 0.3 M HCl solutions used. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Copper selenides occur rarely in nature as bellidoite (Cu2Se), berzelianite (Cu2Se or Cu2-xSe), umang

ite (Cu3Se2), athabascaite (Cu5Se4) and klockmannite (CuSe) [1, 2]. Despite its rarity in nature, the synthetic analogue of berzelianite (Cu2Se or Cu2-xSe) is an important species in copper electrorefining circuits where it constitutes the dominant selenium carrier in copper anodes [3, 4]. Thus, it is the ultimate source of virtually all the by-product selenium produced by the copper 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

1815 

_Dutrizac, Chen_ 



industry and accounts for most of the world’s primary selenium output [5]. The behaviour of Cu2Se in copper electrorefining circuits is complex and commonly involves the reaction of the selenide with dissolved silver to form various AgCuSe and (Ag,Cu)2Se species [6]. In addition to its reaction with dissolved silver, Cu2Se can also dissolve oxidatively to form different copper selenide species · [3, 7-9] and even elemental selenium and CuSeO3 2H2O [10-12]. In the copper electrorefining process it is often assumed that dissolved oxygen is the oxidizing agent, but other oxidants, such as Fe(III) and As(V), could be involved [13]. Despite the importance of the above dissolution reactions for the deportment and recovery of selenium in copper electrorefining operations, very little work has been reported on the kinetics of the selenide oxidation reactions. In contrast, many investigations have been carried out on the kinetics of dissolution of the analogous Cu2S phase [14]. Although it is often assumed that the sulphide and selenide analogues behave in a similar manner, there is little direct evidence to support this assumption. Furthermore, the two systems differ significantly in the presence of the Cu3Se2 phase, the sulphide analogue of which is not detected in the Cu2S leaching system [15]. 

Chalcopyrite (CuFeS2) is the dominant copper mineral in most copper ore deposits, and the conventional means of treating such ores involves flotation to produce a 25-35 % Cu concentrate followed by smelting, converting and refining to yield high purity copper metal. Although the smelting route remains the preferred means of copper production, there is a continuing interest in the treatment of copper concentrates hydrometallurgically. The interest is related both to environmental-hygiene issues associated with the pyrometallurgical route as well as the constantly escalating capital cost of smelters [16]. Numerous lixiviants have been proposed for the treatment of chalcopyrite concentrates, but much of the recent emphasis has been placed on oxygen pressure leaching in sulphate or sulphate/chloride media [17, 18], as well as on cupric chloride or ferric chloride leaching at atmospheric pressure. With respect to the latter lixiviants, there is a consensus that cupric chloride leaching is somewhat more rapid than ferric chloride dissolution. The projected advantages of cupric chloride or ferric chloride leaching at atmospheric pressure include rapid dissolution rates, lower capital costs and predominantly elemental sulphur pr

oduction. Over the years, many chloride-based technologies have been advanced, and progress continues to be made with the Intec, Outotec and Sumitomo processes [19-21]. These, and other, processes have been the subject of a number of detailed reviews [22-24], and the interested reader is referred to those compilations. 

A number of fundamental studies have been carried out to support the development of the cupric chloride leaching option. The fundamental investigations reported up to 1992 were reviewed by Dutrizac [22], and a subsequent review by Gomez et al. discussed some of the electrochemical aspects of the leaching reaction [25]. The CuCl2 leaching of chalcopyrite in complex sulphide concentrates has also been investigated [26, 27], but such concentrates are commonly low grade with respect to copper and the presence of a number of reactive sulphide minerals makes the interpretation of the data for chalcopyrite dissolution difficult. Lundstrom et al. [28] recently carried out an electrochemical study of the dissolution of moderately pure chalcopyrite in chloride media. They showed that the rate increased with increasing temperature and was insensitive to Cu(II)

concentrations less than 9 g/L but increased at higher Cu(II) concentrations. They indicated that the reaction products changed at pH values above 3.0, and the effect of pH on the reaction products formed in the Outotec HydroCopper process was reported in a subsequent study [29]. Skrobian et al. [30] showed that increasing NaCl concentrations accelerated the chalcopyrite leaching rate, and the effect was attributed to the enhanced complexation of the cuprous ion reaction product. The leaching rate seemed to be nearly independent of the particle size of the concentrate used. However, this effect may be a consequence of the dry screening procedure which was apparently used; dry screening is not especially effective for sizing fine materials. The thermodynamic aspects of the chalcopyrite dissolution reaction have been presented by Senanayake and Muir [31] and by Wang et al. [32]. 

As a general observation, little is known about the kinetics of Cu2Se dissolution. Thus, to help clarify the reactions occurring during the oxidative dissolution of Cu2Se, systematic series of kinetic experiments were carried out using Fe(SO4)1.5 - H2SO4 solutions. Ferric sulphate was selected as the oxidant because, unlike dissolved oxygen which is poorly soluble and difficult to control, its concentration could be readily controlled and widely varied in the leaching experiments. There is little consensus among the many previous studies concerning the form of the chalcopyrite dissolution curves, the temperature dependence of the reaction or the effect of the concentrations of CuCl2, HCl and neutral chlorides such as NaCl on the leaching rate. To help resolve the uncertainties and discrepancies related to the dissolut

ion of chalcopyrite in CuCl2 – HCL – NaCl media, systematic series of fundamental leaching experiments were also carried out under the general conditions likely to be encountered in a hydrometallurgical chalcopyrite leaching process. The results of both sets of experiments are summarized in this report. 

#### 2 Experimental Procedures 

The Cu2Se was prepared using a dry synthesis procedure. About 500 g of 4-6 mm 99.99 % Cu shot was hydrogen reduced at 500 °C, and 99.97 % Se was melted under vacuum at about 300 °C to minimize the oxygen content. The hydrogen-reduced copper and a stoichiometric amount selenium were then sealed under vacuum in a silica tube. The silica tube was slowly heated over several hours to 800 °C to react the two elements, and the reacted charge was subsequently homogenized for one week at 800 °C. After cooling, the silica tube was broken open and the charge was ground to minus 150 mesh (-104 µm). The ground Cu2Se was pressed into 13 mm diameter disks at 0.551581 GPa pressure using a carbide-lined die. The pressed disks were not sintered but nonetheless were “hard” and had a density of 6.20 g/cm<sup>3</sup> which corresponds to a theoretical density of 92 %. For some experiments, the ground selenide was wet screened into various mesh sizes; following wet screening, the copper selenide fractions were washed with acetone and dried under vacuum at room temperature. Electron microprobe analysis showed the copper selenide to contain 61.37 % Cu and 38.95 % Se; formula Cu2Se contains 61.68 % Cu and 38.32 % Se. X-ray diffraction analysis of the sized copper selenide fractions detected Cu2Se and Cu2-xSe together with trace amounts of Cu2O; and microscopic examination of the sized fractions and pressed disks detected the

The 13 mm diameter disks of Cu2Se were cast into 25 mm diameter epoxy mounts 12-15 mm high. The mounts were ground flat and polished through 1 µm diamond paste; they were then glued onto a plastic stirring assembly for the leaching tests. For the particulate material, two-gram samples of the wet screened Cu2Se were also subjected to leaching, largely to generate material for the product characterization studies. In both instances, leaching was done in 1.5 or 2.0 L of thermostatically controlled solution, and all the solutions were prepared using reagent grade ferric sulphate and sulphuric acid. Solution sampling was done either using an automatic sampling device which periodically removed and stored 2 mL samples of the leach solution or by manually pipetting 5 mL solution samples which were stored in sealed vials. The collected solution samples were analyzed for Cu, and sometimes for Se, using either inductively coupled plasma analysis or atomic absorption spectroscopy, with matrix

The chalcopyrite leaching experiments were carried out using sized and upgraded chalcopyrite from Messina, Transvaal, South Africa. Selected pieces of high grade chalcopyrite were dry-ground to minus 350 mesh (-45 µm) and were then wet cyclosized in 50 g lots into various fractions: -37 +29 µm, -29 +20 µm, -20 +14 µm and -14 +10 µm. The various fractions were cleaned by repeated passage through a Franz magnetic separator sequentially set to remove impurities more or less magnetic than chalcopyrite. The magnetically upgraded fractions were subjected to froth flotation at pH 6 and pH 10 to eliminate any gangue or middling particles. The cleaned fractions were then re-cyclosized in 15-20 g lots to produce the sized material used for the leaching tests. The final sized fractions were washed thoroughly with acetone and were vacuum dried at room temperature. The cleaned chalcopyrite size fractions assayed 35.8 % Cu, 29.0 % Fe and 33.5 % S; formula CuFeS2 contains 34.6 % Cu, 30.4 % Fe and 34.9 % S. #### 3 Characterization Procedures 

Many of the copper selenide and chalcopyrite reaction products were subjected to X-ray powder diffraction analysi

s using a Rigaku rotating anode with copper radiation. Polished sections of some of the copper selenide reaction products were examined, and identification of the phases was achieved by multiple techniques, including optical microscopy and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy dispersive X-ray (EDX) analysis. Although the various selenide phases are very difficult to differentiate by SEM/EDX analysis, the different phases possess distinctive optical properties. Under the reflected light microscope, Cu2-xSe is light creamy-greyish blue, isotropic or with very faint anisotropy, and exhibiting no bireflectance or internal reflections. Cu3Se2 is optically distinctive with a cherry-red to light red with a bluish tint colour, exhibiting striking bireflectance from violet red to greenish blue-grey and light brownish red, and showing very strong anisotropism from bright orange red to orange yellow and grey-purple. By contrast, the Cu1+xSe phase is light bluish-grey, more greyish than the Cu2-xSe phase, showing weak bireflectance, with anisotropism from light yellow to greyish white. The Cu1+xSe phase exhibits “rough” internal reflections of white to light yellow, which may imply the presence of numerous, tiny, differently orientated crystal domains or non-uniform crystallinity or compositions. The above optical properties are different from those of CuSe (klockmannite). CuSe is smooth light greenish-bluish grey, with strong bireflectance from bluish green to greyish white, strong anisotropism from creamy white to light orange yellow, and exhibiting no internal reflections. Electron microprobe analyses of the reacted copper selenide disks and sized fractions were also carried out to provide complementary quantitative compositional data of the various phases present, and details of all the characterization procedures have been presented previously [33].

Figure 12 illustrates the X-ray diffraction pattern of the Cu1+xSe phase made after 2 h of reaction of the -147 +104 µm (-100 + 150 mesh) material in 0.15 M Fe(SO4)1.5 – 0.3 M H2SO4 solutions at 75 °C. Although the pattern seems to consist of lines corresponding to both CuSe (klockmannite) and Cu2-xSe (berzelianite), the pattern of the Cu1+xSe phase is not identical to that of CuSe (kockmannite), Cu2-xSe (berzelianite) or Cu5Se4 (athabascaite). The lines appearing to correspond to CuSe are broad, suggesting either a significant range of compositions or poor crystallinity; the lines for Cu2-xSe are relatively sharp. Generally similar patterns were realized for compositions ranging from Cu1.31Se1.00 to Cu1.01Se1.00, and the peaks corresponding to Cu2-xSe are prevalent in all the samples. However, the products clearly cannot be interpreted as a mixture of Cu2-xSe + CuSe. The Cu content of the leach products is very low and is less than that of the Cu3Se2 phase which is absent from the samples. Furthermore, optical microscopy of the leached products clearly indicated Cu1+xSe and not Cu2-xSe. Accordingly, it is tentatively postulated that Cu is progressively removed from the Cu2-xSe structure during leaching, and the removal occurs by rapid cuprous ion diffusion through a network of much larger selenide ions. Although the composition becomes significantly copper-deficient relative to Cu2-xSe, the product retains many features of the original Cu2-xSe structure, notably those features corresponding to the original selenide ion network. The resulting structure is metastable, although the equilibrium structure is likely klockmannite (CuSe). However, this is obviously an area requiring further detailed study, especially because several compounds between Cu1.8S and CuS were recently defined in the corresponding Cu-S system [35].

##### 5.2 Effect of the Concentrations of CuCl2, HCl and NaCl 

The dissolution of chalcopyrite requires the oxidation of sulphide ions, and cupric ion is the effective oxidant in cupric chloride leaching processes. Accordingly, the effect of the CuCl2 concentration was investigated using the -29 +20 µm sized chalcopyrite. Leaching tests were carried out at 85 °C using solutions containing 0.3 M HCl and 3.0 M NaCl and at 95 °C using solutions containing 0.3 M HCl and 2.0 M NaCl, in addition to various concentrations of CuCl2 ranging from 0.1 to 1.0 M. The leaching curves obtained in both sets of experiments were similar in form to those shown in Figure 17. Initial rate constants were derived from the leaching curves done at 85 °C and at 95 °C, and these initial rate constants are displayed as a function of the CuCl2 concentration in Figure 19. The initial leaching rates calculated using Equations 8-10 increase gradually but systematically as the CuCl2 concentration increases, and the implication is that the same rate controlling process is operative over the entire CuCl2 concentration range investigated. Although cupric chloride is readily soluble in aqueous media, the cuprous chloride reaction product (Equations 11 and 12) has only a limited solubility. However, the solubility of the cuprous ion is significantly enhanced in the presence of excess chloride ions because of the formation of soluble Cu<sup>+</sup> -Cl complexes. Thus, it is common practice to add sodium chloride to the solution in cupric chloride leaching processes, but the amount of NaCl clearly depends on the concentration of the CuCl reaction product generated. In laboratory kinetic experiments, where dilute CuCl concentrations (< 1000 mg/L Cu<sup>+</sup> ) are encountered, only relatively low NaCl concentrations are required to maintain the cuprous chloride reaction product in solution. Thus, Wilson and Fisher [37] found that increasing the NaCl concentration from 2.8 to 6.2 M had no effect on the chalcopyrite leaching rate, and Bonan et al. [39] presented nearly identical leaching curves for tests carried out in 2.5 and 4.0 M NaCl. These observations are consistent with the findings of Hirato et al. [36] who found that NaCl concentrations in excess of 2.0 M had only a modest effect on the chalcopyrite leaching rate. In contrast, Skrobian et al. [30] reported a 25-30 % increase in the chalcopyrite leaching rate when the NaCl concentration of the leach solution increased from 3.4 to 5.1 M. However, their leach solutions contained 20-30 g/L CuCl, and these concentrations necessitated a higher NaCl concentration to maintain the copper in solution. The present experiments, in which only a few hundred mg/L of cuprous ions were generated, are in general agreement with the previous investigations. #### 6 Conclusions 

The kinetics of dissolution of pressed disks of synthetic Cu2Se in ferric sulphate-sulphuric acid media were investigated over the temperature range from 30 to 95 °C and for a broad range of Fe(SO4)1.5 and H2SO4 concentrations. The dissolution of Cu2Se proceeds in two s

tages: namely, a rapid initial linear stage followed by a much slower second stage. The initial rapid linear stage increases slightly as the temperature increases from 30 to 95 °C and the apparent activation energy is 15 kJ/mol. The initial linear rate increases as the square root of the rotation speed of disks of Cu2Se, and the rate approaches zero as the rotation speed approaches zero. The rate of the initial linear leaching reaction increases as the 0.79 power of the Fe(SO4)1.5 concentration but is nearly independent of the sulphuric acid concentration, for concentrations as high as 1.2 M H2SO4. These variations indicate that the initial rapid linear leaching stage is controlled by the diffusion of ferric ions through the liquid boundary layer to the surface of the copper selenide. For the initial linear leaching stage, the Fe<sup>2+</sup> /Cu<sup>2+</sup> molar ratios of the leach solutions at the end of the experiments are 2.2, and the dissolved Se concentrations are consistently < 0.3 mg/L Se. These values are consistent with the transformation of the Cu2Se into Cu2-xSe, Cu3Se2, Cu1+xSe, CuSe and eventually elemental Se. Mineralogical examination of the leached Cu2Se disks and sized Cu2Se powders support this hypothesis. 

The kinetics of dissolution of closely sized and upgraded fractions of chalcopyrite in CuCl2 – HCl – NaCl solutions were investigated for the range of conditions likely to be encountered in a commercial leaching process. The dissolution of chalcopyrite in cupric chloride media generates cuprous chloride, ferrous chloride and, predominantly, elemental sulphur; less than 5 % sulphate generation occurs. The dissolution reaction seems to obey a linear rate law, but the agglomeration of finely ground chalcopyrite particles by the elemental sulphur reaction product can result in deviations from the linear kinetics, especially at higher temperatures where extensive formation of sulphur occurs. The dissolution rate increases systematically with increasing temperature, and the implication is that only one rate controlling process prevails for the range of temperatures likely to be encountered in a commercial cupric chloride leaching process. The apparent activation energy for chalcopyrite dissolution is approximately 62 kJ/mol; this value is consistent with the range of activation energies reported in the literature for the leaching reaction. The chalcopyrite leaching rate increases with increasing CuCl2 concentrations and the CuCl2 power dependence at 95 °C is 0.29, a value which is in general agreement with previous studies of this leaching system. The chalcopyrite leaching rate in 0.5 M CuCl2 – 2.0 M NaCl media increases gradually with increasing acid

Eng. Maziar Eghbalnia, Prof. David G. Dixon

**Keywords:** Hydrometallurgy, electrochemistry, copper, chalcopyrite, pyrite 

#### Abstract 

The galvanic effect between pyrite and chalcopyrite phases in a chalcopyrite mineral concentrate was evaluated using a novel electrochemical cell. In contrast to previous cells, there is both physical and electrical contact between the mineral phases. Cyclic voltammetric studies were conducted on pure chalcopyrite and a mixture of chalcopyrite and pyrite concentrates in different ratios. The effect of pyrite on chalcopyrite oxidation was determined. In mixtures of chalcopyrite and pyrite, the electrochemical reactivity of the chalcopyrite was increased compared to the chalcopyrite sample. This behaviour is interpreted as being due to galvanic coupling between the two minerals, and the effect of the semiconductive properties of pyrite and their role in charge transfer. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Almost 80 % of the world’s copper originates from Cu-Fe-S ores. Since these minerals are not easily dissolved in aqueous solutions, pyrometallurgy is the main method of copper extraction. However, hydrometallurgical processes have several advantages: smaller scale plants, lower capital investment, lower operating costs, ease of control and the formation of elemental sulphur rather than sulphur dioxide. Thus, there is a substantial body of literature about the hydrometallurgy of copper sulphide mineral [1, 2]. Historically, chalcopyrite has been a difficult mineral to be processed hydrometallurgically. Introduced by Dixon et al. [3], the Galvanox™ (galvanicallyassisted leaching) process has been shown to be a promising advance. Pyrite plays a critical role in the galvanically-assisted leaching process. Unassisted leaching of chalcopyrite is shown in Figure 1. In ferric sulphate media, the overall leaching reaction can be written as:

The aim of the present work is to compare the leaching results with cyclic voltammetry results. Cyclic voltammetry has been used to study the effect of adding pyrite on the chalcopyrite dissolution in the Galvanox<sup>TM</sup> process. For this purpose, carbon paste electrodes (CPE) have been used. Unlike previous studies conducted by Metha and Murr, Nowak et al., Paramguru and Nayak and, Madhuchhanda et al. [5-8], who have used short-circuited galvanic cells, in this study the minerals are in physical and electrical contact. In short circuited galvanic cells, the contact between minerals is through an electrolytic solution while, in the method used in this paper there is both physical and electrical contact between the mineral phases [9]. Cyclic voltammetry with carbon paste electrodes containing mineral particles has been used as an effective tool by Lazaro et al., Urbano et al, and Horta et al. [9-12] to determine the electrochemical properties of minerals, to study the overall reactivity and galvanic interaction of the minerals. 

Electrochemical techniques are one of the most powerful tools to study galvanic interactions between different mineral associations under conditions similar to those found in sulphide mineral concentrates processing. Electrical conductivity is very important in these techniques. Since most sulphide minerals are semiconductors, they show good conductivity. In the solid electrodes, percolation of the electrolyte into the electrode affects the conductivity of the electrode, causing a potential drop due to changes in current resistance (IR) at the interface; because of the hydrophobic binding agent used in carbon paste electrodes, this effect is negligible [9]. In a carbon paste electrode with a non-conducting binder, the sensitivity is high and its residual currents are low because of the small double layer capacitance at the electrode-electrolyte interface [11]. ##### 2.2 Leaching experimentation system 

Batch leaching tests were carried out in a sealed, jacketed, 2.7-L glass reactor as shown in Figure 3. The reactor was maintained at the desired temperature with a circulating hot water bath. The temperature, potential and pH were monitored by three probes inserted into the reactor, connected to a digital controller. The outputs of the three electrodes were recorded by a computer. The controller allowed a redox potential setpoint to be specified. By sending an analogue signal to a gas mass flow valve, the redox potential measured by the electrode inside the reactor was controlled by the oxygen flow rate to maintain the set point. This valve controlled the oxygen flow into the reactor via a sparger from a compressed gas cylinder. The reactor was filled with 1500 g of DI water and the desired mass of sulphuric acid to make a 0.5 M sulphuric acid. Prior to use, the redox probe and pH probes were checked and calibrated. Ferric and ferrous sulphates were added to set a potential for the solution after the solution reached 80 °C. The oxygen flow from a compressed gas cylinder controlled by a multi-channel digital controller sets the potential whenever it fell below the set point. The working electrode was made by mixing 0.4 g of graphite (Fisher grade 38) with 0.6 g of electro-active mineral. After mixing the electroactive mineral and graphite, 0.6 mL of silicone oil (Aldrich) as a non-conducting binder was added. These were mixed to obtain a homogenous paste. Then the paste was placed in a 5 mL plastic syringe with a plunger to push the paste out of the tube in order to renew the surface after each experiment; the surface area was 0.0314 cm<sup>2</sup> . A platinum wire was immersed in the paste to conduct the electricity to the potentiostat. Each electrode was maintained in the electrolyte for 10 min in open circuit prior to scanning. This step proved to be a key point in the reproducibility of the results [10]. 

The cell consisted of a 400 mL glass dish containing the electrolyte solution, the standard calomel reference electrode (SCE), and the platinum counter electrode (dimensions: 5 cm x 2 cm). All potentials are measured and reported relative to the SCE. Nitrogen gas was sparged into the cell

In cyclic voltammetry, a sweep potential is imposed on the sample in the working electrode in order to reach the interfacial energetic conditions that promote the electrochemical reactions. The transferred charges (electrons) associated with the electrochemical reactions are registered as a function of an imposed potential. These cyclic voltammetric studies do not simulate the actual electrochemical assisted leaching process, but they are only used to characterize the surface state evolution and quantify the reactivity of mineral samples. 

This electrochemical study using CPE-chalcopyrite mineral and CPE-chalcopyrite and pyrite mineral has been performed in 0.1 M NaNO3 at a pH around 6.5 (adjusted with HNO3 or NaOH), as the electrolyte. This electrolyte was chosen because it does not interfere with electrochemical reactions of metallic sulphides and does not form complexes with metallic cations. Thus, it is a proper medium for determining galvanic interactions affecting the reactivity of sulphide minerals [11].

#### Abstract 

The world’s energy demands mean that more and more metals are being extracted from ores using hydrometallurgical processes. These processes are much less energy consuming than, for example, pyrometallurgical processes. Hydrometallurgical processes often involve dissolving the metalcontaining ores in an acid. This places high demands on the materials used for construction of hydrometallurgical process equipment. The leaching stage (atmospheric or pressure) is considered to create the harshest conditions for the use of stainless steel. However, the dissolved metal ions present in the leaching solutions may have a beneficial effect on the corrosion properties of stainless steel, as a result of their oxidative effect. This extends the limits of acid concentration and temperature for which it is possible to use stainless steel. This paper contains corrosion results from laboratory corrosion tests, based on sulphuric acid, that simulate hydrometallurgical environments, together with results from field exposures for high-alloyed austenitic stainless steels, as well as the more cost-efficient duplex stainless steel grades. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Due to the world’s energy demands, more

and more metals are being extracted from ores using hydrometallurgical processes, which are less energy consuming than pyrometallurgical processes. Hydrometallurgical processes often involve dissolving the metal-containing ore in an acid for further processing to obtain the desired metal. This places high demands on the materials used for construction of hydrometallurgical process equipment, from a corrosion point of view. Since there are several corrosion mechanisms competing in these types of processes it is difficult to select a cost efficient construction material. Acid solutions with impurities like chloride ions and dissolved metal ions at elevated temperatures complicate the prediction of corrosion. Stainless steels have proven to

be useful materials for construction for hydrometallurgical process equipment since the corrosion resistance of the different stainless steel covers a wide range, from the low-alloyed standard austenitics 304(L) (1.4301/1.4307) and 316(L) (1.4401/1.4404) up to the high alloyed superaustenitic 254 SMO<sup>®</sup> (1.4547) and super-duplex grade 2507 (1.4410). 

In this paper corrosion data that has been gathered over the years are presented, both laboratory corrosion data in simulated environments and results from field tests that could be used as guidelines for materials selection in hydrometallurgical environments. 

#### 2 Stainless steels 

Stainless steels derive their main corrosion resistance from a thin passive layer that forms spontaneously on the surface. The passive layer consists mainly of chromium oxide and has a thickness of 2-3 nm. If the passive layer is damaged and the stainless steel is present in an environment that contains oxygen, the passive layer has the ability to reform. However, if the steel is in an environment that prevents re-passivation, the steel may suffer from corrosion. How corrosion resistant a stainless steel grade is depends on the alloying content. A way of roughly estimating the corrosion resistance of a stainless steel grade is to calculate the pitting resistance equivalent (PRE) value. The PRE value takes into consideration the alloying elements that have a beneficial effect on the resistance to pitting corrosion i.e. chromium, molybdenum and nitrogen. Another way of ranking the stainless steel grades is to measure the critical pitting corrosion temperature (CPT) according to ASTM G150. The CPT value represents the lowest temperature where stable pitting corrosion occurs in a 1 M NaCl solution. A good resistance to pitting corrosion does not necessarily imply good resistance to other types of corrosion, but the alloying elements that have a beneficial influence on the PRE-values often improve the relative resistance to uniform corrosion in most acids as well. 

##### 2.1 Duplex stainless steel 

Duplex stainless steels are characterised by a two-phase microstructure comprising interleaved austenite and ferrite wit

h approximately a 50/50 ratio, see Figure 1. The austenite contributes good ductility and general corrosion resistance, while the ferrite provides high strength and a very good resistance to stress corrosion cracking (SCC). The SCC resistance of duplex grades are only matched by the highest alloyed austenitic grades. Duplex grades also have lower levels of nickel and molybdenum than their austenitic counterparts, resulting in a more stable price. The workhorse duplex stainless steel grade is 2205, EN 1.4462, developed in the 1970’s. Subsequent developments have extended the range to both high-performance super-duplex steels i.e. 2507, EN 1.4410 and more economical lean duplex grades i.e. LDX 2101® , EN 1.4162, where a part of the nickel is replaced by nitrogen and manganese. 1858 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ _Stainless Steels in Hydrometallurgy_ Figure 1: Example of a duplex microstructure. Sulphuric acid is the most commonly used acid in hydrometallurgical processes, since it is cheap and often produced on site at facilities treating sulphide ores. Stainless steels generally show good corrosion resistance in oxidising acids. Sulphuric acid is an acid with dual properties. It is oxidising up to a concentration of about 40 % by weight when it becomes reducing and very corrosive up to about 90 % by weight, when it again becomes oxidising. If uniform corrosion occurs, it causes a uniform removal of material over a large surface, at a more constant rate. This could cause thinning of the wall thickness of a tank or pipe, until the remaining wall is unable to carry the mechanical load. But since the uniform corrosion occurs at a constant rate, laboratory corrosion tests can be performed to predict the corrosion rate in different environments. In pure sulphuric acid conditions the uniform corrosion of a stainless steel increases with acid concentration and temperature as shown in Figure 2. The hydrometallurgical process solutions rarely consist of pure sulphuric acid, impurities like chloride ions and dissolved metal ions are often present. Metal ions like Cu2+ and Fe2+ / Fe3+ have a positive effect on uniform corrosion when added to sulphuric acid. Electrochemical investigations show that oxidising ions like Cu2+ and Fe2+ / Fe3+ increase the open circuit potential of the sulphuric acid 1860 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ _Stainless Steels in Hydrometallurgy_ solution and push the stainless steel into its passive state. The metal ions act like inhibitors for uniform corrosion on stainless steels in sulphuric acid, which make it possible to use standard grades at acid concentrations and temperatures which otherwise would be far too aggressive, see Figure 3. ions are also often present in hydrometallurgical environments. They may originate from the ore itself, groundwater contaminated by geological breakdown of the ore or neighbouring ore bodies, or even by using seawater as make-up water. The chloride content can have three negative effects. The first is increased uniform corrosion rate, above the rate in pure acids. Another effect is to initiate localised corrosion, such as pitting and crevice corrosion. A third mechanism is stress corrosion cracking. All three localised corrosion mechanisms may cause penetration or cracking of a tank or pipe wall and subsequent risk of leakage of solution to the outside, see Figure 4. The combination of chloride ions and metal ions increases the risk of localised corrosion, since the oxidative effect of the metal ions may push the stainless steel not only into its passive state but over the critical potential for initiation of localised corrosion.

The combination of different factors like acid, oxidative metal ions, chlorides and elevated temperatures, complicates the prediction of corrosion, since all the factors affect different types of corrosion. 

#### 4 Tools for materials selection 

The leaching stages (atmospheric or pressure) are most often the harshest process steps for the use of stainless steels. The acid concentrations, chloride levels and temperatures in these environments are often higher than in other steps. But there are possibilities to identify steel grades within the group of super-austenitic and super-duplex grades that can be used for leaching applications as well as other steel grades for less aggressive environments. Different tools like laboratory corrosion tests in simulated environments, field exposures in real applications as well as previous experience is useful when selecting an appropriate material.

#### 6 Conclusions 

- The beneficial effect of dissolved oxidizing ions in the range 9000-29,000 ppm on uniform corrosion is significant compared to pure sulphuric acid. The beneficial effect increases with increasing level of dissolved oxidizing ions. However, the minimum or maximum levels have not been established. 

- Within the 9000-29,000 ppm range of dissolved oxidizing ions, temperature is the most important factor influencing general corrosion on stainless steel. 

- Chloride content is the second most important factor. The chloride effect overshadows the acid concentration when the latter is in the 1-35 % range. 

- The chloride and temperature levels of the field tests performed were too benign to cause general or local corrosion in one year. 

- The standard grade 304L is unsuitable for 10 % sulphuric acid and 100-700 ppm chloride applications. 

- LDX 2101<sup>®</sup> is suitable in a narrower range than 2304, due to selective attack of the ferrite phase in both acid and caustic solutions. 

- At a given chloride content the corrosion resistance in 10 % sulphuric acid increases in the followi

ng order: 316L, LDX 2101<sup>®</sup> , 2304, 904L, 2205, 254 SMO<sup>®</sup> , 2507, 4565, 654 SMO<sup>®</sup> and Ti.

Francois Fleury, Enrique Delgado, Nelson Collao

#### Abstract 

Cobre Las Cruces project, property of Canadian Inmet Mining Corporation, is located approximately 20 km NNW of Seville in Andalucнa in southern Spain, and consists of an open pit mine and a hydrometallurgical plant to produce copper cathodes. 

The project is designed to produce 72,000 tons of copper cathodes Grade A, for 15 years. The plant will process 17.6 million tons of ore with an average grade of 6.22 % copper and for a construction capital cost of € 500 million. 

The geological resources are located at a depth of 150 meters. Two main ore types were encountered: a massive sulphide ore mainly comprised of pyrite and semi-massive ore. The mineralogy is mainly pyrite 65-75 % w/w, digenite and chalcocite 6.2 % w/w, and minor amounts of covellite, chalcopyrite galena and blende. The ore will be crushed, milled and atmospherically leached and the solutions obtained will be treated by solvent extraction and electrowinning, to obtain cathodic copper. 

The main challenge of the project is in the atmospheric leaching at 90 °C and using ferric sulphate for the oxidation of copper. The ferric sulphate will be obtained from leaching of pyrite and oxidized with oxygen, this process has been selected after studies with Outotec, an innovative approach to what is currently being used in this industry. It is expected to have a 92.5 % efficiency of extraction of copper in leaching and three percent of the pyrite to be leached to maintain concentration of iron in the solution. 

This paper shows the results of the operation of the plant and the major milestones that have been affronted and overcome during start up and operation.

#### 1 Introduction 

Cobre Las Cruces project, property of Canadian Inmet Mining Corporation, is located approximately 20 km NNW of Seville in Andalucнa in southern Spain, and consists of an open pit mine and a hydrometallurgical plant to produce copper cathodes. 

The project will be designed for a nominal copper capacity of 72,000 t/y copper cathodes, grade A LME. During the fifteen (15) year lifetime of the project, approx. 17.6 million tonnes of dry ore will be processed, with a total content of 1,097,000 tonnes of copper. The ore which is principally chalcocite copper mineralization will be treated by crushing, milling, atmospheric leaching, solvent extraction and electrowinning. 

Crushing and milling capacities aree designed to handle up to 1.3 million tonnes of dry ore per year. An availability factor is applied to reach an “instantaneous” flowrate. This “availability” is reflecting the actual operating hours of the plant sections and equipment items. To this instantaneous flowrate is then added a design factor (generally 15 %) and the equipment selected will be the next largest size available from the equipment provider. 

Leach, SX capacities are based on a nominal throughput modified to allow for availability to reach instantaneous flows and then a 15 % design factor is added. In EW mass balance it has been applied a design factor of 7.7 % to maintain maximum acceptable current density of 325 A/m<sup>2</sup> . 

The infrastructure required to support the operation is including an adjacent oxygen plant to built and operated by a recognized oxygen production company (outside the project scope), a steam plant, ancillary facilities, and all required administration buildings. The oxygen plant was provided by a recognized oxygen plant operator and supply vendor as a “black box” outside the plant battery limit with oxygen supplied as required “over the fence”. 

The project demands full protection of the underlying “Niebla Posadas” aquifer whose water is to be diverted around the pit by extraction and reinjection wells. To improve water consumption the plant will use almost entirely treated sewage water from the San Jeronimo facility in Sevilla and piped to the site. As we cannot pumped during the dry season, April to September, a water collecting basin with sufficient capacity has been built to supply water during that season. 

All rain water, mine water and contact water runoff will be collected and treated if necessary before its use in the plant or release. 

When in operation the plant will employ approximately 150 staff and operators.

##### 4.6 Neutralization System 

###### 4.6.1 Pre neutralization 

Raffinate and aqueous of water step bleed is fed to the pre neutralization circuit. Flocculants and Ca(OH)2 slurry are premixed with re-circulated pre neutralized solution and then fed into the first neutralization reactor. This pre neutralized solution overflows then to the second neutralization reactor and finally to the thickener. During this process, the sulphuric acid precipitates as gypsum. Raffinate bleed will be neutralized to enable acceptable recoveries of copper in the secondary extraction. The gypsum in the thickener underflow is returned to the leach feed tank. Part of the thickener underflow is re-circulated for seeding purposes. Thickener overflow flows to a secondary PLS tank before to be pumped through polishing filters into the secondary PLS feed tank. Cooled wash water from the leach residue filters is also pumped into the secondary PLS tank.

As with the solvent extraction area the absence of upstream surge in the preceding dry areas forces the EW plant to use the availabilities of the upstream sections. Strong electrolyte from the SX area flows into a strong electrolyte after settler, which acts as a pump tank for the electrolyte filters and it also captures organic entrainment from S1 stage, which may occur during operational disturbances. The separated organic is decanted into a launder from

where is pumped to the crud tank. The strong electrolyte solution is pumped to three dual media electrolyte filters (plus one stand by) into a strong electrolyte surge tank. From here it is pumped via the Electrolyte Interchanger and Trim Heater to a group of “scavenger” cells. These cells provide a final protection for the bulk of the tankhouse “commercial” cells in the event of organic slippage past the Electrolyte Filters due to any bad operation. The scavenger cells are arranged as part of the row of one tier of cells on one side of the electrowinning tankhouse. The “scavenger spent” leaving these cells enters into the main 1885 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ _Fleury, Delgado, Collao_ return manifold for the spent electrolyte from the “commercial” cells of that tier, so enriching this “commercial spent”. This rich feed solution then enters the feed side of the circulation tank. The Electrolyte Circulation Tank consists of two compartments connected via an underflow weir to mix strong electrolyte from the circulating scavenger commercial cell spent electrolyte and the remaining commercial cell spent electrolyte. Additives (guar and cobalt sulphate) are dosed into the EW feed electrolyte. Spent electrolyte is taken from the Electrolyte Circulation Tank back to the solvent extraction through cooling heat exchangers (an electrolyte/electrolyte interchanger) and an Electrolyte Trim Cooler. The tankfarm is equipped with holding tanks. The mixture of scavenger cell spent electrolyte and the majority of the commercial cell spent electrolyte forms the feed to the commercial cells. In the electrolysis cells Cu2+ of CuSO4 is reduced to metallic copper at the cathode blanks and water is decomposed to hydrogen ion and oxygen at the anode. Thus the sulphuric acid content is increased and oxygen is liberated. The spent electrolyte from the cells is returned to the circulation tank. Transformer rectifiers produce direct current which is passed through the electrolyte to achieve this process. Copper cathodes are harvested with an automated tankhouse crane, washed and stripped off from the cathode blanks in a washing and stripping machine. Copper cathode sides are stacked in bundles, which are weighed, strapped and stored. The stripped cathode blanks are returned back to the electrolysis cells. Acid mist which is generated by the liberated oxygen is controlled by removable hoods over each cell with the captured gas ducted to a scrubbing system. Any fugitive acid mist which may escape from the cell hoods during cathode harvesting is controlled by a general building ventilation system using open sides on the building and a ridge ventilator along the roof apex. 1886 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ _A New Technology for Processing Hydrometallurgical Copper Ore_ RIC H ELECTROLYTE CIRCULATION TANK ELECTROWINNING

Leaching of copper from Las Cruces ore was studied earlier at OTC and reported as: Cobre Las Cruces Batch Test Report 03101-ORC-T. #### 6 Conclusion 

The continuous pilot test results demonstrated that leaching of the coarse material –0.30 mm in OKTOP reactors was not feasible because of the high mixing power needed to keep the material in suspension and the high wearing rate of the mixing elements of the agitators. 

The ore had to be ground to 100 % –0.15 mm to ensure adequate agitation and suspension of solids in the leach reactors. The finer material is still very abrasive because a high mixing power is needed to keep the high-density pyrite suspended in the leach reactors and to efficiently disperse the oxygen gas needed for the oxidation. Therefore it is important that the selection of materials of construction for the agitators, and more importantly the agitator blades, must be carefully selected to prevent severe agitator wearing and frequent loss of operating time for changing agitator blades in the commercial operation. 

The copper extraction during both operating periods was up to 94 %, when the oxygen was dispersed, the oxidation potential was maintained at the right level, and/or the Fe<sup>3+</sup> /Fe ratio was high enough (> 20 %). The retention time was 8 hours in both operating periods. The iron extraction was 3 % in both operating periods, which corresponds to the results from the batch tests. 

The calculated oxygen consumption based on pilot plant results was 36-54 kg O2/t ore during the second operating period. 

The calculated unit area for thickening in the second operation period is 0.169-0.192 (m<sup>2</sup> /t/day) and the diameter of thickener is 28-30 m. The demanded filtration area for design capacity is 600-670 m<sup>2</sup> . 

The calculations of filtration area for slurry after thickening (with addition of flocculation reagent) showed that best result were achieved in tests 7 and 4 (1180 and 1265 kg/m<sup>2</sup> h). The average moisture of the cake after filtration was 8.8 % (from 8.0 to 9.7 %).

#### Abstract 

Refined copper produced by means of solvent extraction (SX) accounts for over 20 % of the world production and that technique has become more popular recently as new hydrometallurgical projects dealing with primary copper ores and concentrates are under evaluation or have been implemented in the last years in Chile, USA, etc. 

The low capital and operating costs of SX plants together with the easy operation and the production of top quality electrolytic metals close to the mine site make the economics of the SX processes very attractive, being suitable and feasible in the range of small to medium capacities, where conventional smelting process is not applicable. In some cases, the alternative of obtaining extremely pure salts may be cheaper than metals production. 

Thanks to the commercial success of the Skorpion Zinc integrated refinery in Namibia, producing 150,000 t/y SHG Zn since 2003, a significant expansion of new zinc projects focused on primary and secondary materials is currently underway based on the application of the ZINCEX™ solvent extraction technology. 

Copper SX and zinc SX are mature and well established commercial technologies. Therefore, now is the right time to afford new mining and metallurgical projects dealing with mixed or polymetallic copper and zinc ores and secondary materials. That way, this paper presents relevant design features and technical advances of two industrial projects based on SX applications: (1) Heap leaching of oxidised copper/zinc polymetallic ores to recover both metals in form of the maximum purity cathodes; (2) Processing of flue dusts and electrofilter solid particles from copper smelters to recycle copper and zinc and rejecting some impurities like arsenic. The preliminary evaluation results have been very positive in both projects, showing clearly the technical advantages and the potential profitability to recover those metals by means of SX techniques.

#### 1 Introduction 

In recent years there has been considerable development of hydrometallurgical processes for copper extraction applying solvent extraction (SX) combined with electrowinning for the production of high grade electrolytic copper. As a result, above 20 % of the world copper production [1] is currently achieved from heap leaching operations of oxide copper ores (and also more recently stirred leaching of chalcocite) mainly located in Chile, Arizona (USA), and Australia. 

Solvent extraction of zinc has been successfully applied on several industrial plants using the ZINCEX™ technology. Skorpion Zinc refinery located in Namibia is the major reference producing 150,000 t/y SHG zinc cathodes since 2003 [2]. Besides, this technology is gaining more popularity with the latest trends for zinc recovery from secondary materials. That is the c

ase for Akita Zinc Recycling Co. in Japan [3], which will be producing 20,000 t/y SHG zinc from residual zinc dusts at the end of 2010. 

Copper and zinc solvent extraction are mature and well established commercial technologies, and the mining and metallurgical industries are now in the best position to afford projects dealing with mixed or polymetallic copper and zinc bearing materials [4]. The driving forces behind those industrial projects using SX technologies include both economic and environmental advantages [5]. 

There are a number of key aspects to be considered in the hydrometallurgical processing of mixed copper and zinc primary and secondary materials: 

- Very frequently, those are complex materials and the main metals are distributed as compounds of diverse nature and consequently are very difficult to separate by physical treatment. This characteristic has driven the need to use whole leaching for maximum copper and zinc metals extraction into solution. 

- The whole leaching releases valuable copper and zinc to the pregnant solution but also large quantities of other undesirable components like iron, arsenic, cadmium, etc. 

- Application of SX techniques for copper and zinc recovery from pregnant leaching solutions containing high levels of impurities will require tailored solutions to get the optimum yields applying the best process conditions and design parameters. 

- Other relevant factors like geographical location and available infrastructures, raw materials grade and reserves/availability, acid consumption, power supply and cost, local environmental regulations for disposal, etc, have to be carefully analysed. 

#### 2 Industrial Applications 

A couple of industrial applications is presented and described in this paper. The first application is devoted to oxide copper/zinc ore processing by means of heap leaching, while the second application is focused on the recycling of diverse dusts produced in a copper smelter and containing copper and zinc among other hazardous components like arsenic, etc.

### An Electrochemical Model for Acidic Dissolution of Chalcopyrite (CuFeS2) Mineral 

Ahmad Ghahremaninezhad, Edouard Asselin, David G. Dixon 

The University of British Columbia Materials Engineering Department 309-6350 Stores Road 

Vancouver, BC, V6T 1Z4, Canada 

**Keywords:** Electrochemical dissolution, chalcopyrite, EIS 

#### Abstract 

The dissolution of a massive chalcopyrite electrode (98.1 % chalcopyrite, 1.9 % siderite) was studied in sulfuric acid solution by means of electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) techniques. The studies at open circuit potential (around -235 mV vs. MSE) proved the existence of a thin surface layer on the electrode. This layer was stable up to 100 mV vs. MSE and was assumed to be Cu1-xFe1-yS2 ( _y_ 〉〉 _x_ ) based on reports from previous studies. By increasing the potential to the range of 100-300 mV vs. MSE, the previously formed layer partially dissolved and a second layer (Cu1-x-zS2) formed on the surface. Both of the layers showed the characteristics of passive layers at low potentiodynamic scan rate (0.05 mVs<sup>-1</sup> ) while at high scan rates they acted like pseudo-passive

layers. However, in the potential range of 300 to 420 mV vs. MSE, both of these surface layers dissolved and active dissolution of the electrode started. Different equivalent electrochemical circuits were modeled for each potential range and the model regression results compared with the experimental results of EIS to determine the proposed sequence of chalcopyrite dissolution. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Chalcopyrite is the most abundant copper bearing mineral in the world and its dissolution behavior represents the most important technological consideration in the hydrometallurgical extraction of copper [1]. Since the current pyrometallurgical methods for copper extraction from chalcopyrite have environmental issues, many studies have considered the leaching and dissolution of CuFeS2 in different aqueous media [2-5]. The main problem associated with leaching processes is the slow dissolution rate of the mineral [6]. During the dissolution process, increasing the potential of the chalcopyrite in the anodic direction will cause the formation of surface layers which hinder the dissolution rate of the mineral [7]. The precise composition of the layers is in dispute. Previous studies 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

1909 

_Ghahremaninezhad, Asselin, Dixon_ 



have concluded that these layers could be sulfur [8-9], precipitated iron compounds [8], a solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) – which slows the rate of electron transfer – [10], a metal deficient sulfide [11], or polysulfidic in nature [12-13]. In order to increase the leaching kinetics of chalcopyrite, the characterization of the layers formed during dissolution is essential and electrochemical methods are important to this end. Studies by Biegler [14] show nucleation and growth of a thin two-dimensional sulfide phase on the surface of chalcopyrite during the exposure of a polished sample in H2SO4 solution or air. More studies by Biegler and Swift [15] have shown evidence for nucleation and growth of a 3-dimentional phase at low anodic potentials (around 200 mV vs. OCP). The currenttime behavior of the dissolution process in this potential area has the characteristics of expansion and overlap of localized dissolution centers. Anodic dissolution (around 200 mV vs. OCP) of the chalcopyrite is considered to be a bulk dissolution process which is distinct in mechanism from the surface oxidation process at lower potentials (anodic potentials close to OCP) [16]. The surface oxidation process is detectable as a “prewave” in cyclic voltammetry tests. Technically, the prewave represents the initial stage of the dissolution of chalcopyrite and furthermore, determines the surface properties of the mineral during the rest of the dissolution process. Many publications on chalcopyrite have concentrated on the dissolution behavior in the prewave region [14-16]. Studies by Lazaro and Nicol [17] on the dissolution of chalcopyrite in dilute sulfuric acid solutions have produced some evidence for the formation of

Cu<sup>2+</sup> , Fe<sup>2+</sup> , and soluble sulfur species at the initial stages of dissolution at 60 °C. More kinetic studies on the prewave reaction by Holliday and Richmond [18] have demonstrated a sequential mechanism for the surface oxidation which consists of an initial rate determining step for the production of adsorbed Cu<sup>2+</sup> followed by the production of Fe<sup>2+</sup> ions. These reactions are responsible for making a passive surface layer on the mineral and hindering the dissolution rate. These results are along the same lines as those presented by other workers [16, 19]. Nava et al [20-21] have studied the dissolution of a carbon paste/chalcopyrite electrode in sulfuric acid solution. It was indicated that the dissolution of chalcopyrite starts at low anodic potentials (0.615 ≤ E < 1.015 V vs. SHE) and results in the formation of a non-stoichiometric polysulfide layer of composition Cu1-xFe1-yS2-z. In this potential region the concentration of the dissolved copper ion was found to be very low and anodic stripping voltammetry (ASV) was not able to detect the copper ion in solution. Consequently, Nava et al have concluded that the Cu1-xFe1-yS2-z is indeed a passive film which reduces the dissolution rate of chalcopyrite. At higher potentials (1.015 ≤ E < 1.085 V vs. SHE), a small amount of copper ion was detected in solution which confirmed the partial dissolution of the polysulfide layer. The reaction for chalcopyrite dissolution in this higher potential range was proposed to result in formation of Cu1-mFe1-nS2-p. While this product and the previous one are similar it was shown that the latter sulfide product is an active film as opposed to the former sulfide layer [20-21]. Studies by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) have shown the formation of islands of passive layers on the surface of chalcopyrite electrodes [22]. Another EIS study has demonstrated the active-passive behavior of chalcopyrite but did not point out the passive islands on the surface of electrode [23-25]. In the present study we will concentrate on the electrochemical dissolution of chalcopyrite in simple sulfuric acid solution by EIS method.

#### 2 Experimental 

A high quality natural polycrystalline chalcopyrite sample originating from the Creighton Mine (Canada) was used for electrode fabrication (98.1 % CuFeS2 and 1.9 % FeCO3). Massive electrodes were prepared by cutting the chalcopyrite into approximately cubic shapes with areas of 1 cm<sup>2</sup> exposed to the solution. In order to measure the resistance of the electrode at different potentials, two separate electrical contacts with copper wires were made in the back of the sample with silverloaded epoxy resin (Mg Chemicals). The electrode contacts were protected from the solution by mounting the whole assembly in epoxy resin (LECO), leaving only one face of

the electrode exposed to the solution. Before each test, the exposed face of the electrode was polished with no. 1200 carbide paper to begin each experiment with a fresh surface. Electrochemical experiments were carried out using a conventional three-electrode electrolytic cell; graphite as a counter electrode, and the prepared chalcopyrite electrode as working electrode (WE). A saturated mercury/mercury(I) sulfate electrode (MSE) was used as a reference electrode for all of the electrochemical tests; all further potentials quoted in this study are with respect to the MSE (0.640 V vs. SHE at 20 °C) if not otherwise mentioned. The reference electrode was connected to a Luggin capillary to minimize IR drop. Prior to each test, fresh solutions were prepared from bi-distilled and deionized water, and the samples and counter electrode were degreased by sonicating in acetone and methanol, rinsing with distilled and deionized water and then drying in a stream of air. The electrode potential was allowed to stabilize for 10 min before starting the measurements and, in order to ensure reproducibility, tests were begun only after reaching the same OCP within ±10 mV. The electrolyte used was 0.5 M H2SO4 and all of the experiments were conducted at 25 °C. EIS tests were conducted at different potentials and in the frequency range of 10<sup>–2</sup> to 10<sup>5</sup> Hz with peak to peak amplitude of 10 mV. Electrochemical measurements were performed with a potentiostat/galvanostat PAR 273 connected to Frequency Response Detector PAR 1025 controlled by PowerCorr, PowerStep, and PowerSine software (Princeton Applied Research).

Considering the surface properties and dissolution proc

esses already elucidated at various potentials, the EIS data were fitted to different equivalent electrochemical circuits. Figure 6a shows the modeled circuit for the potential range of OC to 0 V and the calculated Nyquist plots according to the model. Another physical explanation for the CPE would be electrode roughness [32]. _R_ CPE represents the resistance of the CPE in the equivalent circuit. Initially, during the sample preparation a thin layer of Cu1-xFe1-yS2 forms on the surface of the electrode where _y_ 〉〉 _x_ . During electrochemical dissolution of chalcopyrite this layer is stable and its thickness increases with potential according to Reaction (1) (OCP -100 mV vs. MSE). At higher potentials (100 to 300 mV vs. MSE) the previously formed surface layer partially dissolves and a second passive layer (Cu1-x-zS2) forms via Reaction (2). Both of these layers display the characteristics of passive layers at low scan rate (0.05 mVs-1 ) and for high scan rates they are observed to be pseudo-passive. In the potential range of 300 to 400 mV vs. MSE, none of the surface layers are stable and electrochemically active dissolution of the electrode occurs by Reactions (3) to (5). Understanding the surface behavior of chalcopyrite during the electrochemical dissolution was the main goal of this study. The observations of the present study were explained based on the literature _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 1920 _An Electrochemical Model for Acidic Dissolution of Chalcopyrite (CuFeS2) Mineral_ and results of previous studies. Since EIS was the electrochemical technique applied in the present study, different equivalent electrochemical circuits were modeled and compared to experimental results to support the proposed sequence of chalcopyrite dissolution and surface layer formation. ### Selecting between Weak and Strong Extractants on Acid Solutions in Copper SX 

Hans Hein 

Cognis Chile Av. Alonso de Cуrdova 5151, Of. 703 Santiago, Chile 

**Keywords:** Solvent extraction, copper, reagents 

#### Abstract 

Reagents currently available in copper solvent extraction plants or projects may be classified as weak, medium or strong SX extractants. A simple approach given in the past was that weak extractants were suitable for low acid and low copper PLS, whereas strong extractants could be applied on high copper tenor, as well as high acid concentration in pregnant leach solutions. Ketoxime and highly thermodynamically modified aldoxime are considered as weak SX reagents. Their extraction isotherms are less efficient and easy stripping is achieved, even at reduced acid concentration in electrolyte. Pure aldoxime and slightly modified aldoxime are designated as strong extractants, providing efficient extraction from leach solution into organic and difficult stripping of copper into electrolyte. Aldoxime and ketoxime blends may be directed each way. With time, as leaching and SX configurations diversified, the simple and original definition did no longer satisfy the optimum reagent selection. Other parameters like net copper transfer in organic, SX recovery, reagent stability, organic in aqueous as well as aqueous in organic entrainments, plus other aspects have to be considered. The purpose of the present study is to provide some preliminary hints on successful plant configuration and SX extractant selection. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Since copper extractants were discovered and developed by General Mills Chemicals Inc in 1963, company taken over by Henkel in 1977 and ten years ago by Cognis, only three types of oximes had been applied successfully in the copper industry as copper extractants. These oximes are classified as C9 aldoxime, C12 aldoxime and ketoxime. For many years Cognis has been the only company marketing these products worldwide in their pure state as LIX<sup>®</sup> 860N-I, LIX<sup>®</sup> 860-I and LIX<sup>®</sup> 84-I or concentrated as LIX<sup>®</sup> 860N-IC, LIX<sup>®</sup> 860-IC and LIX<sup>®</sup> 84-IC respectively [1]. Cognis Ireland Ltd produces all of t

hem at their production plants in Cork, Ireland. Both aldoximes are considered as
