The main differences between C9 and C12 aldoximes are related to reagent stability, whereas its metallurgical performance is equivalent. Ketoxime may be blended with aldoxime at several proportions, covering the whole range between weak and strong extractants. LIX<sup>®</sup> 984N or its concentrated version LIX<sup>®</sup> 984NC [2], representing a 50/50 percent blend [3] between LIX<sup>®</sup> 84-I and LIX<sup>®</sup> 860N-I or alternatively between LIX<sup>®</sup> 84-IC and LIX<sup>®</sup> 860N-IC, is one of the most common extractants used in copper industry. 

There is another way to control the strength or weakness of copper extractants, considering the same type of oximes mentioned above. A mixture of 5-nonylsalicylaldoxime with a thermodynamic modifier enables aldoxime to become weaker, in other words, extraction isotherms are getting less efficient, whereas strip isotherms generate a lower copper tenor in stripped organic. There are several modifiers offered in the market as a mixture with aldoxime, containing a high flash point hydrocarbon diluent. In view of its physical behaviour, a trend to low viscosity modifiers is noticed. Some of the copper extractants containing low viscosity proprietary modifiers, produced and offered by Cognis, are LIX<sup>®</sup> 612N-LV, LIX<sup>®</sup> 664N-LV and LIX<sup>®</sup> 622N-LV [4]. The three reagents contain different low viscosity modifiers at decreasing degree of modification. In all of them the base aldoxime is LIX<sup>®</sup> 860N-I. Currently Cognis does not offer concentrated versions of modified aldoximes. 

#### 2 Scope of the Study 

Engineering companies and copper producers via hydrometallurgy have difficulties in selecting the most convenient extractant for their particular needs. Usually they rely on technical expertise of reagent suppliers, frequently combined with lab and pilot testing. The general impression is that weak extractants operate well on low copper tenor and low acid in pregnant leach solution (PLS) or aqueous feed to solvent extraction plants. Whenever acidity in PLS increases to less than pH 1.7, current preference is to apply a stronger extractant. Reality has not been quite simple, as new SX configurations [5-7] have been developed. Quite often copper net transfer in organic as well as copper iron selectivity plus reagent stability become important, besides of copper recovery. The purpose of the study is to evaluate weak, medium and strong extractants under selected operational parameters in order to obtain additional conclusions on metallurgical performance, without getting involved at this stage with copper iron selectivity and reagent stability. Consequently, the main objective of the study is to compare copper recovery against copper net transfer in organic. At fir

st non modified reagents will be evaluated, selecting ketoxime LIX<sup>®</sup> 84-I as a weak extractant, aldoxime LIX<sup>®</sup> 860N-I as a strong extractant and LIX<sup>®</sup> 984N as a medium extractant, representing a 50/50 percent blend between LIX<sup>®</sup> 84-I and LIX<sup>®</sup> 860N-I. 

The scope of the study considers to show extraction and strip isotherms, comparing particularly weak, medium and strong extractants, to draw differential isotherms based on two against a single strip stage, to present three McCabe-Thiele diagrams on 2E-2S configuration in comparison to an-

The study covers a range of operating parameters and its results make it feasible to establish basic guidelines. Its scope could not include all parameters usually required for making the right decision on reagent selection like copper iron selectivity, reagent stability, entrainments and others, as the evaluation was focused on copper recovery and copper net transfer. Some conclusions are: 

- Strong extractants allow improved recoveries, nevertheless their copper transfer potential is limited. 

- Weak extractants have great potential in regards to copper net transfer, as long as high recoveries are not particularly forced. 

- Weak extractants improve copper recovery applying a scheme of 3E-1S instead of 2E-2S. 

- Low copper tenor PLS at a reasonable pH favours weak extractants, as known in the past. 

- Modified aldoxime reagents hardly reach the extractant weakness of a ketoxime. 

- Mixtures of modified aldoxime with ketoxime have advantages under particular conditions not evaluated in the present study. 

- Complex SX configurations or key parameters different to the ones considered in the present study require special evaluations for optimum reagent selection.

### MRT Applications in Copper Refining: Bismuth Removal from Copper Electrolyte 

Steven R. Izatt, Neil E. Izatt, John B. Dale, Dr. Ronald L. Bruening 

IBC Advanced Technologies, Inc. 856 East Utah Valley Drive American Fork, Utah, 84003 USA 

**Keywords:** Copper refining, bismuth removal, tankhouse purity control, Molecular Recognition Technology (MRT) 

#### Abstract 

High purity electrolytic copper is an essential commodity in the world’s economy being used primarily to fabricate copper wire. This copper is produced in smelters worldwide using ore obtained from multiple sources and a variety of geographical locations. Copper concentrates from these sources usually contain bismuth at levels up to 0.1 %. Bismuth levels exceeding 2 ppm in the final copper product result in brittleness making the product unsuitable for wire production. IBC Advanced Technologies, Inc. (IBC) has developed an effective bismuth-removal system for the separation of dissolved bismuth from copper electrolyte to reach the desired bismuth levels. The system is integrated into the copper production system and operates continuously. IBC uses a Molecular Recognition Technology (MRT) process to accomplish this separation. In this process, specially designed chelators or ligands are chemically bonded to solid supports such as silica gel to produce a solid-phase system termed SuperLig<sup>®</sup> . This bismuth-removal system has been integrated with the copper refining operation at several refineries. This paper describes the process steps involved in the commercial separation and recovery of bismuth from copper electrolyte solutions. These process steps are absorption, wash 1, pre-elution, main elution, post-elution, wash 2, and bismuth precipitation. Items to control and monitor in each step are given. Limitations of alternate technologies for bismuth control are discussed. Economic benefits of the MRT system to copper refineries where bismuth problems exist are presented. 

#### 1 Introduction 

The major share of world production of high purity electrolytic copper is used to fabricate copper wire [1]. In the production of copper rods, the starting material is commonly a “tough pitch” wirebar of electrolytic copper. The wirebar is subsequently reduced to rod via hot rolling operations. The rods are subsequently drawn into wire. An important factor affecting the hot 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

1941 

_Izatt S., Izatt N., Dale, Bruening_ 



working characteristics of the copper is the nature and quantity of impurities present. Bismuth is well known for its ability to impair the hot working properties of copper. Sp

ecifically, bismuth causes “hot shortness” or brittleness of the copper along the grain boundaries at high temperatures. This effect results from the segregation of low melting point bismuth in minute amounts at the grain boundaries [2]. The resulting copper can crack during subsequent rolling and drawing operations, rendering it unsuitable for wire production. Consequently, copper cathode containing out-ofspecification bismuth, must usually be recycled back to an earlier furnace stage, and recast into anodes. This time-consuming procedure results in substantial additional costs as well as lost copper production. The specification for bismuth in London Metal Exchange (LME) grade copper cathode is 2 ppm maximum. In practice, the actual operating target level is < 0.5 ppm bismuth. 

Bismuth is a relatively rare metal, and is usually associated with lead, copper and lead-silver ores. Consequently, it is generated as a by-product in the smelting and refining processes used to treat these ores. The major geographical sources of bismuth from these ores are in the U.S.A., former Soviet Union states, Mexico, Peru, Canada, and Australia. The largest world source of bismuth is found in China where the bismuth is primarily associated with tungsten/molybdenum ores [3]. 

Copper concentrates from the above countries generally contain bismuth at relatively low concentrations (up to 0.1 % bismuth). However, as sources of higher grade copper concentrates decline, concentrates containing more than 0.1 % bismuth are being more widely processed. Bismuth can often be a particular problem to major international, fully integrated, copper smelters and refiners which often secure copper concentrates from multiple sources and geographical locations with various specifications. 

In the production of copper from sulfide ores, the copper-bearing sulfide concentrates are first smelted to copper matte, oxidized to blister copper, fire refined, and cast into copper anodes. The copper anodes are then refined into high purity copper by electrolysis. In the above pyrometallurgical processes, the bismuth is partially volatilized and collected in the flue dusts. The balance of the bismuth reports with the copper anodes. As the copper anode dissolves in the electrolyte, a portion of the bismuth gradually falls to the cell bottom as an insoluble slime with the remaining portion dissolving in the electrolyte. The problem is to minimize transfer of the bismuth to the copper cathode. Ramachandran has stated that bismuth does not co-deposit with copper under normal electrorefining conditions [4]. Consequently, the major source of bismuth in the cathode may be physical entrapment. Although much discussion continues about the actual mechanisms for bismuth transfer to the copper cathode, it seems clear that minimizing the amount of bismuth in the electrolyte will minimize the amount of bismuth impurity in the copper cathode [5]. 

The MRT bismuth removal system developed by IBC has proven

to be a highly efficient process for separation of dissolved bismuth from the copper electrolyte. IBC estimates that of approximately 100 operating electrolytic copper refineries worldwide, some 60 have a need to better control the bismuth content in their copper cathodes. In this paper, the MRT process for bismuth removal as used commercially in several copper refineries is described, the specifications for its optimal use are

#### 2 Molecular Recognition Technology (MRT) 

The MRT process [6, 7] utilizes “lock and key,” or “host guest” chemistry. MRT is a highly selective, non-ion exchange system, using specially designed chelators or ligands that are chemically bonded to solid supports such as silica gel. The solid phase system (SuperLig<sup>®</sup> ) consists of 250-500 micron size silica particles to which the selective ligand is attached. The SuperLig<sup>®</sup> is packed into fixed bed columns that, in commercial operation, can be built in skid-mounted modular form, and can be fully automated for continuous operation. The feed solution is passed through the column and the target ion is removed from the solution. 

SuperLig<sup>®</sup> products are designed to selectively bind with ions based on multiple parameters such as size, coordination chemistry, and geometry. In contrast, conventional separation methods such as precipitation, ion exchange, and solvent extraction often recognize differences between ions based only on a single parameter (i.e., charge, solubility, size). SuperLig<sup>®</sup> products can bind ions even when they are present in highly acidic or basic solutions. The MRT process exhibits high selectivity, high binding factors, and rapid reaction kinetics, resulting in a very efficient separation [6, 7]. The simple elution chemistry uses small volumes of eluate. Thus, the dilute bismuthcontaining solutions are concentrated upon elution and can be treated to produce a marketable bismuth product of high added value with minimal environmental impact. 

Due to the high selectivity, high loading capacities and rapid loading and release kinetics of the SuperLig<sup>®</sup> products, application of the MRT procedure to commercial scale operation results in substantially lower capital and operating costs than those found in competitive technologies like ion exchange, solvent extraction, classical pH adjustment, and chemical precipitation procedures [6, 8-11]. In the MRT process, relatively small quantities of the appropriate SuperLig<sup>®</sup> product are required, hence the scale of the installation can be smaller, solution wash and elution chemical requirements and volumes are substantially less, and high feed solution flow rates are possible. Higher efficiencies a

re possible due to single pass quantitative removal of the target species and SuperLig<sup>®</sup> products do not introduce contaminants into the process. 

MRT can be used to remove ions to very low levels that are not possible using other technologies. The MRT process can produce commercially pure products that can be sold or recycled. This is an important factor from the standpoint of cost, the environment, and waste disposal. A wide choice of eluant formulations is usually available to ensure compatibility with particular plant requirements. Highly concentrated eluant solutions can be produced from which the simple recovery of a high purity, high value-added product is possible. The result is a readily marketable product and provides significant financial credit to the process.

#### 3 Process Steps 

The process steps for the commercial separation and recovery of bismuth from a copper electrolyte solution are absorption, wash 1, pre-elution, main-elution, post-elution, wash 2, and bismuth precipitation. The description of each of these steps follows. 

##### 3.1 Loading or Absorption Stage 

The process starts from the Electrolyte Tankhouse Circuit (Figure 1), wherein a bleed portion of the electrolyte is pumped continuously into an Electrolyte Buffer Tank, insuring that the electrolyte will be maintained at a constant supply, thus enabling the loading process into the SuperLig<sup>®</sup> 83 Column to continuously operate. A Micron Filter is installed before feeding the electrolyte into the SuperLig<sup>®</sup> Column to prevent slime and other contaminants such as Pb and Sb from building up at the top of the SuperLig<sup>®</sup> 83 Column. The copper electrolyte, containing some of the bismuth, is pumped into the SuperLig<sup>®</sup> 83 Column where the bismuth attaches to the SuperLig<sup>®</sup> 83. The remaining bismuth-free electrolyte is transferred to an Electrolyte Filtered Tank from which it is pumped back to the Electrolyte Tankhouse Circuit. 

The bismuth loading curve in Figure 2 shows removal of the bismuth by the SuperLig<sup>®</sup> 83 from the electrolyte in the SuperLig<sup>®</sup> 83 Column. This loading process stops after the computed loading volume is completed. This loading curve shows that the SuperLig<sup>®</sup> 83 is fully loaded with the bismuth.

##### 3.2 Wash 1 Step 

After loading, the SuperLig<sup>®</sup> 83 Column is washed with 2 M H2SO4 (Figure 3). The purpose of this step is to wash out the copper inside the SuperLig<sup>®</sup> Column and bring it back to the Electrolyte Tankhouse Circuit, thus preventing any loss of copper produ

ct. It is very important to maintain the H2SO4 concentration at 2 M to accomplish the wash. Temperature and flow are also maintained in this step at values that ensure the efficiency of the copper wash. 

##### 3.3 Pre-Elution Step 

In this step, 9 M H2SO4 is heated to 58 ºC and the solution flowrate is properly maintained to control the temperature. The 2 M H2SO4 solution is pushed out of the SuperLig<sup>®</sup> Column (Figure 4) and fed to the Electrolyte Filtered Tank where it is replaced by 9 M H2SO4. 

The pre-elution data in Figure 5 show that the 2 M H2SO4 solution is pushed out by the 9 M H2SO4, which replaces it. This operation is in preparation for the main elution step. At the end of the preelution step, the acid concentration starts to increase and a small amount of bismuth is pushed out of the SuperLig<sup>®</sup> 83 Column.

##### 3.4 Main-Elution Step 

A 9 M H2SO4 solution is pumped into the SuperLig<sup>®</sup> 83 Column, thus detaching the bismuth from the SuperLig<sup>®</sup> 83 resin (Figure 6). The resulting solution is pumped to the Bismuth Product Tank. This is the most critical step in the entire process. The flow rate of the 9 M H2SO4 must be properly controlled and monitored to be able to maintain the required 58 ºC temperature. 

It is very important to continue the elution to the end once it has started. Stopping the elution prematurely can result in bismuth(III) bisulfate precipitation in the SuperLig<sup>®</sup> 83 Column, causing unwanted capacity loss and pressure spikes. 

In the main elution portion of Figure 5, the H2SO4 concentration builds up to 9 M and the bismuth is pumped out of the SuperLig<sup>®</sup> 83 Column. This acid solution goes to the Bismuth Product Tank (Figure 6) for subsequent precipitation. 

##### 3.5 Post-Elution Step 

A 2 M H2SO4 solution is pumped into the SuperLig<sup>®</sup> 83 Column to push the 9 M H2SO4, sequentially, into the Electrolyte Filtered Tank, and into the Electrolyte Tankhouse Circuit (Figure 7). In the post-elution portion of Figure 5, the H2SO4 concentration declines as the 2 M H2SO4 is pumped into the SuperLig<sup>®</sup> 83 Column. Removal of the 9 M H2SO4 is an initial preparation of the SuperLig<sup>®</sup> 83 for the next cycle. 

##### 3.6 Wash 2 Step 

In the final step of the process, the SuperLig<sup>®</sup> 83 is prepared for the next cycle by pushing out the remaining 2 M H2SO4 to a Recycle Acid Tank (Figure 8). This recycled acid is re-used for the Wash 1 step, thus conserving on acid consumption.

#### 4 Bismuth(III) Bisulfate Product 

There does not appear to be any direct end use market for bismuth(III) bisulfate as such. The major commercial bismuth compounds are bismuth(III) oxide and bismuth(III) nitrate for which there are significant markets [12]. The simplest and most common procedure to convert the bismuth(III) bisulfate to bismuth(III) oxide is to leach the bismuth(III) sulfate, and neutralize the resulting solution with sodium carbonate or sodium hydroxide. This proc

edure generates a bismuth(III) oxide which can be readily smelted and reduced to metal, or used as the starting compound in the production of various bismuth products. Bismuth metal can also be produced by using a chloride or fluosilicic acid electrolyte [13]. In this case, bismuth anodes must first be produced by fire refining. Most copper refineries prefer to market the bismuth(III) bisulfate product to a specialized bismuth refiner. It is possible to secure a very high percentage of the then published current world market price for the bismuth metal content in this case. There are various bismuth refining companies prepared to purchase the bismuth(III) bisulfate and convert it to various marketable bismuth products and compounds, or to bismuth metal. 

The international scientific community recognizes that bismuth is one of the safest elements environmentally, and consequently, it has a growing number of applications to alleviate specific toxicity or environmental problems. Due to its unique properties, bismuth has a wide variety of applications. The major trend driving the market demand for bismuth is its use as a non-toxic lead substitute in metal form, and in metal alloys, pigments, and pharmaceuticals [14-17]. For these reasons, IBC projects a stable market outlook for bismuth. The quantities of bismuth generated by the MRT process are not expected to be large enough to have a negative impact on the bismuth price. 

#### 5 Discussion 

The results demonstrate that bismuth removal from copper electrolyte can be done effectively using the MRT process. The process uses readily available sulfuric acid and water reagents. The bismuth loading and elution curves are shown in Figures 2 and 5. In Figure 2, the input bismuth concentration is approximately 600 mg/L. The full loading of the SuperLig<sup>®</sup> is completed with breakthrough occurring at 40 cubic meters of load. In Figure 5, the full elution takes place in only a few bed volumes, which is very important in reducing the reagent costs of the process. Note that the elution is segregated into three distinct portions: pre-elution, main-elution and post-elution. Only the main-elution is directed to the Bismuth Product Tank; the pre- and post-elution portions go to the Electrolyte Tankhouse Circuit to be used during the next elution. Of particular note is the high bismuth concentration achieved during the elution. Peak concentration is near 25 g/L, and this allows for ready precipitation in the Bismuth Product Tank.

### The Rate-Controlling Step of Chalcopyrite Dissolution in Concentrated Cupric Chloride Solution 

Mari Lundstrцm Outotec Oyj Base Metals P.O.

Box 86 02201 Espoo, Finland 

Jari Aromaa, Olof Forsйn Helsinki University of Technology Laboratory of Corrosion and Material Chemistry P.O. Box 6200 02015 TKK, Finland 

**Keywords:** Chalcopyrite, rate-controlling step, chloride leaching, HydroCopper<sup>®</sup> 

#### Abstract 

In hydrometallurgical applications the use of chloride solutions instead of sulfate solutions is becoming more common. HydroCopper<sup>®</sup> , trademarked and registered by Outotec Oyj, is an innovative cupric chloride leaching process, based on the good leaching properties of sulfide minerals in cupric chloride solution. The leaching experiments in this study were carried out under conditions similar to those used in the HydroCopper<sup>®</sup> process, _i.e._ [NaCl] = 250-280 g/l, [Cu<sup>2+</sup> ] = 0-30 g/l and T = 70-90 ºC, pH = 1-3. Electrochemical methods such as anodic and cathodic polarization curves, potentiostatic measurements and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) were used to define the rate-controlling step of chalcopyrite dissolution in cupric chloride solution. The leaching phenomenon was found to be pH dependent in a pH range from 1 to 3. The dissolution of a stationary chalcopyrite was determined to be controlled by diffusion in the reaction product layer at pH = 3, changing to chemical rate control at pH = 1. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Chalcopyrite is the most common copper mineral available in large quantities. Chalcopyrite has been observed to be refractory under hydrometallurgical conditions. Metal recovery in sulfate media is well known by solvent extraction – electrowinning (SX-EW) technology. However, chloridebased processes are of increasing interest. Chalcopyrite has been shown to be less refractory for leaching in chloride solutions. Faster leaching kinetics of sulfide minerals in chloride solutions makes it possible to use atmospheric leaching. High dissolution rates enable the use of smaller solution volumes in subsequent steps. Almost all of the sulfur can be oxidized to the elemental form [1].

This work presents an investigation of chalcopyrite (CuFeS2) dissolution in cupric chloride solutions. Generally, leaching of sulfide minerals is carried out in an oxidizing environment. The anodic oxidation reaction is most likely the oxidation of sulfur in the sulfide mineral. Simultaneously, the cathodic reaction is the reduction of an oxidizing agent. The most commonly used oxidizing agents are oxygen, Fe<sup>3+</sup> , nitric acid, concentrated H2SO4 and Cu<sup>2+</sup> . In cupric chloride solutions, the anodic reaction is the dissolution of chalcopyrite, bornite, covellite, chalcocite or other sulfide minerals. The cathodic reaction can be the reduction of copper(II) ion Cu<sup>2+</sup> , but also the reduction of copper(II) complexes, such as [CuCl]<sup>+</sup> , [CuCl3]<sup>-</sup> and [CuCl4]<sup>2-</sup> . 

The formation of a reaction product layer is char

acteristic for sulfide minerals during leaching. This layer is often suggested to be of elemental sulfur. The elemental sulfur layers can decrease the reactivity of the mineral by hindering the diffusion of oxidants to the reacting mineral surface or metal cations transfer from the sulfide mineral to the solution. In chalcopyrite leaching, the ratecontrolling step can be related to diffusion processes or chemical reactions. The overall reaction rate can be controlled by: 

- (1) Diffusion of a reactant from the bulk solution to the chalcopyrite surface, 

- (2) Diffusion of a reactant or a reaction product through the reaction product layer, 

- (3) Anodic dissolution reaction rate on the chalcopyrite surface or 

- (4) Cathodic reduction reaction on the chalcopyrite or reaction product surface. 

As the reaction product layer grows with time, it can limit the diffusion of oxidants to the chalcopyrite surface or hinder the diffusion of ions away from the surface, both factors limiting the rate of the dissolution reaction. The aim of this work was to determine the rate-controlling step for the dissolution of chalcopyrite in concentrated cupric chloride solution with respect to pH. The hypothesis was that the rate-controlling step is diffusion through the reaction product layer.

A few EIS studies have been carried out on mineral surfaces, but the authors are unaware of any studies on chalcopyrite in cupric chloride solutions at elevated temperatures (90 °C). Those studies gave several interpretations and EIS equivalent circuits for sulfide mineral reaction product layers. Cabral _et al._ [3], Velбsquez _et al._ [4] and Bevilaqua _et al._ [5] suggested a series layer model for both pyrite and chalcopyrite bioleaching and for chalcopyrite in borate solution. Velбsquez _et al._ [6], Shi _et al._ [7] and Nowak _et al._ [8] proposed a parallel layer model for chalcocite in borate solution, marmatite-carbon paste electrodes in ferrous solutions and Cu1.87S in perchloric acid. This latter type of circuit is often used to represent an imperfectly covered electrode [6] and coated surfaces [9]. The equivalent circuit used in the analysis is shown in Figure 2 and it is based on the parallel layer model. The equivalent circuit is based on three possible reactions: the solution can attack the mineral both directly and through the reaction product layer and the solution can attack the reaction product layer directly.

The reported values for the activation energy of diffusion through a liquid phase are from 5-12 kJ/mol [10] to <20 kJ/mol [11]. Chemical and electrochemical reactions are usually more dependent on the temperature and have reported activation 1964 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ _The Rate-Controlling Step of Chalcopyrite Dissolution in Cupric Chloride Solution_ energies greater than 40 kJ/mol [11]. When diffusion takes place through a porous layer, the _Ea_ values are higher than those of diffusion in solution and are in the same range as for chemically controlled reactions. Few activation energies for chalcopyrite leaching in cupric chloride solutions are presented in literature. An activation energy of 134.7 kJ/mol [12] was reported by Wilson and Fisher for chalcopyrite in cupric chloride solution ([Cu2+ ] = 0.79 M, [Cl- ] = 6.23 M, T = 50-97.5 °C). The evaluation of impedance measurements was based on the number of time constants and calculated resistance values. The number of time constants reflects the number of different phases on the sample surface and in some cases also the effect of mass transfer was seen. The values of the different resistances in the equivalent circuit in Figure 2 are inversely related to Faradaic dissolution steps. As the resistive components are connecte

d serial in the equivalent circuit the effect of the components is additive and a total resistance measured at low frequencies sums up all the finite rates of dissolution reaction steps. Figure 6 shows examples of impedance spectra. The spectra show two time constants reflecting two different reaction steps. The low frequency loop describes the reaction product layer but it might also be associated with the diffusion through the layer of reaction products. The high frequency loop reflects the chalcopyrite surface, but might also reflect the behaviour of the reaction product layer. Analysis of impedance spectra was done using the total resistance and charge transfer resistances related to chalcopyrite dissolution and reaction product layer. The total resistance consists of charge transfer resistance of chalcopyrite dissolution, resistance related to the reaction product layer, and in some cases also diffusion. The high frequency loop corresponded to charge transfer resistance of chalcopyrite. At pH = 1 it was 20 Ω at the beginning, increased to 40 Ω in three hours and decreased to 5 Ω after 22 hours. At pH = 2 and pH = 3 chalcopyrite dissolution resistance was approximately 5 Ω during the whole 22 hour test. The low frequency loop corresponded to dissolution through of reaction product layer. At pH = 1 the calculated reaction product layer resistance was 30-40 Ω during the whole test. At pH = 2 the resistance was 30 Ω at the beginning and decreased to 10 Ω during 22 hours. At pH = 3 reaction product layer resistance was 20 Ω at the beginning but increased remarkably with increasing time up to t = 22 h. After 22 hours of leaching the total resistance at pH = 1 was 35 Ω, at pH = 2 it was 10 Ω, but at pH = 3 it was ca 150 Ω [18]. Based on the impedance results we can conclude the pH has a strong effect on the chalcopyrite reaction product layer. At low leaching times the apparent charge transfer resistance is highest at pH = 1 and lowest at pH = 3, however, at longer leaching times this resistance is nearly equal at all pH values. It must be noted that the changes in the apparent charge transfer resistance value can actually reflect the behaviour of the reaction product layer. The behaviour of the reaction product layer changes with time when pH is higher than 1. At pH = 2 the resistance of the reaction product layer decreases with time. At pH = 3 the resistance associated with the reaction product layer was at the first hours similar to that at pH = 2, but increased with time to large values, showing possibly even mass transfer impedance at t = 22 h. These findings suggest that at low pH the rate limiting step can be slow chemical dissolution reaction. At high pH the reaction product layer is more porous and the rate limiting step is likely more diffusion related in that reaction product layer. 1967 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ _Lundstrцm, Aromaa, Forsйn_ 60

Inverse parabolic behaviour at pH = 1.5 suggested that the low dissolution rates at low pH values are related to the slow chemical reaction rate, likely due to formation of a reaction product layer that impedes the dissolution of chalcopyrite. At higher pH values the chalcopyrite leaching behaviour is more parabolic suggesting that the leaching rate is more diffusion controlled, likely by ion diffusion through a thickening reaction product layer [19]. #### 4 Conclusions The rate determining step of chalcopyrite dissolution in cupric chloride solution can be mass transfer in solution, mass transfer through the reaction product layer or electrochemical reaction at the chalcopyrite surface. This study showed that stationary chalcopyrite sample leaching in concentrated cupric chloride solution is strongly dependent on pH. It was shown that cathodic reaction did not limit chalcopyrite dissolution

. Neither did diffusion in the solution limit chalcopyrite dissolution otherwise than possibly at pH = 3 with long leaching times. The possible rate-controlling mechanisms were thus limited to the rate of the anodic leaching reaction or mass transfer through the reaction product layer. 

Activation energies calculated suggested mixed control at pH = 2. Potentiostatic experiments showed that chalcopyrite leaching was inverse parabolic at low pHs, changing into more parabolic at higher pHs. This suggests that the chalcopyrite dissolution was controlled by slow anodic dissolution rate at pH = 1.5, changing into more diffusion controlled process at pH = 3. Also apparent charge transfer resistance, reaction product resistance and total resistance values from EIS measurement supported this conclusion. 

The results show that at pH = 1 chalcopyrite starts to dissolve fast in the beginning, but the reaction product layer or metal deficient layer forming on chalcopyrite impedes dissolution shortly, increasing the resistance for chemical dissolution reaction. With increasing pH the chalcopyrite dissolution is faster during the first leaching hours, however, the formation of other type of reaction product layer decreases the chalcopyrite dissolution rate by hindering the diffusion through the reaction product layer.

### Heap Leaching Solutions Treatment with the ECUPREX Process 

Dr. Massimo Maccagni 

Engitec Technologies S.p.A. Via Borsellino e Falcone, 31 20026 Novate Milanese (MI), Italy 

**Keywords:** Ecuprex, leaching, precipitation, hydrogen sulfide, electrowinning 

#### Abstract 

Copper heap leaching operations are working with lower and lower grade ores and respectively lower copper concentrations in the leaching solutions.  This can create difficulty with the traditional solvent extraction and sulphate electrowinning based processes. 

A new approach can be applied to the treatment of these dilute solutions. 

A significant amount of research has demonstrated the effectiveness of selectively precipitating copper sulphide out of the dilute copper sulphate solutions with hydrogen sulphide. The ECUPREX Process, a hydrometallurgical/electrochemical process based on fluoborate electrowinning, can convert the precipitated copper sulphides to copper cathodes. In the leaching section of this process copper is leached and elemental sulphur is produce

d. This sulphur can be used to produce hydrogen sulphide and recycled in the process as the reactant used to precipitate copper from heap leaching solutions. 

This paper will present this closed loop process in detail together with the pilot plant design criteria. 

#### 1 Introduction 

In recent years, copper hydrometallurgy is becoming more and more important to the overall copper production. 

About 25 % of the World primary output is produced according to this technological approach. Most of this production comes from the heap leaching of oxidised ores or secondary sulphides found along high grade primary sulphides ores in open pit mines. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_

_Maccagni_ 



The leaching medium is usually dilute sulphuric acid and the copper pregnant solution obtained is then treated in a solvent extraction unit to transfer copper to traditional sulphate electrowinning in order to produce pure metallic copper. 

SX-EW is usually described to be a relatively low cost alternative to traditional copper mining and processing. But the process is actually a complement to conventional concentration, smelting and refining rather than a possible replacement. Heap leaching became an interesting development only when a robust and economical solvent extraction technique was developed. 

The oxidised ore body represents a relatively minor share of the available copper resources for an economic extraction. The copper grade in these materials is continually decreasing and now some plants are working with minerals containing less than 0.5 % of copper. 

The result of heap leaching is always a dilute copper solution that has to be treated to recover the leached copper contained in it. Some different acids were taken into consideration but the most suitable and economical is certainly sulphuric acid. 

The recovered solution is usually treated in two main ways: solvent extraction followed by a sulphuric electrowinning or cementation with iron scrap. Cementation is a very simple process, but has a few notable problems: there is no recovery of acid for the heap leaching operations and the solution has to be disposed.  Instead of regenerating acid, there is net acid consumption and a generation of ferrous/ferric sulphate. The use of cementation is becoming less frequent because of economical issues (the cost of iron scrap is increasing and there is no possibility to recover it) and environmental issues (wasting of the ferrous/ferric sulphate solution). 

Engitec studied an alternative solution that takes advantage of its ECUPREX Process, a process which can deal with copper scrap, copper secondary sulphides (chalcocite) and with chemically precipitated sulphides. Through this process it is possible to recover copper from any copper containing solution. 

The process is based on the selective precipitation of copper in the form of sulphide from the acidic solution. The precipitated sulphide is then sent to a fluoborate circuit in which copper s

ulphide is leached taking the copper in solution and, simultaneously, elemental sulphur is produced and recovered as fluoborate leaching residue. The leachate is sent to the electrolysis cell, where copper is plated, while the elemental sulphur is the base reactant to produce the precipitation reactant for the first step of the process. _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 1974 _Heap Leaching solutions treatment with the ECUPREX Process_ #### 2 The Process The process is very simple and it is schematized in Figure 1 flow chart. The possibility to use the elemental sulphur produced during the fluoboric leaching phase is very important for the economics and also for the optimisation of the process because it will avoid having any by product to handle. We have identified two ways: the bio-production and the synthesis. The bio-production process is comparable to the very well known technology for biological sulphate removal. In the anaerobic reactor, sulphate is converted into sulphide. This reduction is performed by the so called sulphate reducing bacteria. In order to make the reduction possible, an electron donor has to be oxidized by the bacteria. The main reaction that occurs in the anaerobic reactor is: 2 S + CH2O + H2O → 2 H2S + CO2 (9) where CH2O represents a hypothetical organic electron donor that is mineralized. When the water contains no organic components, an electron donor has to be added. Examples of organic electron donors are lactate, ethanol, molasses and certain agricultural and food processing wastes. Hydrogen can also be used as electron donor. The choice of an electron donor depends on the sulphur load. For relatively small sulphur loads ethanol is normally used as electron donor. If however, a waste stream is available, the chemical costs can be drastically reduced. For large sulphur loads, hydrogen gas is used, which can be produced (if not available at site) by cracking methanol or by means of a natural gas reformer. In both cases a mixture of H2 and CO2 is produced. The carbon dioxide is used as a carbon source by the bacteria. Some of these packages are used to treat water streams produced in the mining operations and some of them have the goal of recovering copper. We are now investigating another way of producing H2

S through the reaction of elemental sulphur with a hydrogen donor that appears to be promising.

#### 7 Conclusion 

The ECUPREX Technology compared to the traditional SX - EW Technology reveals some technical and environmental advantages resulting in a reduction of the operative cost to convert copper from salt in solution into cathodes. Sulphuric electrowinning is very well known to have the following limitations: 

- high anodic overvoltage (O2 evolution) 

- low cathodic efficiency (90 -93 %) because of the iron content into the electrolyte 

- high bleed, necessary to control the iron build-up 

- high energy consumption (about 2000 kWh/t Cu) 

- anodic O2 evolution will cause the mist problem in the cell room 

- CoSO4 has to be put into the solution to lower the anodic potential preventing in the meantime the lead anode corrosion 

- temperature shocks or shut down and starting up will cause the lead contamination of copper cathode 

- limited lead anode life mainly in case of a high electrolyte acidity 

Through the copper precipitation, with H2S produced in situ, the following typical problems of solvent extraction operations can be avoided: 

- loss of solvent and diluent through the refined solution that can cause a low but constant environmental contamination 

- organics presence in the sulphuric EW loop 

- crud formation because of the presence of suspended solids within the copper solution 

- careful control of the operations feeding into the mixer settler 

- high solvent cost 

- solvent loss increased by evaporation in case of operations run at a high altitude (Andes region)

### CESL Process as Applied to Enargite-Rich Copper Concentrates 

Keith Mayhew, Pardeep Parhar, Henry Salomon-de-Friedberg 

CESL Limited (Teck) 12380 Horseshoe Way Richmond, Canada 

**Keywords:** Enargite, leaching, copper, CESL, scorodite 

#### Abstract 

The CESL Process has been successfully developed for copper, copper/gold, copper/nickel and nickel-bearing concentrates. Recent bench testwork has established that the application of the process can be further extended to include concentrates that contain arsenic, including those with appreciable amounts of the refractory mineral, enargite (Cu3AsS4). 

The present paper reviews the behaviour of arsenic in a number of copper concentrates under standard CESL conditions, and under optimized conditions that led to improved copper extraction from high arsenic, enargite-rich, copper concentrates. Arsenic deportment during the leach is described and characteristics of the precipitated iron-arsenic residue are presented. 

#### 1 Background 

In copper smelting, arsenic is not readily contained and shows up in various smelter slags and dusts, as well as in the downstream copper refinery electrolyte where its concentration may

be up to 20 g/L [1]. In hydrometallurgical processing, leaching of the Cu-As minerals may be challenging and the long term stability of the final residue may be in doubt. Nevertheless, as average arsenic levels continue to rise in copper concentrates as shown in Figure 1 [2], pressure to modify existing processes or introduce new ones will intensify.

A number of pre-treatment approaches have been considered in dealing with arsenic-bearing copper sulphides in concentrate. These have included selective flotation of enargite [3] and tennantite [4] which has proved challenging; sulfidation to convert enargite [5] to a more soluble compound (unsuccessful); and extended grinding [6] which proved equally unsuccessful. Pyrometallurgical roasting to drive off volatile arsenic compounds in oxidizing or neutral atmospheres has also been tested and even practiced [7], but subsequent processing of the As compunds was not fully satisfactory. 

Of the sulphide minerals containing copper, enargite (Cu3AsS4) is abundant and arguably the most challenging to leach [8]. A number of possible routes have been considered. These may be broadly characterized as described in Table 1 (from the review by Filippou et al [8]).

In addition to those listed above are the sulphate/chloride mixed system as represented by the CESL and Platsol processes, Intec’s atmospheric chloro-bromide (Halex) assisted leach, and nitrogen species catalyzed pressure leaching. More recently, the effectiveness of the Galvanox Process in leaching enargite under atmospheric conditions has been described (Riviera-Vasquez and Dixon [9]). 

There is limited information related to the leaching of enargite in copper hydrometallurgical processes. Hurtado-Guzman et al [10] presented modeling information for various copper minerals in the Albion process as applied to Collahuasi concentrates. The estimated copper extraction from enargite was about 60 % after 30 hours of leaching at a P80 grind of 9.2 microns. Nitrogen species catalyzed (NSC) pressure leaching of enargite was described by Anderson and Twidwell [11]. A copper recovery of 95 % after 60 minutes was reported at

a P80 of 10 microns. Two thirds of the sulphur was oxidized to sulphate. The relative roles of nitrates and nitrites in the process were discussed by Baldwin and Van Weert [12]. High temperature pressure oxidation was compared with competing processes by Ferron and Wang [13]. Dreisinger [14] described testing relating to the applicability of high temperature pressure oxidation to El Indio concentrate and ore. The process has been selected for processing Chelopech concentrate [15, 16]. 

The kinetics of enargite leaching in acidic sulphate media under oxidizing conditions was reviewed and studied by Padilla, Rivas, and Ruiz. Their earlier work [17] had shown that enargite leaching was slow at 100 ºC – achieving only 6 % copper extraction in 7 hours. Their later bench study, covering the temperature range of 160 ºC to 220 ºC, indicated that copper leaching from enargite was considerably faster and could exceed 95 % extraction in 2 hours under the most favourable conditions [18].

The leaching of enargite under basic conditions has also received considerable attention. Atmospheric hypochlorite leaching using caustic (pH 12) achieved 99 % enargite conversion within 2 hours at 60 ºC (Mihajlovic et al [19]). Hypochlorite consumption appears to be very high with this process. Sodium sulphide (Na2S) leaching of enargite is reportedly very quick with the help of a pre-grind step. Leaching at 90 ºC, with a considerable excess in reagents, achieved 90 % arsenic dissolution in 15 minutes (Balaz and Achimovicova [20]). Similarly to Na2S leaching, sodium hydrosulphide (NaHS) together with caustic was shown capable of decomposing enargite (Cu3AsS4) to chalcocite (Cu2S). Reaction times at 80 ºC were less than 6 hours and pulp densities were up to 1000 g/L solids (Tongamp et al [21]). Ferric arsenates, and particularly scorodite, appear to be the preferred forms for arsenic disposal. Consequently, acid based processes are currently being favored over the alkaline ones. 

The CESL copper concentrate leaching process has been successfully demonstrated on many chalcopyrite bearing concentrates. This work considered the application of CESL technology to the challenge of enargite leaching. 

#### 2 Experimental Procedure 

All pressure oxidation testing was carried out in a 2 liter Parr titanium autoclave with a magnetic drive agitator assembly. Temperature was controlled by an external heater as well as internal cooling coils. The heater was temperature set point controlled. The cooling coils were fed by pressurized water. Water flow was controlled with a fine needle valve in line with a solenoid that was connected to a second temperature control unit. Both control units received input from a common thermocouple inserted into the thermowell of the autoclave. A rotating shaft with two sixbladed, 5 cm diameter axial impellers provided the required agitation. 

Oxygen was supplied from a

15 kg capacity cylinder situated atop a balance capable of measuring weight differences to the nearest 0.1 g. The gas bleed was manually controlled by a needle valve to maintain the desired oxygen content (85 % dry) in the vapour phase above the slurry. The amount of sulphur _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 1995 _Mayhew, Parhar, Salomon-de-Friedberg_ oxidized affects numerous aspects of the flowsheet, and low sulphur oxidization is usually desirable for an economic process. Sulphur oxidation has a large impact on the autoclave heat balance, the resultant solids density in the vessel, and subsequently the autoclave size and all associated equipment includin

g feed and discharge circuits. In addition to the effect on capital cost, the amount of sulphur oxidation affects the overall autoclave oxygen consumption, as well as the amount of acid that must be neutralized with limestone. Thus the operating cost is also strongly dependent on the degree of sulphur oxidation. #### Abstract 

The Central African Copperbelt has been an important focus point for the international mining industry over the last decade. The Copperbelt, which extends from north-central Zambia into the southern portion of the Katanga province in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), is one of the world’s greatest metallogenic regions containing an estimated 34 % of the world’s cobalt reserves and over 10 % of the world’s copper reserves. The steady improvement in political stability in the region, together with attractive ore grades and improvements in processing technology has brought about a renewed interest in the Copperbelt. 

Various processes have been developed to recover copper and these include both hydrometallurgical and pyrometallurgical processes. The viability of each of these applications depends on numerous factors, such as ore mineralogy and grade, geographical location of the deposit, mining costs, power and water costs, copper recovery, and acid requirements. 

Effective hydrometallurgical extraction methods for copper oxide ore include agitation, vat, dump, heap and in-situ leaching. Agitation leaching is the most prominent process practiced in the Copperbelt due to the favourable copper ore grades. Heap leaching, on the other hand, is a potentially feasible process for treating low grade material, which also includes tailings. 

The last decade has seen a considerable increase in activity in the development of copper heap leaching projects in, especially, South America. While Peru is active in copper heap leaching devel-

The flow sheets are evaluated and the different technical considerations are discussed. A high level capital cost and operating cost comparison is also included to further illustrate the economical differences between the agitated leach process, as practiced in the Copperbelt, and a typical Chilean heap leach process. 

#### 1 Introduction 

A range of different leaching techniques have been employed to treat different oxide ore bodies around the world. Heap leaching has been successfully practiced for treating oxide-copper ores in Chile, while agitation leaching is the prominent process practiced in the African Copperbelt. Processing of these oxide ore bodies usually involve applying an acid solution to the ore, and recovery of metal from the pregnant solution via electrowinning. Prior to electrowinning, solvent extraction (SX) is used in most cases both for purification and concentration of the copper. In rare cases the copper grade of the ore body and subsequent copper tenor achieved in the leaching step is sufficiently high that SX is not required to produce high purity copper by electrowinning. 

Heap leaching could have potential for implementation in the Copperbelt region for the treatment of lower grade copper oxide ore deposits and/or tailings. A small heap leach-SX-EW plant has been successfully piloted at Nkana for Mopani Copper Mines (MCM) [1]. 

Against this background, this paper will provide: 

- An overview of the status of copper operations and projects in the Copperbelt region (DRC and Zambia), 

- A techno-economic comparison of the heap leaching process in Chile compared to the agitated leach process in the African Copperbelt. 

#### 2 Overview of the African Copperbelt 

The Central African Copperbelt is an arcuate zone 600 km long and 50 km wide containing one of the world’s greatest concentrations of copper and cobalt. The Copperbelt extends from north-central Zambia into the southern portion of the Katanga province in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The Copperbelt deposits are remarkable on an international scale, with most having resources of hundreds of millions of tons with ore grades greater than 2 % copper.

The Copperbelt of Africa has a long history of copper hydrometallurgy from the agitation leaching of high grade oxide ores to roast/leach/electrowinning of sulphide copper/cobalt concentrates [2]. Copper mineralization was mined at the turn of the century but was only recovered on large scale from the 1930s [2]. Large towns and mining developments followed and growth continued until the 1970’s when political unrest in the DRC and nationalization in both the DRC and Zambia resulted in a steady downturn in the industry. It is predicted that the Copperbelt region of Zambia and the DRC will become the second-largest copper producing region in the world by 2011. Zambia and the DRC currently account for about 4 % and 2.1 % of world copper production respectively and that is expected to rise to about 5.7 % and 4.9 % respectively by 2013 [3]. Mill discharge is diluted with process water before being pumped to a cyclone. The overflow from the cyclone gravitates to the dewatering thickener feed tank and the underflow from the cyclone gravitates back to the mill feed where it is combined with mill feed and mill inlet dilution water. ###### 3.1.2 Pre-Leach Dewatering Thickener The cyclone overflow is collected in the pre-leach dewatering thickener feed tank. The thickener underflow is pumped to the leach tanks. The thickener overflow is collected in the return water tank, from where it is returned to the milling circuit. _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 2004 _Copper Oxide Agitated Leaching on the African Copperbelt_ ###### 3.1.3 Leaching The dewatering thickener underflow is re-pulped with acid rich copper SX raffinate solution from the raffinate pond to a solids concentration of ~20-30 % before being fed to the leach first leach tank. Leaching is carried out in mechanically agitated tanks. If required, SO2 is occasionally added to the leach tanks as a reductant to ensure dissolution of cobalt. The acidity in the leach is controlled to a pH of typically 1.5-2.2 by addition of concentrated sulphuric acid. Leaching takes place at ambient pressure and temperatures ranging from ambient to up to 60 ºC. ###### 3.1.4 Solid/Liquid Separation The slurry is typically decanted in a counter-current decantation (CCD) circuit, where the overflow from the first CCD thickener is transferred to a clarifier. The two main criteria in a solid liquid separation plant are firstly to ensure suff

icient washing capacity and secondly to reduce the solids content in the PLS to a level that is manageable in the downstream SX circuit. Washing is essential due to the high percentage of occluded solution within the residual gangue. The use of pin bed clarifiers to further reduce the solids content in the PLS is becoming more common. In addition to PLS clarification, settling ponds prior to the SX circuit provide additional surface area and reduce flow rates to allow the fine solids to settle out. 

###### 3.1.5 Copper Solvent Extraction 

Solvent extraction is required to upgrade the copper tenor in solution and/or remove impurities. A typical copper SX plant configuration is two extraction stages, one organic wash stage and two stripping stages. 

In the extraction stages the aqueous phase is contacted counter-currently with an organic phase used in a suitable diluent. The diluent is required as a carrier. This is a kerosene-based chemical and is supplied by many large oil producers [5]. Copper is selectively extracted by the organic phase releasing a proportionate amount of acid to the aqueous phase (raffinate). The bulk of the raffinate is returned to the leaching circuit and the excess raffinate solution forms the cobalt bleed stream to the cobalt recovery plant. 

The loaded organic from the extraction stages is first washed with acidified water and then fed to the stripping stages. Aqueous solution from the wash stage is recycled to the CCD circuit to be used as wash water. 

In the stripping stages the loaded organic is contacted with spent electrolyte produced in the copper electrowinning (EW) circuit. The copper in the organic phase is transferred to the aqueous phase (now called “loaded strip liquor” (LSL)), in exchange for acid and the LSL is collected. The LSL is sent to the electrowinning circuit and forms the feed solution (advance electrolyte) to EW.

###### 3.1.6 Copper Electrowinning 

The electrolytic cells are equipped with anodes (typically Pb-alloy) and stainless steel cathodes. Copper is deposited onto the cathodes. Acid is produced in the cells as a result of the copper deposition reaction. The spent electrolyte solution is drained to the spent electrolyte tank. A portion of the spent electrolyte is sent to the SX stripping circuit and the balance of the spent electrolyte is returned to the electrolyte circulation tank. 

The cathodes are harvested, washed, stripped and returned to the electrowinning cells. The stripped copper sheets are sampled, bundled, weighed and stored for shipment. 

###### 3.1.7 Tailings Neutralisation 

The underflow from the final CCD thickener is pumped to the tailings neutralisation where slaked lime slurry is added to neutralise acid and raise the pH to a value of ~8.0. The heavy metals and impurities in solution precipitate as hydroxides and the neutralised tailings stream is discharged to a tailings storag

e facility. 

###### 3.1.8 Tailings Storage Facility 

The neutralised slurry is pumped to and stored in the tailings storage facility (or tailings dam), where the solids settle permanently in place. Process and rain water is decanted from the settled solids and allowed to flow to the tailings return water pond from where it will be returned to the processing plant via acidification for reuse as wash water in the CCD circuit. 

###### 3.1.9 Site run-off Collection and Water Acidification 

To avoid precipitation of copper in the CCD circuit the pH in this circuit has to be maintained at a level below 3. Contaminated site run-off, tailings return water, cobalt free liquor and any other source of water that is utilized as CCD wash water therefore needs to be acidified. 

##### 3.2 Process Description Heap Leach 

Heap leaching is a mineral processing technology whereby large piles of crushed or run-of-mine ore are leached with various chemical solutions to extract valuable metals. The largest installations in terms of both land area and annual tonnage are associated with copper mines, where copper containing minerals (typically 0.5 %-2 % Cu) are irrigated with a weak sulphuric acid solution. This solution dissolves the copper from the mineral and the ‘‘pregnant leach solution’’ (PLS) passes down through the ore pile and is recovered at the bottom on the ‘‘leach pad’’. For oxide ores, Cu recoveries are typically in the range 75-80 % within 50-100 days [6]. Copper is extracted from the PLS using SX and electrowinning and the acidic solution is recycled back onto the leach pile [7].

The past few decades have seen a considerable increase in activity in the development of copper heap leaching projects in South America. While Perъ is active in copper heap leaching development, the focus of most of the recent activity has been in Chile. This country has been the single largest heap Leach-SX-EW growth location in the world [8]. 

The heap leaching processing route to produce PLS includes several process stages arranged in series: crushing, acid pre-treatment, heap building, and heap irrigation. To optimize copper extraction it is necessary to pay careful attention to the design and operation of each of these stages of the leach process. 

A typical heap leach flow sheet is illustrated in Figure 1B. 

###### 3.2.1 Ore Preparation 

The ore is normally crushed in two or three crushing stages to a nominal size that can vary between 6 mm and 25 mm. To minimize ore haulage cost, the primary crushing is often located near the pit. This is typically done using a single gyratory crusher. The ore that discharges from the primary crusher is fed to the coarse ore conveyor, which discharges it to the coarse ore stockpile. Ore is drawn from this stockpile by multiple draw points equipped with belt feeders, discharging onto the fine-crushing plant feed conveyor. The fi

ne crushing plant uses conventional cone crushers and the screening plants use conventional horizontal vibratory screens. 

Crushed ore may then be agglomerated with concentrated sulphuric acid and water or raffinate solution. Agglomeration, followed by a ‘curing’ period, provides both good percolation and high initial copper tenors in the PLS. 

###### 3.2.2 Ore Handling: Stacking and Reclaiming Systems 

###### Leach Pad Construction 

Two basic methods of pad construction are used for copper heap leaching projects in Chile, these being the re-usable pad and the permanent expanding heap. The re-usable pad or on-off pad method is typically used for oxidized ores with shorter leach times. This involves the construction of a series of durable pads onto which ore is loaded, leached, washed and unloaded for disposal in a spent ore pile. A permanent expanding pad is suitable for mixed and sulphide ores with longer leach cycles. The preparation and placement of ore is done in multiple lifts on a base impervious pad. After leaching, the ore is left in place. 

###### Ore Stacking 

Heap construction methods vary from ore dumping by front-end loaders to conveyor stacking depending on the tonnage rate of the operation. Heap heights vary among 2.5-8 m. Since the agglomerated ore is fragile, free fall discharge between the conveyor and the heap is critical.

#### 4 Technical Considerations 

##### 4.1 Comminution 

The main objective of a crushing facility for a heap leaching facility is to produce a crushed product fine enough to allow ample solution contact with the minerals and to have a rock permeable and stable enough to allow an adequate leaching rate through the heap. For economical crushing plant sizing, coarser top sizes are desired. For good percolation, as coarse a size as possible is desirable. The amount of effort and expense incurred in ore preparation is directly related to the economics of copper recovery. 

In a typical agitation leaching, the required particle size for different types of ore can vary significantly, ranging from 25 micron up to about 1 mm. The objective of an agitation leach ore preparation facility is to produce a product fine enough to allow sufficient area for full wetting of the mineral and allow the particle to remain in suspension. This is typically done using a combination of crushing and milling, specifically primary, secondary and/or tertiary crushing in combination with SAG and/or ball milling. Mills consume large amounts of energy and also need to be designed to consider availability regarding downtime on maintenance. 

##### 4.2 Leach Considerations 

For heap leaching t

o be successful, the stacked ore must be porous enough to allow solution to trickle through it. Ore porosity issues are experienced when ores have high clay content as can be the case with Copperbelt ore. Heap leaching takes place in a solid continuous phase in laminar flow. Heap leaching has much lower recoveries compared to agitation leaching and also lower transfer rates requiring longer processing times. Due to the laminar flow of the solution through the heap, solids entrainment is limited resulting in minimal solution clarification requirements prior to solvent extraction. 

Agitation leaching is carried out in an aqueous continuous phase under a turbulent flow regime. This results in high transfer rates and high recovery. The higher transfer rates obtained under turbulent contact require higher power input to sustain these rates. In addition to increased power requirements, the phase continuity and particle size has an influence on solid transfer to the SX circuit. The finely divided particles are suspended in the aqueous solution which results in increased solids entrainment. Therefore agitation leaching requires additional solution clarification equipment

The difference in dissolution mechanism influences the processing time, recovery and downstream equipment requirements of the plant. 

##### 4.3 Solid-liquid separation 

The solid-liquid separation requirements depend on the type of leaching process. In heap or dump leaching, solids are easily removed by means of natural filtration through the heap. Additionally, traps or solid decantation are typically used before the solution enters a collection pond. The typical arrangement includes two parallel desanding ponds located upstream of the PLS storage pond [8]. 

In the case of an agitation leach circuit, the requirement for a solid liquid separation plant is to ensure sufficient washing capacity and to reduce the solids content in the PLS to a level that will not cause process upsets in the downstream circuit. Washing is essential due to the high percentage of entrained solution within the leach residue. The two methods typically used for solid-liquid separation include multi-stage filtration with counter-current washing, and counter-current decantation and washing. The main factors that influence the selection of methods for solid liquid separation are: the grade of the ore, the filterability and settling characteristics of the leached pulp, the tonnage to be handled, the cost and availability of equipment, local knowledge and preferences. 

##### 4.4 Solvent Extraction Circuit Selection 

There are a range of SX circuit configurations in use in both South America and in the African Copperbelt. The most suitable configuration is

typically judged on a case by case basis. The optimal design is a trade-off between capital and operating costs bearing in mind a number of factors, including the Pregnant Leach Solution (PLS) composition and pH, electrolyte copper and acid concentration, and overall circuit operating philosophy – whether it is maximized for copper recovery or copper transfer and reagent utilization. 

Configurations containing two extraction stages and either one or two stripping stages circuit are the most common configurations used to process ‘high’ PLS copper tenors (4-10 g/l). Series-parallel configurations are also employed at many operations, most notably to process high flow and low copper tenor PLS (1-3 g/l). It is quite common for circuit configuration to be changed from one arrangement to another, to manage changes in copper grade over the life of the operation. 

##### 4.5 Water Balance 

In order to prevent volume and impurity build-up in the copper circuit for Copperbelt based processes, a bleed stream needs to be taken from the acid regenerated stream that exists between the Cu

SX circuit and the leach circuit. The bleed stream typically contains leached cobalt and other impurities and need to be refined to recover the sellable cobalt. 

The bleed stream size is equal to the volume of water added to the copper processing circuit, minus the volume losses in the circuit. Numerous studies have been done to minimize this bleed stream as larger volumes require larger equipment, and lower cobalt concentrations require upgrading steps to ensure adequate purification and cobalt concentrations for the cobalt electrowinning process. 

A few initiatives in aim to decrease the amount of water added to the circuit, hence decreasing the bleed stream volume, include the following: 

- Milling in raffinate, where the milling is done with an acidic medium which is recycled from the copper circuit, thus no water is added to the mill circuit which will make its way into the copper circuit. 

- Filtration after thickening instead of thickening only after milling. This ensures that most of the water added to the mill stays within the milling circuit and prevents excess water flowing into the copper circuit. 

- Changing the CCD circuit to filtration, or a combination of both, which allows for enhanced solids washing efficiency thus requires less wash water to be added to the copper circuit. 

In comparison, heap leach operations do not incorporate milling and solid/liquid separation steps and hence do not typically require a water bleed from the circuit. 

##### 4.6 Tailings Disposal 

In an agitated leach circuit, the tailings from the solid-liquid separation circuit need to be neutralized and disposed of in a safe manner. The requirement for limestone/lime as neutralizing agent and the need for tailing ponds contribute to the operating and capital cost of an agitated leach facili

ty. The maintenance on a heap leach operation is more compared to an agitated leach due to the high maintenance associated with the upfront ROM material handling and the liner and piping maintenance associated with the heap itself. #### 6 Further Considerations ##### 6.1 Location and Climatic Considerations Heap leaching projects in South America are located in a belt that covers the southern region of Peru and the Northern region of Chile. The climate is typically arid with high evaporation rates. Sources of water at these plants are typically limited and have high levels of impurities. Other operations are located in the milder coastal climate but also have problems obtaining make-up water. Some even use sea water for this purpose. The Copperbelt stretches from the northern and eastern parts of Zambia and into the DRC. This area is classified as humid subtropical or tropical wet and dry. There are two main seasons, the rainy season (November to April) corresponding to summer, and the dry season (May/June to October/November), corresponding to winter. The

rainy season is characterized by heavy downpours with high average rainfalls. 

In areas of high rainfall such as the Copperbelt, solution balance problems can arise in heap leaching operations resulting in the need to treat and discharge process water. The stability of the heap and associated percolation efficiencies need to be considered, including the treatment of depleted heaps that will be affected. 

##### 6.2 Ease of operation 

The number of unit operations and the nature thereof, makes an agitation leach circuit more challenging to operate than a heap leach circuit. Since the leaching operation of heap leach requires limited operator control and, due to the absence of a solid-liquid separation circuit and tailings neutralization facility, heap leaching operations require less intensive control and fewer operators; however maintenance costs for a heap leaching operation is considerably higher compared to that of an agitated leach operation, as can also be seen from Table 6 .

##### 6.3 Infrastructure 

Large scale copper mining since the 1930’s in the Copperbelt brought great industrial interest to this part of Africa resulting in the development of infrastructure to service the various industries and especially the mines. The nationalization of the Zambian and Congolese mines in the late 60’s had a large impact on the infrastructure and economy of these areas. However, following the first democratic elections in Zambia in the late 1990’s and Congo in 2001, structural reforms have been put in place to stimulate economic activity and encourage foreign investment. The steady improvement in political stability in the region together with attractive ore grades and improvements in processing technology have brought about a renewed interest in the Copperbelt. 

Over the last few years both developed countries and the developing world have started investing in improving infrastructure in Africa. For example both China and India have committed billions of dollars, particularly in Angola, the DRC and Zambia. In addition the World Bank, the African Development Bank (AfDB), the European Community (EC), Britain and a number of other donors have pledged approximately US$1.2 billion towards the upgrading of the existing north-south corridor system which connects the Copperbelt to the ports of South Africa. The objective of this initiative is to improve Africa’s competitiveness by upgrading transport, trade opportunities and energy supply. 

#### 7 Conclusion 

The low capital and operating costs of heap leach/SX/EW operations together with the relatively simple operation and the direct production of cathode copper close to the mine site make the economics of the process attractive. Technical considerations like ore amenability to the different leaching steps, water balance issues, impurities and economics need to be closely considered in the process s

election process. 

In areas of high rainfall such as the African Copperbelt, solution balance problems are inevitable in heap leaching operations resulting in the need to manage, treat and discharge large volumes of process water. Several pilot scale heap-leaching plants have been operated over the last few years to try to better understand how best to manage this issues. 

Heap leaching is unlikely to displace agitated leaching in the Copperbelt both because of the inherent problems associated with the solution balance and the very high copper grades of the ores.

**Keywords:** Hydrometallurgy, concentrate, chalcopyrite, pressure leaching 

#### Abstract 

Pressure leaching is an attractive alternative to process copper concentrates without atmospheric pollution as produced by pyrometallurgical processing. In the present work, we discuss some experimental data obtained in the pressure leaching of a chalcopyrite concentrate in H2SO4-O2 system. The leaching experiments were carried out in a 2 liter batch pressure reactor using mono-sized chalcopyrite concentrate samples. The main variables studied included stirring speed, temperature, partial pressure of oxygen, sulfuric acid concentration, particle size, and leaching time. The results showed that a stirring speed over 700 rpm was sufficient to obtain adequate suspension of the particles and good oxygen distribution. The variable that affected most the dissolution rate of copper from the concentrate was the temperature. At 160<sup>o</sup> C, the copper dissolution from a mono-size -75+53 µm concentrate sample was relatively slow and about 90 percent of copper was dissolved in 60 minutes, while at 190 º

C, the dissolution was very rapid and complete copper extraction was obtained in about 10 minutes. On the other hand, the partial pressure of oxygen between 517 to 1034 kPa and the sulfuric acid concentration from 5 to 20 g/l affected little the dissolution rate of copper. 

#### 1 Introduction 

In recent years, research on the leaching of copper concentrates has augmented considerably, mainly due to the increasingly stringent restrictions on environmental pollution dictated in most countries which have increased the costs of the pyrometallurgical treatment [1]. Among the alternative methods investigated, the pressure leaching processes in sulfate media was preferred in part due to the commercial success of this technology in the treatment of zinc concentrates [2, 3], refractory gold ores and concentrates [4, 5], and also because most sulfate media processes can be easily integrated with heap leaching operations existing in most mining companies. In this manner, the available solvent extraction and electrowinning capacity, can be used in the process.

Considering the above, a number of different processes have been developed to treat copper concentrates, which can be classified according to the temperature of operation as low, medium and high temperature pressure leaching [6-8]. All three categories of pressure leaching processes have reached some level of industrial application to treat copper concentrates. 

The low temperature pressure leaching processes [9, 10] operate at temperatures lower than the melting point of elemental sulfur (119 °C). Generally, these processes involve a very fine grinding of the concentrates to accelerate the dissolution kinetics of the refractory copper minerals such as chalcopyrite with slow kinetics at low temperatures. In some cases, catalysts such as chloride or bromide ions are used to enhance the mineral dissolution reactions in the leaching system. In those processes, most of the sulfide sulfur is oxidized to elemental sulfur. Therefore, the dissolution reaction of chalcopyrite can be written as: 

CuFeS2(s) + O2(g) + 2H2SO4(a) = CuSO4(a) + FeSO4(a) + 2H2O + 2Sº(s) (1) 

The ferrous sulfate can be oxidized to ferric sulfate according to: 

2FeSO4(a) + H2SO4(a) + 0.5O2(g) = Fe2(SO4)3(a) + H2O (2) 

The ferric ions produced will aid in the dissolution of chalcopyrite. Depending on the conditions, the ferric iron hydrolysis will occur to a certain extent to produce a goethite precipitate or some type of jarosite depending on the cations available in the leaching system. 

The medium temperature pressure leaching processes [11-16] operate in the temperature range of 140 to 180 °C and they require the use of specific reagents to minimize the wetting of the sulfide minerals with liquid sulfur in addition to fine grinding. The use of sulfur dispersion agents is to prevent the slowing down of the leaching kinetics by the formation of a liquid sulfur

layer over the sulfide particles. In these processes, the sulfide sulfur oxidizes to elemental sulfur partially and to sulfate. Therefore, in addition to Reaction (1) the following leaching reaction should be considered: 

CuFeS2(s) + 4O2(g) = CuSO4(a) + FeSO4(a) (3) 

The proportion of elemental sulfur and sulfate produced in the leach can change widely depending on the mineral composition of the concentrate and the operating conditions, specially the acidity and the temperature. The oxidation of ferrous sulphate, Reaction (2) will be faster under this higher temperature condition and the iron will precipitate as hematite although some jarosite has been observe to form at high acidity [1]. Finally, the high temperature pressure leaching processes operate at temperatures over 200 ºC, usually around 220 ºC, and they are also called total pressure oxidation processes [8, 17] because under these leaching conditions most of the sulfide sulfur oxidizes to sulfate, i.e. Reaction (3) is the dominant leaching reaction. The main characteristic of these processes is a very high leaching kinetics of the sulfide minerals present in the concentrates. The ferric iron generated in the system will precipitate mainly as hematite, with the formation of some basis iron sulfate at high acidity [1, 6].
