### The Behavior of Magnetite on Mo Recovery from Copper Slags via Acidic Leaching 

Mario Sбnchez Josй Palacios Universidad de Concepciуn Universidad de Atacama Departamento de Ingenierнa Metalъrgica Departamento de Ingenierнa Metalъrgica Casilla 53-C CRIDESAT Concepciуn, Chile Copiapу, Chile 

**Keywords:** Slags, copper recovery, molybdenum recovery, roasting, leaching 

#### Abstract 

Recovery valuable species from copper slag have been studied via pyrometallurgical and hydrometallurgical processes, and the main objective has been to recover copper. However, the slags contain iron, copper and molybdenum, among others elements, and oxides, and the molybdenum has become the most attractive element considering its commercial value and the amount contained in the slag, which is approximately 25 % of the molybdenum contained in the ore feed to molybdenite concentration plant. The recovery of molybdenum has shown as being very influenced by the phases present in the slag and its association, and the content of magnetite present in the slag. Therefore, a characterization of the slag containing molybdenum and the behavior of magnetite on the recovery of molybdenum via acidic leaching are presented in this work. 

#### 1 Introduction 

The pyrometallurgical process for cleaning copper slag is the common practice to recover the copper contained in the slag, producing a final slag with approximately 1 % of copper which is eventually deposited in slag dumps. Chile produces approximately 4 million tons per year, which is equivalent to 2.2 ton of slag per ton of copper produced. This slag is quite stable from an environmental point of view. However, its treatment becomes attractive due to: a) elements or compounds with a commercial value contained in the slag; b) low availability of areas nearby the smelters for dumping the slag and c) high cost of the slag transportation from the smelter to the slag dump. 

The slag utilization and metals extraction from copper slag have been reported [1], and it was shown the possibility of being used as cement, filling and abrasive material, and the extraction of metals by using hydrometallurgical or Pyro-hydrometallurgical processes at laboratory scale.

However, the actual use of the slag is very restricted, and the metals extraction have been limited to copper recovery by a reduction process in melted phase, or by flotation to recover the

copper sulfide and partially the metallic copper contained in the slag. 

Molybdenum is present in most of the Chilean copper slags. In the copper concentrates, it is present as molybdenite, and during the smelting step, it pass on to the slag. The molybdenum distribution between slag, matte and metallic copper was studied at 1300 °C under copper smelting conditions [2], and it was reported that molybdenum content in the slag increases with the increasing of copper content in the matte. Also, it was identified as a sulfide of copper and molybdenum in the matte (Cu1.9Mo2.0S2.8), and as a separate phase of iron and molybdenum oxides, containing 0.5 to 1.0 % Mo, in the slag. The stoichiometry of these oxides varies from 58.3 % Fe - 15.5 % Mo to 21.0 % Fe - 56.3 % Mo. 

In the 1960s, Kennecott developed a process to recover molybdenum from copper slag at pilot scale [3], in which a matte of copper and molybdenum sulfides is produced by adding pyrite and coal to the melt at 1350 °C, and the produced matte is oxidized and leached to recover almost 85 % of molybdenum. The complexity of this process was to form the matte containing Cu-Mo-Fe-S, which required a mechanical stirring for higher molybdenum recovery. Also, copper and molybdenum recovery from copper slags was studied by using a combined process of oxy-sulfating roasting of slag mixed with copper concentrate at 680 °C in a fluidized bed reactor followed by a sulfuric leaching of the obtained calcine at 40 ºC [4]. The recovery of copper and molybdenum was 90 % and 70 % respectively. 

Treatment for adding value to copper slags for obtaining products with commercial value, considering all the species contained in the slag, have been reported by the authors [5, 6]. Also, the extraction of molybdenum after reduction of the slag by using coke at 1200 °C was reported [7], and it was shown that although the molybdenum extraction was not higher than 20 %, the extraction increases as the magnetite content in the slag decreases for rapidly cooled slag where the magnetite content was reduced from 18 % to 1-2 %. Thus, the present work shows the results of the feasibility study, at laboratory scale, the effect of magnetite on the molybdenum recovering from copper slags by using hydrometallurgical processes after an oxidizing roasting for obtaining hematite and soluble molybdenum oxide. Therefore, the behavior of magnetite on the mechanisms of molybdenum entrapment in the slag and its further release via acidic leaching is described in this paper. 

#### 2 Theoretical Considerations 

The slag is homogenous in the molten state, and it retains a homogeneous state when is rapidly cooled, and when the slag is slowly cooled, a ferrous silicate and oxides phases are precipitated. Molybdenum in the slag is associated to iron, and in the presence of oxygen the Fe-Mo-O system shows several oxides [8], such as the non-stoichiometric MoFeO with an oxygen content which never exceeds 33 at. % and MoFe2O4, an inverse spin

el which gives a solid solution with magnetite

Thus, under oxidative conditions the molybdenum contained in the iron spinel is liberated in the soluble form of molybdenum trioxide and hematite, which is insoluble in an acid medium, according to the following schematic reaction: 

· FeOx MoO2 + yO2 = Fe2O3 + MoO3 



The iron silicate and iron oxide are also oxidized according to:

Therefore, the magnetite content in the slag represent an indicator of the amount of molybdenum possible to be dissolved in an acidic solution.

The molybdenum recovery also increases compared with the extraction obtained in the direct leaching of unroasted slag under the same conditions of temperature and acidity due to its oxidation to the soluble form according to Reaction (1). 

Thus, molybdenum should be oxidized to Mo<sup>6+</sup> to be dissolved in weak acid solutions, and Fe<sup>+3</sup> and Mo<sup>6+</sup> can be obtained by oxidation. Also, other compounds in which molybdenum is hexavalent; MoFeO5 and Fe2(MoO4)3 have been reported by Morgenstern et al. [16]. Therefore, it can be concluded that molybdenum is present in the reduced state Mo<sup>+4</sup> in the presence of magnetite. ### The Marcobre Vat Leach System: A New Look at an Old Process 

Ph.D., P. Eng. W. Joseph Schlitt B. Eng Adam Johnston Hydrometal, Inc. Transmin Metallurgical Consultants P.O. Box 309 Calle La Perricholi 110 Knightsen, CA 94548, USA San Isidro 27, Lima, Peru 

**Keywords:** Hydrometallurgy, copper, vat leaching, bottle roll tests, column tests, pilot tests 

#### Abstract 

Marcobre S.A.C. is in advanced development of the Mina Justa copper property in Peru, having recently issued a definitive feasibility study for the project. Based on a progression of metallurgical tests, vat leaching followed by solvent extraction-electrowinning is proposed as the processing route for the oxide ore. This option gives better recovery at lower acid consumption than conventional heap leaching. 

#### 1 Introduction 

In the early 20<sup>th</sup> century, vat leaching was a popular route for treating fast-leaching oxide and carbonate ores. The process provided high metallurgical recoveries and was capable of producing very high-grade leach solutions suitable for feeding to direct electrowinning operations. Today, other types of leach operations are more widely used. Only Mantos Blancos, Chile continues to operate a large-scale vat leach system. This provides part of the feed to their solvent extractionelectrowinning (SX-EW) operation. 

This may be about to change. Marcobre S.A.C. (Marcobre) has been working to develop its Mina Justa copper project at Marcona, Peru. The main deposit consists of a high-grade sulfide zone that responds well to conventional flotation. The sulfide is overlain with a considerable tonnage of oxide material with variable characteristics. Initial testing gave high leach recoveries. However, it was clear that acid consumption would be very high. 

This led to some preliminary work on high intensity leaching. The success of these tests suggested that a vat leach approach might be more suitable for the ore than heap leaching. This resulted in a vat development program that started with batch tests and concluded with testing in an integrated pilot plant. This paper discusses the testwork program and the resulting design for t

he vat system.

The vat approach offers several advantages over heap leaching for Marcobre and it may be applicable to other projects as well. 

#### 2 Historical Perspective 

Copper vat leaching technology was developed in the early part of the 20<sup>th</sup> century and is still in use today. It proved to be effective for treating fast leaching non-sulfide ores, particularly the carbonate, oxide, silicate and exotic ores that were being discovered in Chile and elsewhere. A key advantage was the ability to operate the vats counter currently so that high pregnant leach solution (PLS) grades were achieved. Then after some purification steps, the PLS was advanced as feed to a direct electrowinning operation. This recovered the copper in cathode form and was the route used in virtually all vat operations prior to use of SX-EW. 

The best known vat leach operation was Chuquicamata located in Chile’s Atacama Desert. This was built in 1916 and operated continuously until November 2006. Certainly this 90-year run is something of a record for a hydrometallurgical plant. The plant has been well documented in the literature. Rose [1] described the initial operation and Eichrodt [2] explained the complex solution management practices. Campbell [3] described the plant after modifications in the 1930’s and McArthur and Leaphart [4] provided an updated description just prior to the advent of SX-EW. Figure 1 shows these vats after shutdown.

At Chuquicamata there were 12 vats in line, each holding about 10 kt of ore crushed to minus 10 mesh (-2 mm). Up until the 1950’s, the ore graded nearly 2 % Cu and contained large amounts of brochantite [Cu4(SO4)(OH)6] and antlerite [Cu3(SO4)(OH)4]. These natural sulfates were watersoluble, requiring no external acid for leaching. However, the resulting copper sulfate still generated acid during electrolysis, making the process nearly self-sufficient in acid. Copper recovery from such ore ranged from 88 to 94 %, with tank house feed maintained at 25 g/L. In later years, as the sulfide content increased, vat recovery dropped to an average of 80 %. 

More details on this and other vat leach operations have been summarized by Schlitt [5]. With appropriate ore, vat leaching is characterized by a high level of recovery and a short leach cycle time when compared to conventional heap or dump leaching. Thus, the in-process inventory of copper is much lower than it is for a heap or dump leach. Nevertheless, only one large scale vat leach plant is still in operation. This is at Mantos Blancos in Chile. As described by Mendoza [6] the Mantos Blancos vat system closely parallels the old Chuquicamata design, except that recovery utilizes modern SX-EW technology. The vats at M

antos Blancos are integrated into a larger leach system that includes sulfide heap leaching, an agitated tailings leach and mine waste dump leaching. 

#### 3 Overview of the Marcobre Project 

Mina Justa is one of several copper projects being developed in Peru. Marcobre has been conducting metallurgical studies on the project since 2005. The work has progressed to the point where plant design and engineering, capital and operating cost estimates, and a financial evaluation of the project have be undertaken. A definitive feasibility study (DFS) on the oxide portion of the project was completed in mid-2009 and a corresponding NI 43-101 report has been filed with the Canadian securities commission. 

The Marcona copper property is owned by Marcobre, a private closed corporation with limited liability. Marcobre was incorporated under the laws of Peru in 2004. Chariot Resources Limited of Toronto, Canada indirectly owns 70 % of Marcobre, while Korea Resources Corporation and LSNikko Copper Inc. indirectly own 30 %. 

The Marcona copper property is located approximately 400 kilometers southeast of Lima in the province of Nazca, department of Ica, in the southern Peruvian coastal belt. The center of the Marcona copper property lies approximately 25 kilometers north of the coastal town of San Juan de Marcona. Figure 2 is a map showing the project location and concessions.

The Marcona copper property consists of iron oxide-copper (silver-gold) deposits and prospects that are part of a very large iron oxide-rich hydrothermal system associated with the Marcona iron ore deposits located a few kilometers to the southwest. Based on the parameters generated during the comminution testwork program, modeling of potential crushing circuits was undertaken. #### 4 Initial Testwork 

##### 4.1 Bottle Roll Leach Tests 

The initial bottle roll tests on the concession were done by Rio Tinto’s Peruvian exploration subsidiary and predate Marcobre’s acquisition of the property. Rio Tinto ran two sets of tests but the locations of the samples are now unknown. In the first set the head grades ranged from 0.2 % to more than 5.0 % Cu (average of 2.80 % CuT). Recovery was also variable, ranging from 11.2 to 96.5 %, (average of 72.5 %). Gangue acid consumption (GAC) ranged from minus 5 kg/t (acid generation) to 48.9 kg/t (average of 32.6 kg/t). 

In the second set of tests, the head grades ranged from 0.28 to 2.00 % CuT (average of 0.69 % CuT). The acid soluble content varied from 0.25 to 1.83 % (CuSS), with an average of 0.66 %. Extractions ranged from 56 to 93 % of CuT, with an average of 81 %. Total acid consumption (TAC) varied from 6 to 138 kg/t, with an average of 64 kg/t. The average GAC was 55 kg/t. Both sets of tests showed that the oxide ore was readily leachable, but was generally characterized as a high acid consumer. Results in the second set were similar to the results obtained by Marcobre in their bottle roll program.

#### 5 Vat Leach Tests 

Based on the information shown in Figures 6 and 7 and the improved results at higher flows and lower acid levels, a high intensity vat leach appeared to hold some potential. When numerous individual batch vat tests gave promising results, a two-phase vat leach pilot program was developed. The objectives of the pilot plant program were as follows: 

1. Provide the data needed to support the DFS for the leach portion of the project. 

2. Determine the leach kinetics for different materials and the recoveries that could be expected with a 6-day vat leach cycle. 

3. Determine the sulfuric acid consumption rate as a function of rock properties and various process parameters. 

4. Provide samples for SX compatibility tests and environmental assessments. 

##### 5.1 Phase 1 Tests 

Five general composites from the Mina Justa deposit were used in the majority of the pilot tests. These represented both types of ore, material from different depths and areas, and high- and lowgrade material. Other composites were also tested, including one from the Magnetite Manto deposit. Grades ranged from 0.36 to 1.30 % CuT. Characterization of these composites included density determinations, complete chemical analyses (both wet and ICP) and XRD analyses. 

The pilot plant consisted of 15 vats each 100 mm in diameter with a working height of 7 m. The vats were fabricated from PVC pipe. They were connected in series and were operated in a countercurrent mode with up-flowing leach solution. In normal operation six vats were under active leach, one was being loaded, one was draining, three were in maintenance and four were on stand-by ready for loading. To avoid recoveries above 100 %, the recovery of total copper is capped at 95 %. The minimum GAC is set at 15 kg/t for design purposes. Gangue acid consumption is used, as this defines the amount of acid that must be supplied externally. As indicated, the relationship between grade and recovery is positive, but the relationship between head grade and GAC is negative. The reason for the negative relationship between GAC and the head grade is that higher grade material produces more copper and generates a larger acid credit, reducing net acid consumption. It is important to note that total acid consumption is independent of head grade. This confirms that total acid consumption is an inherent rock property that depends on the makeup of the gangue, not the copper grade. 

An effort was made to correlate five resource parameters with recovery and acid consumption. The five were mineralogy, lithology, depth in the deposit, the zone within the deposit and the mining year. The latter is obviously an imposed constraint and not an inherent property of the deposit. Of these, only depth had much impact on recovery, with recovery declining as depth increases. 

#### 6 Conclusions 

1. An extensive metallurgical program has demonstrated that for the Marcobre oxide ore, vat leaching is a better option than heap leaching. Recoveries are comparable, but the vat leach has faster kinetics and a lower GAC value for a given recovery

. 

2. The recovery of copper is primarily dependent on the ratio of acid soluble to total copper. However, there is also a lesser dependency on head grade. Over the life of the mine, leach recovery is projected to average 74.5 % of CuT or 92.0 % of CuSS. 

3. Total acid consumption is independent of the copper head grade, depending primarily on the nature of the gangue. However, gangue acid consumption is inversely related to head grade due to its effect on recovery and the resulting acid credit. Life-of-mine, GAC is projected to average 42 kg/t of ore. 

4. Using the pilot plant data, recovery and GAC can be defined as follows: Recovery of CuT [%] = [86.5 + 9.3(CuSS)](CuSS/CuT) GAC, kg/t = 50.07e<sup>-0.47[%CuSS]</sup> . 

5. Other optimum vat leach criteria are as follows: a) Crush size - P100 of 8 mm, b) Cure acid dosage - 15 kg/t, c) Acid level in irrigating solution - 11 g/L, d) Irrigation rate – 700 L/m<sup>2</sup> -h, e) Vat height - 7 m, f) Active leach cycle - 6 d, g) PLS tenor - 9 g/L Cu.

### Getting More Out of Your Copper SX Plant 

Matthew Soderstrom, Troy Bednarski, Hector Yaсez, Alexis Soto, Eduardo Kamenetzky, Violina Cocalia Cytec Industries Inc.

#### Abstract 

A significant economic consideration for concentrate producers is by-product credits. What if this concept could be applied to a copper solvent extraction (SX) operation as well? Due to large solution inventories, a number of copper SX operations contain significant minor metal values within the leach liquor. These metals values tend to build up in the leach solution over time until an equilibrium is reached. It may be possible to recover these metals economically since they exist in the solution ‘for free’ (no additional mining or leaching costs) [1]. Cytec has an active development project for the recovery of certain of these trace metals via SX or alternative routes – without negatively affecting the primary copper recovery process. This paper will review a solvent extraction and crystallization route for the recovery of molybdenum from copper SX liquors (patent pending). 

#### 1 Background 

The recovery of Mo is practiced in the catalyst industry through solvent extraction from an acidic sulfate leach solution [2, 3]. Solvent extraction has also been studied for the recovery of Mo from acid leach solution of molybdenite (MoS2) concentrate [4-6]. The process presented here based on solvent extraction with a formulated phosphinic acid extractant is a flowsheet that concentrates the Mo from a Cu SX raffinate solution and resolves a number of practical physical, chemical and kinetic operating issues. With appropriate modifications the process is also applicable to the recovery of Mo from other industrial processes. 

#### 2 Solvent Extraction and Process Development 

A modified phosphinic acid reagent formulation was developed for the molybdenum extraction process. A common problem for recovering molybdenum from these streams in the past has been finding a formulation which would have the right selectivity and kinetic properties to allow the low Mo concentration to be efficiently extracted without altering the standard Cu SX-EW process. Due

to the unique properties of the formulation it is possible to selectively remove molybdenum while leaving the majority of the impurity elements behind in the leach liquor. Ideally the recovery process would take place downstream of the standard copper SX plant, removing the molybdenum from the acidified copper raffinate stream. 

Figure 1 shows the loading characteristics of the phosphinic acid formulatio

n for Fe, Al, and Vanadium. Due to the extremely strong complex formed between the formulation and molybdenum, molybdenum loading is nearly stoichiometric even at a pH of 0.1. As shown, the Fe, Al, and would also be extracted from solutions at typical Cu raffinate pH values (pH 1.2-1.6), however their loading is significantly reduced at higher acidities or lower pH values. Therefore, molybdenum may be separated from these other common impurities by increasing the raffinate acidity prior to the Mo recovery stage. 



Figure 1: Impurity Loading as a Function of pH 

The majority of other elements which would typically be present in the leach liquor (Cu, Zn, Mg, Si, etc…) are only extracted at much higher pH’s than normally encountered in copper SX processing (pH >3). 

Once the molybdenum has been extracted from the aqueous leach solution the next step was to develop a process for the recovery of the molybdenum from the organic phase. Although known that Mo could be removed from organics by utilizing a basic media for stripping, previous processes failed in part due to third-phase formation / physical separation difficulties. 

In order to avoid or minimize third-phase formation, the new formulation contains a phase modifier which enhances the phase separation characteristics. In addition the stripping solution and stripping conditions are closely controlled to maximize Mo stripping while minimizing the formation of the basic salt of the phosphinic acid.

##### 2.1 Molybdenum Extraction 

Molybdenum extraction is believed to proceed according to the equation below: 

MoO22+ +2(H2R2)org- MoO2(HR2)2 org + 2H+ (1) 

The reaction is largely non-reversible due to the strength of the molybdenum ligand complex. The kinetics of extraction are surprisingly fast. In a dynamic rig run (3 minute mixer retention time) greater than 90 % recovery of molybdenum was achieved from a real raffinate solution initially containing <10 ppm Mo. 

Figure 2 shows a Mo extract isotherm along with a McCabe Thiele diagram. The isotherm was generated using a copper raffinate solution containing 40 ppm Mo and an initial acidity of 20 g/l H2SO4. The organic was made up to a 10 vol. % solution of the extractant formulation in diluent. 



Figure 2: Molybdenum Extraction Isotherm 

As shown, the extractant formulation could theoretically load up to 5 g/l Mo from the 40 ppm feed. Due to the low feed pH, the loading of impurities into the organic phase was minimal. 

Since Mo is typically present in these leach liquors at very low concentrations (5-100 ppm), it is advantageous to extract the Mo while utilizing a very low flow O/A ratio. Organic recycle may be utilized to maintain proper mixing characteristics. By concentrating Mo in the organic within the extract circuit, the downstream equipment required for organic processing is minimized. 

As shown by the McCabe Thiele diagram, using an extract O/A

ratio of 0.025 and a single extraction stage, the Mo recovery would be expected to be ~80 % while concentrating the Mo in the organic phase from 40 ppm to ~1200 ppm (30 times concentration). In order to maintain the organic loading in extract constant, the organic flowrate for the downstream scrubbing and stripping operations would be ~30 times lower than the initial raffinate flowrate into the extraction section.

##### 2.2 Impurity Scrubbing 

Acidification of the raffinate stream prior to molybdenum extraction, can greatly reduce the coextraction of impurities, depending on the final molybdenum product purity required a scrub stage may also be necessary. Acidified water may be used to remove any co-extracted impurities and the process may be optimized to achieve the desired metal separation. 

##### 2.3 Molybdenum Stripping 

Due to the very strong Mo extractant complex, Mo can only be partially back extracted with acid. Molybdenum stripping is best achieved using a base. Molybdenum stripping with ammonium hydroxide is believed to involve a speciation change reaction according to Equation 2. Equation 3 then shows the possible stripping reaction. 

Speciation Change: 



Stripping Reaction: 

MoO2(HR2)2 org + 2NH4OH ↔ (NH4)2MoO4 + 2H2R2 org (3) 

Under these conditions, the formation of the ammonium salt of the phosphinic acid formulation is minimized. However the choice of the base and the ratio of base to ligand / metal must be carefully controlled to prevent third phase formation. Under proper conditions, the Mo may be successfully stripped from the organic minimizing the circulating load of Mo and maximizing extraction. 

In the pilotings completed to date, the Mo was stripped from the organic phase using a strip solution containing ammonia and ammonium carbonate. Presence of ammonium carbonate greatly enhanced the physical separation between the phases and minimized the transfer of base back with the organic into extract. 

In order to produce a concentrated strip liquor it is advantageous to run a high flow O/A ratio within strip. Aqueous recycle may be used to achieve the necessary mixing conditions. Concentrated base should be utilized to achieve the optimum stripping conditions while minimizing dilution effects. 

##### 2.4 Crystallization 

Molybdate crystals in different forms may be produced from the concentrated strip liquor utilizing multiple methods such as distillation, cooling, selective solubility, etc. In the trials run to date, the molybdenum was recovered from the strip liquor by adjusting the pH of the concentrated solution using sulfuric acid. This was done on a batch basis but could also be achieved continuously by taking a small bleed stream from the aqueous strip liquor. Ammonium molybdate can also be produced in situ through adjustment of the strip liquor pH.

#### 4 Conclusions 

Mo was successfully extracted from copper raffinate liquor, concentrated and purified via an SX route. The molybdenum was extracted from a feed containing ~70 ppm, was concentrated within the organic phase to ~2 g/l, and was then stripped producing a strip liquor containing ~45-50 g/l Mo (> 600Ч concentration). ### Arsenic Inertization from Copper Pyrometallurgy through Phases of the Alunite Supergroup 

J. Viсals, A. Sunyer, E. Torres, V. Beltran, N. Llorca 

University of Barcelona Department of Materials Science and Metallurgical Engineering Martн i Franquйs 1, 08028 Barcelona, Spain 

**Keywords:** Arsenic, copper, waste, inertization, stabilization, alunite 

#### Abstract 

Arsenical wastes including flash smelting dusts as well as calcium arsenates produced from gas cleaning steps of the copper pyrometallurgy were investigated. The inertization process consists basically of three steps: 1) Arsenic leaching, 2) Ozone treatment to convert arsenic species into As<sup>V</sup> , and 3) Hydrothermal precipitation in Na<sup>+</sup> -Al<sup>3+</sup> -SO42--AsO43- media at ~200 °C, using aluminium and sodium sulfates as reactants. Under optimal conditions, the precipitates consist mainly of a complex arsenical natroalunite with - in some conditions - trace to minor amounts of mansfieldite or scorodite, depending on the solution composition and temperature. The precipitation rate is fast (≤ 15 min) and the major effect on phase composition and arsenic solubility of the precipitates was the initial Al/As molar ratio in the liquid. Minimum arsenic solubility was obtained with precipitates containing arsenical natroalunite, free or with only traces of mansfieldite or scorodite. This was achieved for Al/As ≥ 3 in the liquid media, the arsenic solubility being 0.01-0.02 mg/L at pH ~7, depending on the phase composition. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Arsenic is one of the most common toxic impurities in raw materials and final wastes of base and precious metal industries. In copper pyrometallurgy, arsenic is mainly concentrated in wastes of gas cleaning steps as well as in electrolyte and anode slime of the electrorefining process [1]. Numerous methods for arsenic inertization were investigated such as the precipitation of calcium arsenates, ferrihydrite and scorodite [2]. Scorodite generation has been extensively studied [3-5], even at industrial scale [6], due to its relatively good stability. Scorodite precipitation can be verified hydrothermally and also at ~95 °C with precise control of supersaturation and seeding. Nevertheless, As-solubility in scorodite (typically 0.05-1 mg/L) [7, 8] may exceed the maximum permitted for inert wastes. For this reason, the research on other As-bearing phases could be interesting.

Phases of the alunite supergroup are common in the Earth`s surface [9], where most of them were produced by weathering of polymetallic sulfide deposits and further natural precipitation [10]. These natural phases exhibit great stability in supergenic conditions, decomposing only in strong acid [11] or alkaline media [12]. They consist of structures AB2(TO4)(OH)6, in which A can be monovalent (Na, K, Ag, H3O etc.) or divalent (Pb, Sr, Ba, Ca), B is usually trivalent (Al, Fe, rare earth) and TO4 is principally SO4, AsO4 or PO4. These phases have also a great possibility of stoichiometric changes, such as the simultaneous substitution of an alkaline plus SO4 by a divalent plus AsO4 or PO4, or two alkaline by a divalent plus a vacancy, etc. For this reasons, phases of the alunite supergroup may be proposed as a host for stabilizing a variety of toxic heavy metals [13, 14]. 

Possibilities for arsenic inertization through alunite-type phases are, of course, evident. For instance, the co-inertization of As & Pb through beudantite (PbFe3(SO4)(AsO4)(OH)6) precipitation [13]. Another possibility could be the incorporation of the AsO4 group in a diluted solid solution – with low thermodynamic activity – in simple alunites. Natroalunite (NaAl3(SO4)2(OH)6) was selected for the present laboratory-scale study. 



Figure 1: Schematic diagram of the inertization process. 

Figure 1 shows a schema of the process. Waste is treated with H2SO4 in suitable conditions for As leaching. The resulting solution (or slurry) is ozonized to transform all arsenic species into As<sup>V</sup> . Ozonation was preferred because it did not introduce new pollutants in the circuit. Hydrothermal precipitation is verified at ~200 °C using aluminium and sodium sulfates as reagents. After the treatment, the liquid can be recycled in a plant to recover the possible valuable elements (Cu, Ni, etc.) and finally, to the cleaning steps of the final effluent. Since hydrothermal precipitation in a single step does not eliminate all As from the liquid, an optional step of pH adjustment (to ~3.5) can be verified to recycle the remnant As & Al to the hydrothermal step. 

Two kinds of wastes were tested in this study: A) “Calcium arsenate” obtained by lime precipitation of a final plant effluent from the electrolytic section of a pyrometallurgical plant and B) Flash

#### 2 Experimental methods 

Original wastes, intermediate products and all hydrothermal precipitates were studied by chemical analysis (ICP), X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (S

EM). Quantitative microanalysis of different phases was obtained by energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) at 20 kV, 0.6 nA, 30 s, through a JEOL JSM-840 instrument provided with an INCA-250 analyzer. 

Leaching experiments on original wastes or intermediate products were conducted in a conventional thermostatic reactor coupled with magnetic stirring. The addition of leaching agent (H2SO4), ORP and pH were monitored. The degree of solubilization for selected elements was measured by sampling at different times and solution analysis (ICP). Particular conditions are described jointly with the experimental results. After leaching, the resulting solution or slurry was ozonized in the same reactor injecting an O2/O3 mixture through a fritted glass diffuser. Ozone was produced in a TRIOGEN generator at 0.75 L/min with an ozone mass flow of 3.36x10<sup>-2</sup> g/min. 

Hydrothermal experiments were performed in a PARR 4563 autoclave reactor, provided with temperature, pressure and stirring controllers. After the leaching and ozonation steps, the solution (or slurry) was placed into the reactor with the reagents (Al & Na sulfates). The system was heated to working temperature at a rate of 5 °C/min. Then the system was also cooled to room temperature at a rate of 5 °C/min. The hydrothermal product was filtered, washed and characterized as described. The conditions of each group of tests are reported with the corresponding results. 

The solubility of hydrothermal products at different pH’s was studied by stirring 0.50 g of solid into 50 mL solution at 25 °C during 24 h. These solutions were prepared by convenient dilution of H2SO4 or NaOH stock solutions. Eventual pH changes during these leaching tests were corrected by addition of small volumes of dilute H2SO4 or NaOH. Three consecutive leaching tests were performed for each pH. After each leaching the slurry was filtered and the solution was analyzed for As by ICP-MS.

#### 7 Conclusions 

Hydrothermal precipitation of As(V) in acid Na<sup>+</sup> -Al<sup>3+</sup> -SO42- media at ~200 °C, using aluminium and sodium sulfates as reactants, may be an alternative for arsenic inertization from wastes of copper pyrometallurgy. Under optimal conditions, the precipitates consist mainly of a complex arsenical natroalunite. The precipitation rate is fast (≤ 15 min) and the major effect on phase composition and arsenic solubility of the precipitates was the Al/As molar ratio in the initial liquid. Minimum arsenic solubility was obtained with precipitates containing arsenical natroalunite free or with only traces of mansfieldite or scorodite. This was achieved for Al/As ≥ 3 in the liquid media, the arsenic solubilities being 0.01-0.02 mg/l at pH ~7, depending on the phase composition.

### Solvent Extraction of Metals and Cyanide from Waste Cyanide Solution by LIX 7950 

Feng Xie, David Dreisinger 

University of British Columbia Department of Materials Engineering 309-6350 Stores Road, Vancouver, BC, V6T 1Z4, Canada 

**Keywords:** Solvent extraction, metal, cyanide, LIX 7950 

#### Abstract 

Solvent extraction of metals and cyanide from waste cyanide solution with the guanidine extractant LIX 7950 has been investigated. Gold and copper can be effectively extracted from alkaline cyanide solutions by the extractant. High cyanide levels tend to depress extraction of copper, but exhibit insignificant effect on extraction of gold. The extraction of the mixture solution of metal cyanide complexes with the extractant has been studied and an extraction sequence of Au > Ag > Zn > Ni > Cu > Fe was observed. The free cyanide remains in the aqueous phase due to the preferential extraction of metal cyanide species over CN<sup>–</sup> . The important findings suggest a possible solution to the separation of metal cyanides and free cyanide in cyanide effluents by which metal cyanides can be concentrated into a small volume of solution and the barren cyanide solution recycled to the cyanidation process. 

#### 1 Introduction 

The cyanidation process is still the dominant technique for gold ore treatment. The use of highly toxic cyanide in the gold mining industry has attracted great public concern especially after several cyanide spill disasters happened over the last couple years [1]. Environmental constraints controlling the discharge of cyanide from gold plants are being tightened by the local governments worldwide. The concentration of free cyanide and the WAD (weak-acid-dissociable) cyanide species discharged into the tailing should be controlled below a strict limit, at many sites 50 mg/L to tails and 0.1 mg/L or less in any discharge to a receiving waterway [2]. The treatment of effluents with high levels of cyanide and metals (especially valuable metals such as copper) using the INCO SO2/Air, hydrogen peroxide or Caro’s acid oxidation techniques could severely decrease the profitability of the process [3-5]. Acidification, Volatilization, and Reneutralization (AVR) and some

modified processes thereof have been developed and practiced in some gold operations,

however the high consumption and cost of reagents has significantly limited their application [2, 6]. The indirect recovery of metals and cyanide with pre-concentration by activated carbon has been proposed. The low adsorption capability of activated carbons has severely hampered their wide application in practice [2, 7]. Strong base and guanidine-based resins were also used to recover metals and cyanide from cyanide solutions [8-10]. In the Augment process, CuCN-precipitated resin is used as the adsorbent for the adsorption of soluble copper cyanide from the leachate of coppercontaining ore. The loaded copper cyanide species are eluted from the resin using a concentrated copper cyanide solution having a molar ratio of cyanide to copper (CN/Cu) of approximately four. The resin can be regenerated via conversion to the CuCN form with sulfuric acid and the eluate is submitted to electrowinning to produce copper cathodes [11]. One potential disadvantage of the processes is that the precipitated CuCN may block the resin pores, decreasing the opportunity for additional metal cyanide complexes to be adsorbed into the resin [8, 11]. Solvent extraction technology offers an alternative method for metal and cyanide recovery from waste cyanide solution. Some solvents have been suggested for recovery of metal and cyanide from waste cyanide solution. The use of LIX 7820 (a solvent mixture of Aliquat 336 and nonylphenol) to recover copper from cyanide solution has been proposed [12, 13]. The recovery of copper and cyanide by guanidine extractants (LIX 79 and LIX 7950) has also been investigated [14, 15]. The guanidine extractant is capable of being prontonated to form an ion-pair with the metal cyanide complexes at pH below 11 and is converted to the neutral guanidine functionality resulting in metal stripping [15]. These investigations proved that copper can be effectively extracted from alkaline cyanide solutions by the proposed extraction systems and the cyanide levels and the presence of other anions may potentially affect the extraction of copper and cyanide. In this work, continuous laboratory tests on the use of the reagents LIX 7950 and for metal and cyanide recovery from waste cyanide solution have been conducted which focus on the extraction and stripping behaviors of gold, silver and copper cyanides under different cyanide to copper molar ratios. The potential application of the two extraction systems for recovery of copper and cyanide from waste cyanide solution is discussed. 

#### 2 Experimental 

The extractant LIX 7950 was used as supplied by the manufacturer. N-dodecane was used as diluent and 1-dodecanol as modifier. Synthetic gold and copper cyanide solutions were made up from NaCN and AuCN and Cu(CNC)2, respectively. The mixture of metal cyanide solution was prepared · · from the corresponding me

tal cyanides (Zn(CN)2, Ni(CN)2 4H2O, K4Fe(CN)6 3H2O, respectively). All the chemicals were reagent grade. The extraction and stripping tests were carried out in a sealed beaker and mixing was provided by a mechanical agitator with glass impellers. Equilibrium pH was adjusted by direct addition of concentrated H2SO4 solution (50 % v/v) or NaOH solution (2 mol/L). All the extraction and stripping tests were conducted at indoor temperature. When equilibrium was reached, phase separation _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 2088 _Solvent Extraction of Metals and Cyanide from Waste Cyanide Solution by LIX 7950_ was conducted in a separatory funnel. Samples of the aqueous solution were filtered to remove any entrained organic before analysis. The organic samples for stripping were filtered with 1 PS Phase Separation paper. The copper content in the aqueous sample was analyzed by atomic absorption spectrophotometry (AAS) and copper in the organic phase was calculated by mass balance. Total cyanide content in the aqueous solution was determined by a standard distillation method and the cyanide content in the organic phase was calculated by mass balance. It was confirmed that good agreement between analytical and calculated results was obtained (> 95 %). #### 3 Results and Discussion ##### 3.1 Effect of contact time The influence of contact time on copper extraction by LIX 7950 was first examined and the results are shown in Figure 1. The influence of the contacting time on the extraction of other metal cyanide solutions (Au, Ag, Zn, Ni, Fe cyanide solutions) with the extractant also exhibited similar behaviors. The results are in accordance with those reports that the extraction kinetics of gold from cyanide solution with guanidine extractants and modified amines were usually fast [15]. In general, those complexes with lower CN- coordination numbers were extracted preferentially over those with higher numbers and the lower charged metal cyanide complexes are extracted preferentially over higher 2- 3- charged complexes. The speciation calculation show that low a high cyanide to copper molar ratio favors the 3- formation of the complexes with high coordination numbers (Cu(CN)4 ) [19]. Hence a low CN/Cu ratio favors the extraction of copper cyanide species. That cyanide concentration exhibited negligible effect on gold extraction is probably because gold coordination in cyanide solution is relative simple and only complex Au(CN)2- ions occur. #### 4 Conclusions 

The recovery of metals and cyanide from cyanide solution by the guanidine extractant LIX 7950 has been investigated. The low pH favors the extraction of gold and copper by the extractant. High cyanide levels tend to depress copper loading, but exhibit insignificant effect on gold extraction. A selectivity order of Au > Ag > Zn > Ni > Cu > Fe with the extractant has been observed. The free cyanide remains in the aqueous phase due to the preferential extraction of metal cyanide species over CN<sup>-</sup> . The effective stripping of loaded copper and cyanide can be accomplished by using moderate strong sodium hydroxide solutions (0.5-1 mol/L). The presence of small amount of NaCN in the stripping solution favors the stripping of the loaded copper and cyanide. The important findings suggest a possible solution to the separation of metal cyanides and free cyanide in cyanide effluents by which metal cyanides can be concentrated into a small volume of solution and the barren cyanide solution recycled to the cyanidation process.
